<![CDATA[Irish Times Feeds]]>https://www.irishtimes.comSun, 25 Oct 2026 18:08:08 +0000en1hourly1<![CDATA[Trump is about to discover the political cost of inflation]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/economy/2026/10/23/trump-is-about-to-discover-the-political-cost-of-inflation/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/economy/2026/10/23/trump-is-about-to-discover-the-political-cost-of-inflation/Fri, 23 Oct 2026 05:00:01 +0000The great slayer of political careers – inflation – has come for Donald Trump.

The irony is that it won’t be the racist rhetoric, his role in the Capitol riots, or the self-sabotaging tariffs that remove the Teflon, but something entirely more mundane: gas prices.

They have averaged over $4 a gallon for a record 169 days, a timeline that runs concurrent with the Iran war. The average cost of gas in California, the most expensive state, has been over $6 since late September.

Car ownership is a necessity in many parts of the US, with motorists spending on average two-thirds more on fuel than their European counterparts. That’s why fuel costs are such a flashpoint.

The country’s 196,000 gas stations and their price billboards serve as a daily reminder of Trump’s failed war aims, a political burden he now carries into the midterm elections. Polls suggest he will lose big.

US and Israel draw up plans for renewed strikes on Iran after midterm elections

The latest Reuters/Ipsos survey indicates Trump’s approval rating has fallen to a record low of 31 per cent. It was 44 per cent at the same point in his first term.

More worrying for Trump’s avowedly pro-business administration is that more than two-thirds (68 per cent) of voters disapprove of his handling of the economy, including 37 per cent of republicans.

Asked which party they would vote ⁠for if the elections were held today, some ​47 per cent of registered voters chose Democrats, while 35 per cent chose republicans.

The 12-point advantage in favour of Democrats ​is the widest in the current election cycle and could, if translated into actual votes, see the Democrats seize control of both houses, the House of Representatives and the Senate.

What are the US midterms? A visual guide

This would hobble Trump’s presidency as Democrats would be in a position to block cabinet and judicial appointments while having subpoena powers to investigate the administration.

The top Democrat on the House oversight committee, Robert Garcia of California, says he will prioritise the examination of Trump’s family businesses, the Epstein files, immigration enforcement, corporate profiteering, and how US health secretary Robert Kennedy jnr has handled vaccines.

US inflation accelerated to 3.7 per cent (in annual terms) in September, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics. This was faster than the annual growth in wages (3 per cent), meaning real wages are falling.

Trump’s big mistake has been to dismiss this marker or at least be insensitive to it, repeatedly telling voters that the economy is great and that they’ve never had it so good.

“We have the hottest country anywhere in the world,” he repeatedly says at rallies.

To be fair, the US economy is faring better than many had predicted in the wake of his sweeping “Liberation Day” tariffs in 2025. Unemployment has been at or below 4.5 per cent for 60 consecutive months, a postwar record. Consumer spending remains solid while business investment is being fuelled by the AI boom.

But Trump is falling into the same trap as his predecessor, Joe Biden, in talking up the macroeconomy when consumers and households are being screwed by the micro one: prices.

Jame Carville’s’s famous maxim, “It’s the economy, stupid”, might need to be refined to “It’s the price economy, stupid”, to highlight what matters most to voters in the 2020s.

The Irish Government has learned not to make political capital out of its turbocharged GDP numbers or its windfall taxes, as it only antagonises households in the grip of a price squeeze.

But Trump can’t help himself.

US inflation peaked at 9 per cent in June 2022 as the reopening of the economy after the pandemic led to a burst in price growth. A year later it had fallen to 3.1 per cent and by Trump’s election win in November 2024, it was down to 2.6 per cent. It had been expected to fall to the Federal Reserve’s target rate of 2 per cent by the end of 2025, paving the way for growth-affirming interest rate cuts.

But Trump destroyed that trajectory by imposing tariffs on imported goods. Inflation stopped falling and started to rise again, hitting 3 per cent in September 2025.

Even with the tariffs, US inflation would probably have slowed again this year if the US leader hadn’t gone to war with Iran, triggering a spike in global oil prices.

This has not just driven up petrol prices but also the cost of diesel, the fuel needed to transport everything.

The full ramifications of Trump’s war can be seen through the prism of producer prices, which surged by 6.3 per cent in September. This will translate into further consumer price inflation in the coming months.

High inflation is also resulting in upward pressure on interest rates, further anchoring household spending and Trump’s poll ratings.

Trump’s political shtick has always been to proclaim everything he touches gold. It won’t wash this time.

]]>Jacquelyn Martin<![CDATA[What limits apply to the new personal investment accounts? ]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/10/25/what-limits-apply-to-the-new-personal-investment-accounts/https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/10/25/what-limits-apply-to-the-new-personal-investment-accounts/Sun, 25 Oct 2026 10:00:00 +0000The Finance Bill published last week puts further detail on and provides legislative underpinning for the new personal investment accounts. So we are taking the chance this week to run through in a quick-fire style a series of recent readers’ questions on various aspects of the personal investment account scheme as providers start working on the shape of products that they will offer under the scheme.

As a non-resident Irish citizen but with a PPSN, can I invest in the proposed investment scheme?

BP

No, you cannot open an account unless you are over 18, resident in the State and hold a PPS number. The fact that you are an Irish citizen is irrelevant. And if someone opens an account and subsequently moves outside the State, they can no longer contribute to the account during any period when they are non-resident.

Money you would put in the investment scheme would be money you had likely already paid tax on (maybe at 52 per cent or 55 per cent if you are self employed). Why should this money be taxed again? It makes more sense to tax gain, not original contributions. It isn’t like you are getting a tax credit or deduction with your contributions. This investment scheme doesn’t make sense to me. You could actually lose money and yet still pay the 1 per cent tax.

AM

Taxing money you have already paid tax on is nothing new in Ireland or other jurisdictions – think VAT, excise on petrol and even customs duty on online shopping outside the EU. Or deposit interest retention tax (Dirt), capital gains tax and exit tax on savings and investments.

You are certainly correct that you could be taxed at 1 per cent on part of your fund even if it makes a loss in a given year, as long as its balance exceeds €50,000. That is the outcome of the Government decision to follow the Swedish model for such investments rather than the UK individual savings account model. I can only assume that was done (a) for simplicity and (b) to allow the Government set the tax rate at as low an advertised figure as possible.

Can I invest overseas in the new scheme?

RW

You can as long as it is through an investment account provider registered with Revenue for the purposes of providing these accounts. A register will be available as the scheme gets up and running. What investments they offer and in which markets remains to be seen.

My wife and I will have approx €60k to deposit in the investment scheme next July. Are we limited to a total of €12,000 deposited annually or could we both take out a separate plan to let us deposit €24,000 during the year?

BN

You are each limited to contributions of up to €12,000 in any tax year. You cannot hold a joint account but you can each hold an account, allowing you to invest €24,000 between you.

First-time buyers account for almost two-thirds of Irish mortgage transactions

Can I transfer my existing vanguard ETF to this investment account (new one) without any tax if it’s less than €12k threshold? Or should I sell this and transfer?

AP

This has cropped up a few times. The purpose of the new personal investment account is to encourage new investment by people of savings largely held in deposit accounts.

There is nothing to stop you moving money from an existing investment – such as your Vanguard ETF – to one of these new accounts as long as you stay within the contribution limits but each will be treated on a stand-alone basis so you will have to settle any tax due on the Vanguard investment before lodging the money to one of the new accounts.

In sum, no, you will not be able to avoid existing tax liabilities on an investment simply by transferring it to one of the personal investment accounts.

Am I reading the rules wrong, or could investors do the following: build up gains under the €50k limit and when nearing it, withdrawing some funds (free of CGT). Rinse and repeat, like making bread from a sourdough starter?

BL

As long as the balance of the account stays below €50,000, no tax is due. The account provider will be obliged to keep tabs on the account balance each day over the course of the year and if the balance exceeds it on any day, the account starts being liable for tax.

But as long as the particular investment is liquid enough, there is nothing to stop you withdrawing funds from the accounts on occasion as you approach the limit to avoid tax, although you obviously are limiting your potential investment gains.

Tech sell-off deepens, dents rate hike bets

Will dividend income within the personal investment account be tax free (up to €50k value), can you move existing investments to the new account without triggering a taxable event and finally will you be able to fully choose your own investments or will a fund manager do it for you?

OC

Dividend income on investments within the new personal investment account will be tax free subject, as you say, to the €50,000 tax free balance. Transfers from other investments will trigger any tax provisions attaching to those investments as stated above. You will be able to choose from the investment options offered by one or other fund provider. We don’t yet know how much flexibility that will offer though we do know that you will not be able to get interest in any uninvested cash held in your account.

Is there any age limit to the investment scheme? Myself and my wife plan to set up an account in each of my two kids’ names (ages 16 and 12). We want to fund this by the two of us giving them €3,000 each (€6,000 per child) as this is the limit of the small gift exemption. Is there anything preventing us from doing this and what, if any, tax liabilities apply?

GOC

There is an age limit and neither of your children will be eligible for at least a couple of years. No one under the age of 18 can hold one of these new accounts. You, as an adult, cannot open one in the name of your child and you cannot hold more than one account. However, you and your wife can each open an account in each individual’s name.

]]><![CDATA[Musk won his battle with Swedish union but it is still business as usual]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/technology/big-tech/2026/10/25/musk-won-his-battle-with-swedish-union-but-it-is-still-business-as-usual/https://www.irishtimes.com/technology/big-tech/2026/10/25/musk-won-his-battle-with-swedish-union-but-it-is-still-business-as-usual/Sun, 25 Oct 2026 08:00:00 +0000One of my bugbears about journalists – myself included – is that we tend to pile into stories when they first develop, explain why they matter, then forget about them and move on to the next new thing. But there is value in paying attention to how stories end.

Take, for example, the battle that broke out three years ago between Elon Musk and Sweden’s trade union movement. In 2023, a group of Tesla mechanics in Sweden went on strike over their employer’s refusal to sign a collective agreement with their union, IF Metall.

Other unions joined in. They halted postal deliveries, waste collection and the unloading of cars at ports.

The stakes were high. Musk did not want to set a precedent that he would recognise unions anywhere. And Sweden’s trade unions did not want to allow Tesla to undermine the country’s labour market model, in which government regulation takes a back seat and employers and unions negotiate the rules between themselves.

Journalists flocked to cover it. Musk called it “insane”. But how did it end?

Musk won. This summer, IF Metall announced that it was calling off the strike after more than 1,000 days because Tesla had bought out all the striking members.

“Without workers on strike, there is no strike,” said Veli-Pekka Säikkälä, the collective bargaining secretary at LO, the Swedish trade union confederation, in a statement at the time.

What does it mean that Musk was victorious? For the global labour movement – and indeed anyone with ambitions to curb the power of the tech titans of our age – it is hardly encouraging that even one of the strongest trade union movements in the world could not force Tesla to the table.

After all, the Swedish unions have high membership levels, deep pockets and a supportive institutional set-up, all things that elude unions in many other countries.

In the US, for example, trade unions thought they had secured a historic victory in 2022 when workers in an Amazon warehouse in Staten Island voted to form a union. But more than four years later, Amazon has still not even negotiated a contract.

But while the “Swedish model” could not break Musk, it does not seem as if Musk has broken the Swedish model either. Although trade union officials did worry that Tesla could be the thin end of the wedge, those I spoke to on a recent visit to Stockholm took some solace from the fact that they have continued to sign collective agreements with other companies, including with tech firms that will help to shape the future of the economy.

After a year of negotiations, for example, including a strike threat, video games company King (maker of Candy Crush) signed a collective agreement with Swedish unions last month.

“The Tesla strike is important because it’s an emblematic company in the green transition – at least it was,” German Bender of the think tank Arena Idé, who wrote a book on the conflict, tells me. “But the strike ended, the union lost, and the Swedish model hasn’t crumbled.”

What if the strike had gone the other way and Musk had been the one to lose? Entering into the Swedish way of doing things could have given him an insight into a very different type of trade unionism from the American style he knows and dislikes.

Although they have become known in recent years for their fight with Tesla, in fact, Sweden has the most pro-technology trade unionists I have come across.

Susan Schurman, professor of labour studies and employment relations at Rutgers University, says that Nordic unions in general understand that it is vital for employers to remain competitive in export-led economies.

“They don’t focus on restraining technology; they focus on: ‘How do we incorporate this in a way that will help our companies remain competitive and make sure our members get their fair share of the profits?’” she tells me. “American unions have not historically thought this way.”

Indeed, the Nordic region’s powerful unions have hardly held companies back on implementing the latest tech. Sweden has been called the Silicon Valley of Europe because of its high number of start-ups.

Meanwhile, the percentage of businesses that have adopted artificial intelligence is higher in Denmark, Finland and Sweden than any other country in the OECD’s database – and well in excess of the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development average.

]]>Colin Keegan<![CDATA[Irish business leaders on the move: 10 key leadership changes in 2025 and 2026]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/09/24/irish-business-leaders-on-the-move-10-key-leadership-changes-in-2025-and-2026/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/09/24/irish-business-leaders-on-the-move-10-key-leadership-changes-in-2025-and-2026/Thu, 24 Sep 2026 09:00:00 +0000Corporate Ireland has felt its fair share of movement at board level over the past year, from the appointment of a managing director tasked with the overhaul of national operations to the disputed ousting of a chairman.

Marian Finnegan

After nearly 30 years of working for the country’s largest real estate agency, Marian Finnegan’s service to Sherry Fitzgerald led to her taking up the group’s chief executive role in September last year.

She is the first woman at the helm of the company, which employs 360 people in over 100 offices. Within six months of Finnegan’s promotion to the top job, the firm specialising in residential properties acquired its rival Knight Frank, which focuses on commercial properties.

In an interview with The Irish Times, Finnegan said she saw a “tiny” job advertisement on the back page of this newspaper for an economist position at the firm in 1996. After 29 years, while managing director of the residential arm of the company, Finnegan said “it felt like the natural next step” to head the business.

The top position had been left vacant since February 2025 following the exit of Steven McKenna, who has since founded his own advisory firm.

Kenny Jacobs

In February of this year, the High Court heard Kenny Jacobs would “voluntarily step down” as chief executive of the DAA, which operates Dublin and Cork airports, after an out-of-court settlement closed the lawsuit brought against the semi-State body.

Suspended from his position just before Christmas following a months-long rift with DAA colleagues, Jacobs had previously agreed an exit package with its board, however Minister for Transport Darragh O’Brien refused to sign off on it.

Following an ugly court case – what is seen as the fieriest feud to engulf the airport operator in decades – Jacobs ultimately left with a parting sum in the region of €480,000.

In July, the Cork-born businessman was appointed chairman and president of Manna, the drone delivery service that paused operations in Ireland the previous month and is now focusing on the US and UK markets.

Garry Moroney

Marking a departure from the managing director title bestowed on previous commercial leaders of The Irish Times Group, tech-exec-turned-media-mogul Garry Moroney was appointed its first chief executive in November 2025.

He took over in January 2026 from the interim chief executive Michael Sheehan, who reverted to his previous position of chief financial officer. Previously chief executive of travel management platform Roomex, Moroney had founded two companies before this and worked at McKinsey at the start of his career.

Alongside this newspaper, the group owns the Irish Examiner and Echo, a range of regional newspapers and websites MyHome.ie and RIP.ie. In early August, it announced its intention to wind down breakingnews.ie.

Deirdre Veldon, the former deputy editor of The Irish Times, stepped down as the group’s managing director in September 2025 having served in the position since late 2022.

Andrew Yaxley

UK-based Tesco Group reshuffled its Irish operations in August, with former Tesco Ireland chief executive Andrew Yaxley returning to lead the all-island business here after eight years in Britain.

He effectively traded roles with Geoff Byrne, who will take over as chief executive of the wholesaler Booker Group in September. Both men will continue to sit on the group’s executive committee.

Yaxley, who has worked for the supermarket giant for over 25 years in Ireland, Britain and Czech Republic, had been head of the Irish arm of the retailer from 2015 to 2018.

Not long after his appointment, the UK-based parent company announced its intention to save £1 billion (€866 million) over the next three years through supply chain reform and job cuts.

It is understood some 150 jobs are at risk within the group’s 1,200 person-strong workforce in Ireland. Louise Ryan left the managing director role in June, after one year in the post.

Caroline Bocquel

Moving from the top job at Ireland’s Seafood Development Agency (Bord Iascaigh Mhara) to the top job at the State’s national tourism development authority, Caroline Bocquel was appointed chief executive of Fáilte Ireland in November last year.

The first woman to lead the State agency, she previously chaired the audit and risk committee in the Environmental Protection Agency and, before that, served as chief financial officer of the global charity Goal.

Fáilte Ireland’s previous chief executive, Paul Kelly, left the tourism authority in March after eight years in the post. He now serves as chief executive of the Royal Dublin Society (RDS).

Albert Manifold

In an unexpected move that attracted international headlines, Templeogue-born Albert Manifold was ousted as chairman of British oil and gas giant BP with immediate effect in late May.

The company said “serious concerns” were raised with relation to “important governance standards, oversight and conduct”. Manifold said he was removed “without warning and without explanation” and rejected “lies” spread about his personal and professional conduct.

Shares in BP dropped 4 per cent on the London Stock Exchange the day Manifold was removed, as many investors questioned the stability of the company. The same day, Ian Tyler was appointed as BP’s interim chair.

Eoin Tonge

Primark returned to its Irish leadership roots with the appointment of Eoin Tonge as its chief executive in March this year, 17 years after its founder Arthur Ryan left the position.

Between the two, from 2009 to 2025, the role was held by British-born Paul Marchant, who resigned in March last year following an investigation into alleged inappropriate behaviour towards a female colleague.

Tonge had acted as interim chief executive from the conclusion of the investigation but was announced as a permanent successor a year later.

The retailer’s parent company, Associated British Foods, is moving forward with plans to demerge the fashion giant from grocery businesses under its portfolio by late 2027.

With the exit of David McRedmond after a decade as the head of An Post in August, the chief executive title is to pass next to Fergal Leamy, the former head of Coillte, the State-owned forestry company and Glen Dimplex, a privately-owned manufacturing and heating group.

She now oversees the long-awaited Dublin MetroLink and a Dart-like service in Cork city. Upon her appointment, Shaw said she was “excited to begin work to continue the journey of improving transport for the people of Ireland”.

The nearby Aviva Stadium looms large on one side, Liberty Hall can be seen on another and there are wonderful views in the distance of the Dublin mountains and the bay.

The rooftop has a few levels, with a small amphitheatre for outdoor gatherings, some neatly clipped lawns and a forest of colourful shrubs and trees.

It’s a statement investment by EY. So much so that O’Keeffe won’t disclose how many millions were spent on fit-out costs, only that it was delivered “on budget and on time”.

Two of the floors are an acre each in size, and the new HQ can accommodate 3,500 “colleagues and about 600 external guests” at any one time, O’Keeffe says.

On the ground floor, it has three meeting rooms that are available for use by the near 670 alumni of its successful and high profile EY Entrepreneur of the Year programme.

Totalling just under 18,000sq m (190,000 sq ft) of plush office space, it is about 50 per cent bigger than its previous, dated properties in the capital.

EY is very much in growth mode. When O’Keeffe took over as managing partner in 2018, the Big Four accounting firm had annual revenues of about €250 million on the island of Ireland. In the year to the end of June 2025, its fee income was €850 million.

O’Keeffe won’t be drawn on the figure for the year to the end of June 2026 but it’s expected to nudge €900 million.

“Business is good,” he says. “We are well on our way to reaching our strategic objective of becoming a billion euro turnover business over the next number of years.

“We changed our strategy last year because we were watching the world change, from a geopolitical perspective, from a technology and AI perspective and from a national versus global perspective.

“So we changed our strategy around IQ and EQ, all around behaviours. We have digitalised all of our business.

“We have pivoted around how we go to market. We make sure we have an industry lens and a sector lens in everything we do, not just a service lens.”

He describes how EY goes to “market together” with its alliance partners, namechecking Microsoft, SAP, Service Now and Snowflake.

“We became the Microsoft partner of the year for their full ecosystem. We did the exact same with SAP. We also decided that we would export a lot of our capability in Ireland into other [EY] member firms where they needed our support and our help.”

He cites the Nordic countries and the US as examples of where some of its key staff are deployed to work on projects for big clients of sister firms.

He says the Irish firm has spent a “significant amount of money” on training and upskilling its staff so it can deliver for clients.

This all feeds into a plan to achieve turnover of €1.3 billion by 2031, whichwould represent growth of about €400 million over the period.

More than half of Irish business leaders worried over ‘sophisticated cyber attacks’ by AI

O’Keeffe estimates that EY is the largest Big Four firm in the market, some 40 per cent bigger than KPMG, in second place.

EY employs 5,600 staff on the island (it has 157 equity partners), with 4,400 in the Republic and 3,500 allocated to Dublin. About 2,000 of its staff were not born in Ireland and some 100 nationalities are represented at the firm.

Which brings us to the impact of artificial intelligence on EY’s business, specifically the potential impact on its graduate programme and overall headcount.

“An awful lot of this has yet to be determined and figured out,” says O’Keeffe, while adding that the firm has the largest AI and data analytics practice of any professional services firm on the island, with a team of 350 people.

Within EY, he says it has “embedded AI tooling in our own methodologies in how we actually perform our work on behalf of clients”.

“In our insurance business, we’ve got very specific tools. You could even go into journal entry testing or predictive analytics and sample sizing right through to diligence and corporate finance and also into tax. They are all our own tools.”

When search engines came out, people said there will be no need for professional services. [AI] is no different and there will be winners and losers ... things will change but we will continue to grow

Frank O’Keeffe

It is also using Microsoft Copilot and Anthropic’s Claude on a day-to-day basis. “We have nearly one and a half thousand technology consultants that you could tag to being AI ... but everybody else is using AI tools and processes and licenses to make sure that we do the most effective roles to support our clients. And we believe we’re ahead of the our competition.”

Amid tales of hallucination, does he trust the accuracy of AI tools?

“We have very rigorous quality control measures when it comes to anything that we produce for the external marketplace. Everything gets reviewed by a human ... we work together as teams to ensure we’re using the technology in the right way and that we’ve got the right processes and controls and oversight in place to ensure we can stand over everything we deliver into the market.”

PwC published ‘thought leadership’ reports marred by AI hallucinations

He acknowledges that mistakes can and probably will happen, adding that the firm needs to remain “vigilant” in terms of the quality of information it uses and disseminates.

He says EY took on 400 new graduates in September across the island, a “very similar number” to a year ago. “And we’re currently assessing the business need for 2027.”

He’s not convinced that AI will replace graduates in huge numbers. “We’ve always invested in the next generation of talent an we’ll continue to do that as a significant employer of graduates.”

He says today’s graduates have a head start in terms of their abilities on digitalisation, AI and technology, meaning they could rise up the ranks more quickly than would have been the case in the past.

Will the graduate number always be around the 400 mark?

“Nobody can give you that answer. It has yet to be determined. The market is shifting, the way of work is shifting and we have to determine what that will look like over the next number of years.”

Graduate recruitment slowdown by firms like KPMG in UK sends shiver down spine of south Co Dublin

Looking out five years, will EY still have 5,600 staff? “At least, he says. “But I also think the ways of working will change and what our people will be doing will be different. If you remember, when the search engines came out, people said there will be no need for professional services. This is no different and there will be winners and losers ... things will change but we will continue to grow.”

O’Keeffe is a glass-half-full person and is confident on the future growth prospects for the Irish economy. EY provides audit or advisory services to many of the big multinationals that operate here.

Does he worry that the recent corporation tax windfalls are at risk by one or more of the tech or pharma giants pulling out?

“That’s something that the Government and the IDA need to be really conscious of,” he says. “They need to stay really close to all of the individual companies and they need to explain the attractiveness of Ireland.

“The Government is very pro-business but they need to stay close to what are the issues that those corporation face globally.”

Ireland’s corporate tax advantage is over. So what’s the plan?

He also makes the point that Ireland needs to be seen as a welcoming place for senior executives and other “talent” that those same multinationals employ here.

“We need to make clear that we’re a welcoming country with humility, which has brilliant talent. Only six generations ago our people had to be leave this island because there was nothing here for our talent.

“Now we have an opportunity to ... bring people from around the world to Ireland. But we cannot do that if we show any signs of xenophobia within our country, and we’ve seen it in pockets, especially in 2025.”

Is the Government right to tighten the rules on immigration?

“We have to be very mindful of people who have already committed to building their lives here and naturalising themselves. We have to be very clever on who comes here for the benefit of the country. That’s a tricky balance for the Government, no doubt. But we need to attract high-end jobs so that we have the best talent coming to the country, because they will also share their experiences and help others develop and grow to that level of talent. We need to make sure that we’re not losing our ability ... to bring the right people that this country needs to continue its success in the years ahead.”

Unlike most of its rivals, there is no term mandate in place for EY managing partners. O’Keeffe has been in situ for eight years now. Does he intend to see the new five-year strategy plan through?

“I hope so. I have all the energy in the world but that will be determined by my fellow partners. The time has flown by and we’ve had so much change from Brexit to Covid to wars, you name it.

“I wake up every morning with lots of energy and still believe I’ll be doing it [the job] tomorrow, next year and hopefully the year after.”

CV

Name: Frank O’Keeffe.

Age: 53.

Job: Managing Partner, EY Ireland.

Family: Married to Susan, four children.

Hobbies: Golf, GAA, rugby.

Something you might expect: “Passionate about the interconnected forces of people, business, technology and the geopolitics shaping our world.”

Something that might surprise: “For all the seriousness of my day job, I don’t take myself too seriously and I’m usually happiest when there’s a bit of fun and laughter around.”

Leadership style: “I’d describe it as open, collaborative and straightforward. I try to give people the trust and space to be at their best. I’m a big believer in listening, staying curious and bringing people with me. And I’ve always thought a bit of humour helps, particularly when things get challenging.”

]]>Sean Gallup<![CDATA[Sex tourism concerns led Dublin-based Airbnb to suspend account]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/crime-law/courts/2026/10/23/sex-tourism-concerns-led-dublin-based-airbnb-to-suspend-account/https://www.irishtimes.com/crime-law/courts/2026/10/23/sex-tourism-concerns-led-dublin-based-airbnb-to-suspend-account/Fri, 23 Oct 2026 17:50:59 +0000Airbnb, which has its European, Middle East and Africa headquarters in Dublin, has successfully opposed High Court proceedings requiring it to reinstate the account of a Colombian property letting company which was terminated due to concerns about a breach of its ban on listings for sex tourism.

Medellín-based Turisvivienda SAS operates a portfolio of short-term rentals in the Colombian city which are close to the nightlife area and described as akin to Dublin’s Temple Bar.

Turisvivienda brought injunction proceedings in the High Court against Airbnb Ireland Unlimited Company, as under the terms of service between the parties, the Irish courts have exclusive jurisdiction to determine disputes between them.

Judge Marguerite Bolger refused the injunction application, saying she was not satisfied that Turisvivienda had established a strong case that it would succeed at trial that Airbnb’s conclusions before it disabled the account were unreasonable, groundless and/or unlawful.

The judge said that under its terms of service relating to its sex tourism policy, Airbnb does not permit paid sexual services at a listing, even in locations where these activities are legal.

She said there are long-standing issues in Colombia, and in particular in Medellín, in relation to sex tourism and sex trafficking. Sex work is not illegal in Colombia for sex workers aged 18 years or over.

Since September 2024, Airbnb has actively engaged with the authorities in Medellín on this issue and has recently removed over 150 Medellín-based hosts from its platform under its policies on sex work.

Turisvivienda said it has also proactively put steps in place to prevent sex work in its properties, which include 24-hour security, the display of an anti-sex tourism statement in its listing descriptions and around the properties and requiring all guests and visitors to sign a contract prohibiting sex work and providing personal ID.

On June 21st last year, Turisvivienda filed a safety report with Airbnb about a guest’s behaviour and was unhappy with the response to its complaint. Two days later, it was advised that, following an investigation, its account was being terminated for violating the defendant’s sex work policies.

Turisvivienda appealed and provided documentary evidence on its policy to prevent sex tourism.

Airbnb later responded, saying it had identified “direct on-platform communications with booking guests that violate our Terms of Service, specifically our policies prohibiting sex tourism”.

It listed extracts from online conversations between Turisvivienda and its guests, including references to the phrase “guest friendly”, which it described to Airbnb as “a common coded phrase used by sex tourists travelling to Colombia to connect with hosts that permit sex work in their listings”.

Airbnb also said that although this term is not solely an indicator of complicity in sex tourism, it is “a strong signal when observed in combination with other indicators”.

Turisvivinda’s founder and 90 per cent shareholder, David Emch, sought to have the dispute dealt with by arbitration at the International Centre for Dispute Resolution (ICDR) but an arbitrator found the ICDR lacked jurisdiction to decide the claim.

Last May Turisvivienda brought an application here for an injunction to have its account restored.

It claimed Airbnb was in breach of contract for reasons including that it failed to follow its own terms of service and by disabling its account for a reason not provided for in the contract.

As part of its case, an affidavit was sworn by one of its employees who responded to posts on the Airbnb system. The employee said she understood the use in some guest queries of the words “girls” and “chicks” not to refer to sex workers, but simply to be alternative terms to describe women.

She described her understanding of a message from a guest, “get me a bride”, as meaning “the fact that the guest was hoping to find someone to marry while visiting Medellin, and I did not think it appropriate or necessary for me to respond”.

Airbnb opposed the injunction application.

Bolger said it was not for the court to determine whether the communications did or did not indicate sex work but rather to decide whether Airbnb’s conclusion that they did was reasonable and lawful.

She was not satisfied Turisvivienda had established a strong case that it would succeed at trial.

She also said that in the absence of a statable claim that Turisvivienda’s financial viability is seriously at risk, its losses to date are entirely financial, for which it can be adequately compensated in damages.

]]>stockcam<![CDATA[Builder Clearwater Construction owes creditors €2.4m]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/23/builder-clearwater-construction-owes-creditors-24m/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/23/builder-clearwater-construction-owes-creditors-24m/Fri, 23 Oct 2026 18:09:35 +0000A building company that folded leaving sports clubs with bills for unfinished work owes creditors more than €2 million.

Grangecon, Wicklow-based Clearwater Construction & Landscaping Ltd, known to most customers as CWC, ceased trading earlier this month.

Creditors heard on Friday that the business has a deficit, the difference between liabilities and assets, of €2.37 million.

The firm, run by director PJ Norton, owes €2.06 million to unsecured creditors, mostly suppliers with unpaid bills or customers with unfinished work.

They voted to appoint KPMG as joint liquidator with another firm instead of the company’s nominees, Eoin Massey and Anthony Glennon of Friel Stafford.

Clearwater owes Revenue €230,176, including €87,412 in PAYE and PRSI along with €64,239 in unpaid VAT and more than €33,000 in corporation tax.

An estimation of the realisable value of Clearwater’s assets comes €5,011, according to a statement of affairs given to shareholders on Friday that was seen by The Irish Times.

Sports organisations, many of them in the southeast, are owed significant sums for work that has yet to be completed.

Building company ceases trading, leaving sports clubs with bills for unfinished work

Leaving the meeting, which ran for 90 minutes in a hotel in Stillorgan, Dublin, creditors said they did not expect to receive the sums they are due from Clearwater.

A spokesman for Kilmacthomas GAA Club in Co Waterford, said the organisation paid Clearwater a €50,000 deposit to secure an astroturf pitch in July after the company sought the payment.

“We had concerns about a making a payment at that level but we did our due diligence, we had our contracts in place and had our solicitor review them, but then the purchase was never made by Clearwater,” he said.

The spokesman pointed out that many of the organisations now left with unfinished work had paid Clearwater with money received through the Government’s Sports Capital Grants scheme, one the main funding sources for community groups across the Republic.

All of them also rely heavily on voluntary raising efforts by members and their committees, he added.

Jamie Farrell, chairman of Bunclody Association Football Club in Co Wexford confirmed that the meeting heard that Clearwater began to experience difficulties in March and these had become more serious by July.

His organisation paid Clearwater €313,000 for work left incomplete as a result of the company’s failure.

He said he hoped that the liquidators “act on behalf of creditors and that they look into the company in great detail”.

The well-known Athboy Celtic Association Football Club in Co Meath is owed €135,800 according to a list of creditors.

Following news that the company ceased trading the week before last, several of the organisations hit complained that Clearwater had not been communicating with them.

Norton refused to comment following Friday’s meeting.

   <title>Rekordbeteiligung zeichnet sich ab</title>
   <description>Bei der vorgezogenen Parlamentswahl in Serbien hat sich am Sonntag eine Rekordbeteiligung abgezeichnet.    <title>Handelsangestellte sollen sich „umorientieren“</title>
   <description>Der Chef des Instituts für Höhere Studien (IHS), Holger Bonin, hat bei den Lohnverhandlungen für „differenzierte Abschlüsse“ plädiert.    <description>Nach den gewaltsamen Protesten der Vorwoche sind in Frankreich am Samstag erneut Hunderttausende auf die Straße gegangenen. Notes From Poland https://notesfrompoland.com regular summaries of news from Poland Sun, 25 Oct 2026 17:59:56 +0000 en-US hourly 1 https://wordpress.org/?v=6.9 https://notesfrompoland.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/10/cropped-2019-10-29_1838-32x32.png Notes From Poland https://notesfrompoland.com 32 32 Time is running out for Germany to pay Polish WWII victims the compensation they deserve [Opinion] https://notesfrompoland.com/2026/10/25/time-is-running-out-for-germany-to-pay-polish-wwii-victims-the-compensation-they-deserve-opinion/ Sun, 25 Oct 2026 14:10:55 +0000 https://notesfrompoland.com/?p=105968 Philipp Fritz There are 30,000-50,000 such survivors, but their number dwindles every week.]]>

Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work!

Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support.

By Philipp Fritz, Warsaw correspondent for Die Welt (which first published this article in German here)

Negotiations on compensation for the still-living victims of the German occupation of Poland have been going on for years. There are some 30,000 to 50,000 such survivors, but their number dwindles every week. Berlin should act now.

No “humanitarian gesture” has emerged. “The draft budget currently reflects the fact that no decision has been made,” said Josef Hinterseher, a German foreign office spokesman, at a press conference in late September.

He thereby confirmed what many observers had suspected: survivors of concentration camps, ghettos and death marches, former forced workers and participants in the Warsaw Uprising who are still living in Poland will not receive any compensation, one-off payment or monthly pension from the German government.

The German chancellor has announced that his country will offer support to surviving Polish victims of WW2 and will help strengthen Poland’s eastern border.

However, in both cases he did not provide details of what these measures will involve in practice https://t.co/gKX6142Alo

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 2, 2024

Just a few sentences later, Hinterseher moved onto the next subject – the fact that two Russian oligarchs were to be removed from the EU’s sanctions list. Or at least, that Berlin had not been successful in opposing this decision.

The fact that these two issues were dealt with publicly one after the other shows that the German government is quicker to reach a decision that makes Putin’s supporters’ lives easier than it is with victims of the Nazi terror. It is a declaration of moral bankruptcy.

Warsaw and Berlin have been negotiating compensation for the last remaining victims of the German occupation of Poland for years. There are between 30,000 and 50,000 of them – aged over 90, often living alone and in poor health. Their numbers are dwindling every week.

The fact that talks are taking place in Berlin ministries but without any decision being taken is met with sadness and fury in Poland.

 

Increasingly, Poles are getting the impression that, even if the Germans manage to put up memorials, they cannot offer survivors tangible help when it is asked for. It is a common view that in Berlin the descendants of the perpetrators are simply waiting for the victims to die so that this pesky issue will sort itself out.

Should that happen, those left behind will not forget, and the Germans will hardly be able to forgive themselves.

Warsaw is no longer demanding war reparations from Berlin. In December 2023, Donald Tusk’s government switched to talking about “making amends”.

Polish foreign minister @sikorskiradek has called on Germany to “think creatively” about compensating Poland for WWII.

On a visit to Berlin, he also said that the new government would "end the cold war" waged by the former ruling PiS party against Germany https://t.co/kZ62nUuqqO

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) January 31, 2024

This is not just splitting hairs. In so doing, Tusk put the ball in the German government’s court, giving it the chance to take action and, through a gesture recognising suffering and providing a relatively small sum of money, to offer people tangible help and do a service to the German-Polish relationship.

Former German Chancellor Olaf Scholz is reported to have offered Tusk a one-off payment in 2024, but Poland’s prime minister turned the sum down as insufficient. Instead, Polish diplomats are demanding monthly pensions.

In any case, we are talking about a few hundred million euro: a relatively small amount compared to the equivalent of €1.3 trillion that Poland’s former ruling national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) party once demanded from Germany, and also in comparison to many other budget items – and yet still there is nothing about compensation in the budget planning.

Poland is seeking $1.3 trillion in war reparations from Germany, but Berlin says the issue was legally settled long ago.

Legal scholar @MPiatkowski1 examines the arguments of both sides, explains the legal context, and looks at what could come next https://t.co/xsKAY2TukS

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 9, 2022

Rumour has it that, in return for compensation, German foreign ministry officials are asking for a kind of Polish guarantee that in future there will be no more demands for reparations, or at least that at least the German gesture will receive good press in Poland.

If that is true, it would be thoroughly indecent, bringing to mind an image of a perpetrator trying to buy his victim’s silence. This reflects a belief in objectification, an ugly bureaucratic mentality stemming from a system in which “work” in a ghetto counts towards statutory pension contributions, but no one can bring themselves to pay compensation.

This issue can be resolved at the very top. Chancellor Friedrich Merz would have to work with the relevant ministries – the foreign office and finance ministry – to provide for compensation for the victims in the budget. This would be a belated but major and morally right gesture. If politics is too slow – time really is of the essence – then civil society should take it upon itself to show where it stands.

Donations for the still living victims of the German tyranny or a fund from which survivors would receive monthly payments can be created from within society. Business can also get involved. German corporations which were guilty of, for instance, exploiting forced labourers in occupied Poland, or those that emerged from them, such as BASF, Siemens, Volkswagen, BMW and Deutsche Bank, could contribute.

Poland covers almost all the costs of maintaining former Nazi-German camps on its territory. It has spent more on this than Germany has paid in compensation to Polish war victims

It's time for Germany to fund preservation of the sites, argues @W_Kononczuk https://t.co/08nf4c2jMz

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) January 25, 2026

Right now, since its state elections in September, Germany gives the impression of a country whose compass for right and wrong is broken.

As of 6 October, the state parliament of Sachsen-Anhalt has as its vice-president Hans-Thomas Tillschneider of the AfD, a man who wrote on X that “the Poles have been getting on my nerves for a long time now”. In Berlin, not only did the left-wing Die Linke celebrate their electoral success with Israel haters and antisemites, they even tolerate them in their ranks. It is shameful.

But now Germany, and particularly its government, has the opportunity to show that the rhetoric of responsibility for the victims is not merely empty words. That, contrary to a mood that does not support it, they are doing what is morally right. Time is running out, Germany – it’s your last chance.

By Aleks Szczerbiak

Political scandals generate intense media attention and public outrage but rarely produce dramatic shifts in party support that they once did.

They are now more likely to affect electoral outcomes indirectly by demobilising softer, less committed voters and influencing turnout, particularly among supporters of the government disappointed by its apparent underperformance and broken election promises.

The hospital scandal

Two high-profile political scandals dominated the Polish news agenda for much of this summer. The first centred on irregularities at Warsaw’s Southern Hospital (Szpital Południowy) and involved a young and relatively inexperienced doctor, Dawid Kacprzyk.

In spite of his lack of a specialist qualification, Kacprzyk coordinated the hospital’s emergency department and reportedly earned a staggering 1.6 million złoty (€366,000) in the previous year alone. He also served as a Warsaw district councilor for the liberal-centrist Civic Coalition (KO) grouping, Poland’s main governing party led by Prime Minister Donald Tusk.

Public outrage intensified following reports that the hospital had operated a dedicated “VIP path” or special lounge where ruling-party-linked politicians and their families were allowed faster access and medical examinations without the usual queues faced by ordinary patients.

Further claims emerged, including a whistleblower surgeon alleging that supervisory failures contributed to patient deaths and of improper private business activity in the hospital morgue.

Poland’s health minister has unveiled a set of reforms intended to “rebuild trust” in public hospitals following a series of reports about exorbitant pay for some doctors and that politically connected patients could skip queues and use a "VIP lounge" https://t.co/pidAHxohc4

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 8, 2026

For its part, KO insisted that the scandal was the personal misconduct of one former party member rather than a general problem affecting the entire healthcare system. They noted that Kacprzyk quickly resigned his council seat and hospital role, and that party-aligned Warsaw mayor Rafał Trzaskowski had dismissed the hospital board and two of his deputy mayors overseeing the city’s health services.

KO argued that no specific names of preferential VIP patients had been publicly confirmed, any irregularities were being fully investigated by prosecutors and independent bodies, and political and legal accountability would follow if ethical breaches or crimes were proven. The government also pledged systemic reforms including measures to curb excessive pay for doctors.

Nonetheless, the scandal struck a deep chord with the Polish public, triggering massive negative media and political fallout that aligned perfectly with the right-wing opposition’s narrative painting KO as part of a “Warsaw elite” that enjoys special privileges at the expense of ordinary citizens.

The cryptocurrency scandal

The second major summer scandal centred on allegations of financial impropriety and political entanglement involving Zondacrypto, once Poland’s largest crypto trading platform, that claimed over a million users but earlier this year collapsed abruptly after thousands of retail investors were unable to access their funds.

However, what began as a major financial scandal escalated into political warfare, providing the government with powerful ammunition to attack the right-wing Law and Justice (PiS), Poland’s ruling party between 2015 and 2023 and currently the main opposition grouping, party-aligned President Karol Nawrocki, and the broader conservative political eco-system over payments and donations made by the crypto firm.

Prosecutors are investigating possible criminal offences relating to financing by Zondacrypto, a collapsed crypto firm, of organisations and individuals linked to the right-wing opposition, including the Polish version of US conservative conference CPAC https://t.co/swceV864nA

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 26, 2026

For example, Zondacrypto sponsored the 2025 Polish edition of the Conservative Political Action Committee (CPAC) conference attended by the then-presidential candidate Nawrocki, advertised heavily with conservative media outlets such as the TV Republika television network, and made donations to foundations linked to high-ranking PiS figures such as former justice minister Zbigniew Ziobro.

The government also tried to entangle Nawrocki, who repeatedly vetoed its cryptocurrency regulation laws, into the scandal, arguing that he was protecting the shady interests of the industry and its political beneficiaries at the expense of ordinary Poles (the Tusk administration lacks the three-fifths parliamentary majority required to overturn a presidential veto).

For their part, PiS and the broader Polish right dismissed the government’s accusations as a smear campaign and sought to shift blame for the scandal onto the Tusk administration for inadequate oversight to protect investors. Figures on the right, including those connected to foundations that received money, framed these dealings as legitimate sponsorships common across the media and other organisations.

The president of the Polish Olympic Committee has been detained as part of a criminal investigation into Zondacrypto, a crypto firm that collapsed earlier this year and was a major sponsor of Poland's Olympic team https://t.co/QPG7ejAImD

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 27, 2026

PiS rejected claims that the party or associated groups received funds from the firm and defended Nawrocki’s vetoes as necessary against flawed legislation.

Nonetheless, opinion polls found that most respondents linked the scandal to PiS and the right-wing opposition, providing the government with numerous attack lines to force them onto the defensive.

The diminishing impact of scandals

It is worth recalling how an earlier era of post-communist politics scandals possessed much greater transformative, system-altering capacity and could act as catalysts for the restructuring of the electoral landscape.

For example, at the beginning of the 2000s, the so-called “Rywin scandal” was widely seen as a decisive factor in the near-destruction as a political force of the previously powerful, and then-governing, communist-successor Democratic Left Alliance (SLD). The scandal erupted in late 2002 when film producer Lew Rywin allegedly solicited a large bribe from the Agora media group, publisher of the influential liberal-left Gazeta Wyborcza newspaper, in exchange for media legislation changes while claiming to act on behalf of a “group holding power” (grupa trzymająca władzę) linked to the ruling party.

A high-profile parliamentary investigative commission, sustained media focus, and a series of follow-on scandals and accumulation of allegations of deep-seated influence peddling by post-communist networks created a powerful narrative of systemic bribery and corruption, completely discrediting the SLD as a competent governing force.

Having won a substantial victory in the 2001 parliamentary election, securing 41% of the votes, its support collapsed to only 11% at the next 2005 poll. This helped clear the way for the rise of the KO (originally Civic Platform)-PiS duopoly that has structured the Polish party system ever since, thereby establishing a precedent that scandals were electorally fatal transgressions.

 

The contrast with the recent hospital and cryptocurrency scandals is instructive and illustrates a broader transformation in the relationship between political misconduct and electoral politics in Poland.

Whereas in the more fluid party system of the early post-communist period a cluster of major scandals or single-event shocks could rapidly destroy dominant parties and restructure competition, now – although they still generate intense, high-octane political and media outrage – such controversies appear to slide off the main political actors with remarkably little immediate consequence.

Indeed, neither of these recent scandals produced the dramatic shift in headline polling numbers that some observers, drawing on historical precedent, might have anticipated given the intensity of the media coverage.

Scandal-neutralising structural shifts

This change stems from three interlocking shifts in the structural dynamics of Poland’s political system. Taken together, they have substantially diminished the capacity of scandals to move headline poll numbers and trigger the kind of large-scale systemic realignments seen in an earlier era of post-communist politics.

Firstly, the sheer velocity of modern political communication prevents single-issue-based scandals from sustaining public focus. In the early 2000s, a major corruption scandal could dominate the news headlines for months through concentrated media attention. The Rywin scandal unfolded through prolonged televised parliamentary commission hearings, keeping the story alive and allowing public outrage to build into a sustained narrative that slowly drained the ruling party’s legitimacy.

Today, digital algorithms and the 24-hour news cycle ensure that a major story, whether about healthcare management or cryptocurrency, moves at a breathtaking pace and is overtaken rapidly as public attention moves onto the next domestic controversy, international development, or strategic counter-narrative.

Seven people have been charged in relation to alleged corruption in the issuing of Polish visas to foreign nationals

The scandal has engulfed the government since last week, but officials say the opposition is exaggerating the scale and nature of the case https://t.co/iHnIShb1pQ

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 15, 2023

This hyper-accelerated news cycle means that even a high-profile case that generates intense short-term media coverage does not remain the dominant story for long enough to produce cumulative, system-level damage by limiting the time window in which a scandal can convert temporary disapproval into lasting shifts in voting intentions. Scandals thereby become a form of ambient “background noise” in Polish public life rather than a singular focal point for popular outrage.

Secondly, and perhaps most formidably, the protective shield of deep polarisation and socio-political division renders large segments of the electorate relatively impervious to allegations against “their” side. After 2005, the Polish party system crystallised around a durable “post-transition” socio-economic divide reinforced by cultural and geopolitical fault lines.

In this deeply fractured and highly polarised landscape, with large segments of the electorate embedded within hostile camps, when a scandal like the hospital crisis or cryptocurrency controversy breaks, voters interpret allegations levelled against “their” party through a tribal filter as a politically motivated hit job or the work of hostile media.

So even severe scandals are shaped by, and largely confirm, existing political loyalties and rarely trigger cross-camp voter defections. This is a sharp contrast with the early 2000s, when the party system was still fluid and electoral volatility high.

How does voting work? What do polls suggest the outcome will be? Which issues may animate the campaign? And what role will President Nawrocki play? https://t.co/fmdoFpBaxz

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 15, 2026

Thirdly, the parties themselves have become far more professional at message discipline and crisis management. Today’s parties are centralised media machines staffed by sophisticated public relations strategists who view a scandal not as a moral crisis but a communication problem requiring aggressive damage containment.

Rather than allowing a controversy to fester, they immediately launch counterattacks, accusing their opponents of far greater historical or concurrent corruption, and ruthlessly enforce internal party discipline and message conformity.

They also deploy well-rehearsed crisis management playbooks including: personnel sanctions; framing the problem as local or individual responsibility, or residual rather than systemic failure; ordering visible audits, investigations, or reforms to demonstrate “taking action”; and co-ordinated messaging that seeks to close the story quickly and shift the focus back onto the other side’s weaknesses or broader policy issues.

Differential mobilisation, not voter persuasion

Yet while polarisation and professional crisis management allow parties to survive the immediate news cycle, this does not mean that scandals have become irrelevant. Rather, their effects are more subtle and delayed through the “slow-burn” mechanism of differential turnout by selectively demobilising specific voter segments.

Although in a highly polarised polity the most committed hard-core partisans are relatively immune to negative information about “their” side, soft or conditional supporters may become disillusioned, or simply less motivated, when repeated scandals reinforce a narrative of self-interest or incompetence.

The net result is a gradual, cumulative, asymmetric demobilisation of one camp that does not fully register in standard inter-election voting intention surveys, which generally show expressed party preferences among those willing to answer but not necessarily the intensity of that preference or the probability that a respondent will actually turn out to vote.

In Poland’s deeply polarised political landscape, the next parliamentary election, scheduled for autumn 2027, is unlikely to be determined by persuading voters to cross the ideological divide. Rather differential levels of electoral turnout and mobilisation are likely to be the key, specifically: whichever side’s core base is more motivated to – and peripheral, less ideologically committed “softer” supporters are demotivated from – showing up on polling day.

Young Poles are bucking the international trend by turning out at a higher rate than the oldest voters in recent elections.

We spoke with experts and young voters to find out more about the growing frustrations that are driving this political engagement https://t.co/y1JpYYmbjb

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 11, 2025

And in a context where the election is likely to be closely fought, and relatively small differences in participation rates could prove decisive, although they may not produce dramatic changes in headline party polling preferences, scandals can still play a significant role. However, we are only likely to see the full impact of any such scandals when voters eventually go to the polls and actual turnout patterns are revealed.

Given the general disillusionment with the current government and growing narrative of its underperformance and failure to deliver on its electoral promises, scandals are more likely to contribute to the demobilisation of the governing camp. It is anyway inherently more difficult for incumbent parties to mobilise their disillusioned supporters to turn out and vote than it is for motivated oppositions to rally their base to oust them.

Indeed, revealed voter preferences in the summer 2025 presidential election – when Nawrocki won an unexpected victory over Trzaskowski, the ruling party-backed favourite – and more recently the severe setback for KO in the Kraków mayoral by-election, suggest that government supporters are already showing greater reluctance to vote.

So, while their effects are routinely neutralised by fast-moving news, tribal shielding and professional spin, scandals still matter in Polish politics, although the battleground has shifted from voter persuasion to differential mobilisation.

The government’s majority in parliament has approved two bills that would liberalise Poland’s strict abortion laws. One would reverse the 2020 constitutional court ruling introducing a near-total ban on abortion; the other would decriminalise providing help to women in obtaining unlawful abortions.

However, it appears likely that both measures will be vetoed by President Karol Nawrocki, who is aligned with the right-wing opposition. His chief of staff reiterated on Tuesday that Nawrocki “supports the protection of life from conception to natural death”.

— Aleksandra LEO (@AleksandraLeo) October 20, 2026

When Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s ruling coalition, which ranges from left to centre right, took power in December 2023 from the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) government, it pledged to soften abortion laws.

However, since then, it has failed to do so, largely due to disputes between more conservative and liberal elements within the coalition. But now, a year ahead of parliamentary elections, that has changed, with the more powerful lower-house Sejm pushing through two abortion bills on Tuesday.

One would once again allow abortions to be carried out in cases where a severe foetal abnormality is diagnosed. That would reverse a ruling by the Constitutional Tribunal (TK) in 2020 outlawing such abortions, which the TK found contravened various constitutional principles, including the right to life.

That judgement, which went into force in January 2021, means that abortion is currently only allowed in two cases: when a pregnancy results from a crime (such as rape or incest) or when it threatens the mother’s life or health. In Europe, only Malta has a stricter abortion law.

The ruling was issued when the TK was stacked with PiS-appointed judges – including three who had been illegitimately appointed – and regarded as being under the control of the then-ruling party. It prompted the largest protests Poland has witnessed since the communist era.

 

In the Sejm vote on Tuesday, 233 MPs were in favour of the new bill, with 203 opposed. Support came from parties in Tusk’s coalition, as well as the small left-wing Together (Razem).

Tusk’s centrist Civic Coalition (KO) and The Left (Lewica), one of its coalition partners, have previously expressed support for an even greater liberalisation of the law, allowing abortion on demand up to the 12th week of pregnancy. However, all of their MPs voted in favour of the compromise option on the table.

Meanwhile, five MPs from the centre-right Polish People’s Party (PSL), the most conservative element of the coalition, joined with the right-wing and far-right opposition in voting against the bill.

How MPs from each parliamentary caucus voted on the bill to allow abortions when a severe foetal abnormality is diagnosed (za = for, przeciw = against, wstrzymało się = abstained, nie głosowało = did not vote)

In a separate vote, the Sejm also approved a bill that would decriminalise the act of helping a woman obtain an unlawful abortion. Currently, that is an offence that carries a prison sentence of up to three years.

A previous attempt to pass such a bill was defeated in 2024, after most PSL MPs joined with the opposition to block it. That prompted Tusk to declare that abortion reform would be impossible during the current parliamentary term.

However, on Tuesday, 217 MPs voted in favour and 213 against, meaning the bill was approved. A total of 27 MPs failed to attend the vote, including 10 from PiS, among them party leader Jarosław Kaczyński. If they had participated, the bill would likely have been rejected.

All MPs from KO, The Left and Razem voted in favour of the bill, as did almost all from the centrist Poland 2050. However, 14 PSL MPs joined with the opposition in voting against it, including PSL’s leader, deputy prime minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz.

Both the bills approved by the Sejm now pass to the upper-house Senate, which can propose amendments but not block the passage of legislation. Tusk’s coalition has an even larger majority in the Senate than the Sejm.

Once final versions of the bills are approved by parliament, they pass to the president, who can sign them into law, veto them, or ask the TK to assess whether they comply with the constitution.

Given that Nawrocki is aligned with the right-wing opposition, has vetoed a record number of government bills, and has declared his opposition to abortion, it appears very unlikely that he will sign either bill into law.

“I received a medal from the Americans for helping them, for treating Americans. I didn’t have to do that. We treated them with our own Polish medicines,” they added.

Tusk then added his own remarks, stating: “I would like these words to reach our allies. So that no one will ever again downplay the efforts of our soldiers. Wherever our allies, including our closest ally, the Americans, have needed our participation, Polish soldiers stood shoulder to shoulder with them.”

Tusk also referenced Nawrocki’s silence on the matter. “Frankly, I was also counting on the president speaking out on this matter. But it seems I miscalculated.”

 

Tusk is the first European head of government to directly criticise Hegseth’s remarks, although a spokesperson for British Prime Minister Andy Burnham did say on Monday that it was “wrong to diminish the role” of British personnel, 457 of whom died in Afghanistan.

Of the 3,621 coalition deaths during the war in Afghanistan, around two thirds were Americans (2,461). The rest came from 31 different countries, with Poland’s 44 fatalities the seventh most of any nation.

Hegseth’s remarks are not the first time that the Trump administration has caused anger in Poland by downplaying allies’ role in Afghanistan. In January, Trump himself suggested that other countries had “stayed a little back, a little off the front lines”.

That prompted General Roman Polko, who commanded Poland’s GROM special forces unit in Iraq and Afghanistan, to call the US president “a coward who has never been on the front lines”.

The Polish government has also clashed with the US on other issues. In January, Tusk joined other European leaders in calling for Greenland’s sovereignty to be respected, following Trump’s calls for the island to be brought under US control.

The following month, Tusk declared that Poland would not be a “vassal” of the US and suggested that Nawrocki wanted Poland to be too subservient to Washington. Czarzasty has twice this year clashed with the US ambassador over critical remarks he made towards Trump.

However, at the same time, the Polish government has sought to maintain positive relations with Washington, given the United States’ role as Poland’s most important security partner. In June, Poland formally requested that the US establish a new permanent military base on its territory.

Hegseth himself has praised Poland, calling it a “model ally” last year. The US State Department this month also announced that it was pushing for Poland to be allowed to join the G20 “as soon as possible”, pointing to its “growing leadership position in the international arena”.
