City AM https://www.cityam.com/ London's Business Newspaper Sun, 25 Oct 2026 15:29:57 +0000 en-GB hourly 1 https://wordpress.org/?v=7.1.3 https://www.cityam.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/09/app_launcher_icon_final_rounded.png?w=32 City AM https://www.cityam.com/ 32 32 213406410 Google, OpenAI and Anthropic back £100m UK AI biosecurity lab https://www.cityam.com/google-openai-and-anthropic-back-100m-uk-ai-biosecurity-lab/ Sun, 25 Oct 2026 15:29:45 +0000 https://www.cityam.com/?p=2471226

Google Deepmind, OpenAI and Anthropic are backing a new £100m British AI biosecurity laboratory as the government unveils more than £600m in funding to tackle emerging technological threats. The lab will use AI to detect and monitor biological threats, bringing together some of the world’s largest AI developers as ministers seek to strengthen Britain’s defences. [...]]]>

Google Deepmind, OpenAI and Anthropic are backing a new £100m British AI biosecurity laboratory as the government unveils more than £600m in funding to tackle emerging technological threats.

The lab will use AI to detect and monitor biological threats, bringing together some of the world’s largest AI developers as ministers seek to strengthen Britain’s defences.

OpenAI and Anthropic will provide up to £200m in AI model credits, giving researchers access to their technology, while Google’s Deepmind and London-based life sciences startup Basecamp Research will support the initiative.

The investment forms part of a £165m National AI Biosecurity Initiative announced ahead of Wednesday’s Budget, with a further £65m allocated to biological surveillance and the development of treatments and other countermeasures against dangerous pathogens.

AI minister Kanishka Narayan said the government wanted to establish the facility as a leading international centre for biosecurity research.

“Our new AI Biosecurity Lab will be a major new global institution, bringing together world-leading scientific expertise to protect people from emerging biological threats and ensure Britain leads the world in AI safety and security,” he said.

“As AI becomes more powerful, Britain must have the capabilities to protect its people and shape its own future”.

Britain ramps up AI security spending

The biosecurity project is the largest individual initiative in a wider government funding package targeting cybersecurity, domestic AI development and research into the technology’s economic impact.

The UK’s AI Security Institute will receive an additional £120m to expand its testing of advanced models and research into emerging risks.

A further £130m will be directed towards strengthening cybersecurity, including £60m for a National Cyber Shield designed to use autonomous AI systems to detect and respond to threats.

The remaining £70m will establish a National Exposure and Real-Time Vulnerability Centre, using AI to identify weaknesses across critical infrastructure and the wider economy.

The investment follows growing government interest in deploying advanced models for defensive purposes.

Narayan recently revealed that the government had spent just £13,000 using AI to identify 500 previously unknown cybersecurity vulnerabilities across parts of the public sector.

An additional £60m will be invested through the Sovereign AI Fund to support British businesses developing robotics, autonomous systems and industrial AI, alongside £60m for research and procurement of domestic AI technology.

The package includes £18m for a chip-design academy and £23m over three years for the AI Economics Institute, which will examine the technology’s impact on productivity, employment and living standards.

The government is also allocating £30m to regional mayors to support local AI initiatives.

]]> 2471226Saskia Koopman Saskia Koopman Healey to unveil billions in defence spending as Tories demand he resign https://www.cityam.com/healey-to-unveil-billions-in-defence-spending-as-tories-demand-he-resign/ Sun, 25 Oct 2026 11:16:43 +0000 https://www.cityam.com/?p=2471208

John Healey is set to announce billions of pounds in new defence investment in Wednesday’s Budget as the Conservatives demand he resign unless he commits to spending three per cent of GDP on the military by 2030. The chancellor is expected to channel additional funding through the National Wealth Fund and British Business Bank, backing [...]]]>

John Healey is set to announce billions of pounds in new defence investment in Wednesday’s Budget as the Conservatives demand he resign unless he commits to spending three per cent of GDP on the military by 2030.

The chancellor is expected to channel additional funding through the National Wealth Fund and British Business Bank, backing British defence manufacturers and military technology firms while seeking to boost domestic jobs.

The investment will be financed through long-term borrowing rather than spending cuts, the Sunday Times reported, with drone manufacturers and artificial intelligence companies among those expected to benefit.

The approach would allow the Treasury to increase defence investment without breaching its fiscal rules, as funding provided through public financial institutions is treated differently from conventional government spending where it is expected to generate financial returns.

It would also count towards Nato’s defence spending targets, offering Healey a way to increase military investment while facing pressure to balance the public finances.

The announcement comes four months after Healey resigned as defence secretary under former prime minister Keir Starmer, arguing that the government had failed to commit sufficient funding to the armed forces.

He had demanded a timetable to increase defence spending to three per cent of GDP by 2030, ahead of Nato’s wider target of 3.5 per cent by 2035.

However, the chancellor has since said that a full timetable for reaching the target will not be published until next year’s spending review.

Tories demand Healey’s resignation

Shadow chancellor Andrew Griffith has called on Healey to resign unless Wednesday’s Budget sets out a fully funded plan to reach the three per cent target.

“By the end of his Budget statement, John Healey must have fully funded three per cent defence spending, or resign”, Griffith said.

“We are living in an era of extraordinary threats, and yet the Chancellor is dithering over finding the money to pay the country’s insurance premium”.

The Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) has estimated that reaching three per cent of GDP would require an additional £17.3bn in 2029 to 2030.

Conservative shadow defence secretary James Cartlidge welcomed the proposed investment but accused Labour of adopting a policy previously put forward by his party.

“I welcome Labour copying our idea, particularly if that means getting more cash to UK start-ups and defence tech businesses”, he said.

However, Cartlidge warned that investment in emerging technologies would not remove the need for additional funding for military training, equipment and ammunition.

Defence secretary Wes Streeting rejected the criticism, accusing the Conservatives of leaving the armed forces underfunded.

“Kemi Badenoch’s Conservatives shrunk the British Army to its smallest size since the Napoleonic era and left a £17 billion hole in the equipment plan”, he said.

“Their fantasy economics won’t keep Britain safe, just as their reckless hollowing out of our armed forces didn’t when they were in power”.

The row follows a warning from Streeting that Britain must be prepared for the possibility of conflict by 2030 as Russia expands its military capabilities.

Writing in The Telegraph on Saturday, he said the UK had “a little over 1,000 days” to ensure it could defend itself alongside Nato allies. “To prevent the worst, we have to prepare for it”, he said.

The Treasury is reportedly preparing to provide £20.4bn in additional support to the National Wealth Fund and British Business Bank from 2028-29, although the amount ultimately directed towards defence has not been confirmed.

]]> 2471208Saskia Koopman Saskia Koopman Healey’s startup adviser quits ahead of Budget over ‘sideshow’ treatment of entrepreneurs https://www.cityam.com/healeys-startup-adviser-quits-ahead-of-budget-over-sideshow-treatment-of-entrepreneurs/ Sun, 25 Oct 2026 10:50:43 +0000 https://www.cityam.com/?p=2471201

The Treasury’s entrepreneurship adviser is stepping down after accusing ministers of treating Britain’s fastest-growing companies as a “sideshow” while directing taxpayer money towards traditional industries. Alex Depledge, appointed by former chancellor Rachel Reeves in June 2025, will leave the role on Thursday, a day after John Healey delivers his first Budget. “Keeping scale-ups on the [...]]]>

The Treasury’s entrepreneurship adviser is stepping down after accusing ministers of treating Britain’s fastest-growing companies as a “sideshow” while directing taxpayer money towards traditional industries.

Alex Depledge, appointed by former chancellor Rachel Reeves in June 2025, will leave the role on Thursday, a day after John Healey delivers his first Budget.

“Keeping scale-ups on the fringes underestimates the contribution of our greatest companies, and we need to support and develop them on British shores at all costs”, she told The Sunday Times.

“We treat them as a bit of a sideshow”.

Depledge, who founded property technology firm Resi and cleaning marketplace Hassle.com, argued that ministers were overlooking high-growth businesses in favour of established industries.

“Where’s the real economy? They think it’s over here with steel, cars and hard hats, that this is the “main event'”, she said. “And my argument has always been: no, scale-ups are the main event”.

Her departure comes amid mounting frustration among British founders over taxes, access to investment and the government’s approach to economic growth.

Depledge also criticised the disruption caused by July’s change of chancellor, saying she had been forced to repeat arguments she had already won under Reeves.

“With John Healey and Johnny Reynolds, I had to relitigate all the arguments I had already won – and win them again”, she said.

While she held fortnightly meetings with Reeves, Depledge said she had “barely any face time” with Healey.

Founders press chancellor ahead of Budget

Depledge declined to disclose the measures she had proposed for Wednesday’s Budget but suggested they could include new incentives for company founders.

Last year, she helped secure an expansion of the Enterprise Management Incentives scheme, which allows growing businesses to offer tax-advantaged share options to employees.

Her exit comes as entrepreneurs urge Healey to protect Business Asset Disposal Relief, which reduces the tax paid by qualifying business owners when they sell their companies.

A group of founders has also called for tax breaks for entrepreneurs who reinvest the proceeds of business sales into other British companies.

Meanwhile, a survey of 400 scale-up founders by business network Helm found that 73 per cent were not at all confident the Budget would be good for business.

Healey has ruled out an increase in capital gains tax and pledged to back entrepreneurs who take risks and build profitable companies.

But Depledge warned that Britain risked missing out on the economic benefits of AI unless it moved faster to support domestic technology firms.

“We are in grave danger of not having a seat at the table”, she said. “The window is 18 months. That’s it”.

She also called for more pension fund investment in British growth companies, arguing that too much domestic capital was flowing overseas.

“There’s £3t trillion of capital sitting there that is not working for our pensioners and it’s not working for our high-growth companies”, she said.

Depledge previously told City AM that Britain’s startup environment had deteriorated over several years, arguing that founders needed better access to funding and incentives to retain talent.

“This has been a slow decline, right? That didn’t start with this current government”, she said last year.

Depledge said her decision to leave was also driven by a desire to return to business, adding: “At my very core, I’m an entrepreneur.”

]]> 2471201Saskia Koopman Saskia Koopman Burnham sparks Brexit row over return to EU free movement https://www.cityam.com/burnham-sparks-brexit-row-over-return-to-eu-free-movement/ Sun, 25 Oct 2026 09:47:40 +0000 https://www.cityam.com/?p=2471198

Andy Burnham has been accused of “betraying Brexit Britain” and threatening to hand control of the country’s borders back to Brussels after suggesting the UK could restore freedom of movement with the European Union. Reform UK leader Nigel Farage branded the remarks a betrayal of voters, while the Conservatives vowed to oppose any attempt to [...]]]>

Andy Burnham has been accused of “betraying Brexit Britain” and threatening to hand control of the country’s borders back to Brussels after suggesting the UK could restore freedom of movement with the European Union.

Reform UK leader Nigel Farage branded the remarks a betrayal of voters, while the Conservatives vowed to oppose any attempt to reverse one of the central outcomes of the 2016 referendum.

The backlash follows an interview with The Sunday Times in which Burnham called for an “honest discussion” about restoring free movement, arguing that immigration patterns had changed since Britain left the EU.

“Freedom of movement had very significant challenges associated with it and I spoke about them in my previous time in parliament”, Burnham said.

“But, at the same time, it was a type of immigration that perhaps wasn’t as difficult [as now]”.

He argued that EU migration had often been temporary, with workers spending several years in Britain before returning home, whereas more recent arrivals were increasingly settling permanently.

“The balance of migration has changed, hasn’t it, since then? I think we’ve just got to have an honest discussion about those things”, he added.

Tories and Reform attack Brexit shift

“This is a total betrayal of Brexit Britain and Burnham’s Makerfield pitch”, Farage said.

“He is also deluded to say immigration was different when we were members of the EU. We will fight this dishonesty”.

Shadow home secretary Chris Philp accused the prime minister of seeking to surrender control of Britain’s immigration system.

“Andy Burnham knows full well that a return to EU free movement would mean handing back control of our borders and allowing uncontrolled migration from across Europe”, he said.

“The British people voted to end free movement, and there can be no return to it”.

Philp added that the Conservatives would oppose any attempt to restore the arrangement, arguing that immigration policy should be determined in Britain rather than Brussels.

Burnham, who became prime minister in July, has increasingly signalled his willingness to reconsider Britain’s relationship with the EU.

Last month, he said the government should examine options ranging from closer economic cooperation to rejoining the single market, customs union or EU itself.

However, Labour’s 2024 manifesto ruled out a return to free movement, the single market and the customs union.

Burnham has not committed to restoring free movement but said keeping Britain outside the arrangement would not be a red line in future negotiations.

He also ruled out recommending that Britain adopt the euro or join the Schengen passport-free travel area.

The debate comes ahead of a planned UK-EU summit in Brussels on 20 November, where Burnham is expected to discuss closer ties with European leaders.

The world of fashion has so often been seen as belonging to a select few outposts in London, Milan, Paris and New York. But in 2026 it now belongs, at least in part, to sport. 

That’s not to say Roman Abramovich is buying Vogue or the Saudi Arabian Public Investment Fund ponders whether to back Alexander McQueen or Vivienne Westwood on a daily basis; but suits, belts and couture are now undoubtedly embedded within the sports sector. And nowhere is that more true than in Formula 1.

Having signed a 10-year, $1bn deal with LVMH – the parent company of Louis Vuitton, Christian Dior, Tag Heuer and many more luxury brands – Formula 1 has placed fashion front and centre of its outward-facing commercial aesthetic.

Teams now have fashion labels as sponsors, traditional sports apparel brands are delivering entire collections to the paddock, and next year the grid will gain a fashion house as a primary sponsor when two of the 22 cars will race under the Gucci Racing Alpine Formula One Team brand.

Formula 1 mass-market appeal

“Every livery, suit and piece of trackside branding is broadcast globally across every session, all weekend. Few sports offer a mixture of mass-market appeal and exclusivity,” Niklas Oppermann, co-founder of Williams Racing sponsor Carl Friedrik, tells City AM.

“The sport has such a rich design and engineering heritage to draw from: liveries, typography, materials, decades of visual history per team, which gives us a deep creative archive to reinterpret through our own lens.

“Our latest collection with Williams, called Grove, looks back to F1’s 1990s heyday, using a classic chestnut-and-cream palette alongside motifs that nod to the era, while still feeling distinctly us. We’ve also limited each style to just 80 units, reflecting the sense of exclusivity that has always been part of the sport’s appeal.”

Trade publication The Sponsor’s Sean Connell says that, having traditionally relied on cultural moments like the Oscars or one of the world’s fashion weeks, fashion now sees Formula 1 as a travelling catwalk.

Lewis Hamilton was a co-chair of the 2025 Met Gala – brainchild of former Vogue editor Anna Wintour – and last year attended his eighth edition of the charity ball. And while the only other Formula 1 driver to attend the New York event is Daniel Ricciardo, the likes of Charles Leclerc and George Russell have been seen on catwalk front rows.

Challenges

“The challenge now is that the early-adopter advantage is disappearing,” warns Connell. “More fashion and luxury brands are entering Formula 1, which means simply being present is no longer enough. Brands now have to work harder to genuinely stand out and create meaningful cultural impact.”

Alex Royce, head of sport at consumer brand agency Hope and Glory, points out that “A$AP Rocky becoming creative director for the Puma/F1 partnership demonstrated a strategic move into high fashion and streetwear”, and that Hamilton’s long-standing (and now finished) association with Tommy Hilfiger was a huge boon for Mercedes.

Adds Richard Exon of creative agency Joint: “For fashion brands, it’s an irresistible combination of glamour, jeopardy, celebrity and conspicuous wealth, played out across some of the world’s most aspirational destinations.”

Formula 1’s global fanbase has grown 12 per cent year-on-year, and it is getting younger and more female.

Formula 1 future

It has branched out way beyond the track and its traditional markets. Fashion, one expert says, has no language. But it’s clear Formula 1 is now seen as a showcase opportunity for the best and brightest in the luxury world – whether that be high-end or streetwear.

“F1’s global fanbase is still growing, so there’s more room to absorb additional brand partners without necessarily diluting, at least in the near term,” adds Oppermann, whose latest collection is available online. 

“It’s up to fashion brands to create meaningful partnerships and products that resonate with the sport’s audience. Ultimately, the equity that comes with being a F1 team partner signals credibility and ambition, and puts us in company with brands we admire.”

Amendments to Fifa’s Disciplinary Code from January 2027 have attracted attention, but most of the changes have already been binding for almost six months.

The May 2026 edition of the Code introduced changes affecting clubs, players, agents and their advisers, while January will introduce further changes around domestic enforcement.

The immediate exposure

Deadlines are one of the most important changes. Time limits now expire at midnight Eastern Standard Time on the final day rather than midnight Central European Time – in effect, six hours later than before.

A deadline falling on a weekend or US federal holiday rolls forward to the next working day, and Zurich public holidays no longer count. The risk is miscalculation: parties must now track a foreign time zone and the US holiday calendar.

The year-end pause no longer protects internal appeals. While most time limits remain paused between 20 December and 5 January, appeals under article 60 are excluded.

Take a club that receives the reasons for a decision on 19 December. Previously, the clock stopped the following day. Now the three-day window to announce an appeal runs on through the festive period.

A legal team away until 5 January could return to find the decision final, regardless of its merits, although there is some flexibility with extensions available in certain circumstances.

Decisions, appeals and sanctions

A single judge of the Disciplinary Committee may now decide any matter under the Code. A panel must now decide discrimination and match manipulation cases, unless the case is “deemed urgent”.

Doping cases no longer fall within that guarantee. They go directly to the Appeal Committee, removing one internal stage.

Internal appeals also carry greater cost risk. Proceedings before the Disciplinary Committee generally remain free, but before the Appeal Committee costs fall on the sanctioned party.

Where no sanction is imposed, costs are allocated according to the degree of success rather than automatically borne by Fifa.

For players or officials who admit to a discrimination offence, up to half their sanction may be converted into Fifa-approved educational, communication and training initiatives.

A team that leaves the field in protest at a refereeing decision, as we saw at in the Africa Cup of Nations final this year, now forfeits the match, with no replay.

Agents: creditors, sharper risk

Article 21, which sanctions failure to comply with decisions, now names football agents and match agents among the creditors it protects.

This gives an agent holding a Fifa or CAS decision over unpaid sums, such as commission, access to Fifa’s enforcement machinery.

In practice, this means that an agent with an unpaid award can ask Fifa’s Disciplinary Committee to act, potentially resulting in a club being barred from registering new players until it pays. During a transfer window, this creates significant leverage.

The same provision runs the other way: an agent who ignores a decision against him risks suspension of the licence he trades on.

What changes in January 2027?

The January 2027 edition, approved by the Bureau of the Fifa Council in June 2026, concerns decisions of national dispute resolution chambers (NDRCs) recognised under Fifa’s regulations.

Where a member association fails to enforce a final and binding decision of a recognised NDRC within 60 days, Fifa’s Disciplinary Committee becomes automatically competent to enforce it against the club or individual concerned. From January, Fifa can act directly where an association fails to do so.

A player who wins before his national chamber but remains unpaid can, after 60 days, take the matter to Fifa, which may impose a registration ban.

Important questions remain, including when the 60 days begin, how finality will be proved and whether the new route applies to decisions that became final before 1 January 2027.

Fifa’s disciplinary decisions are not routinely published, and appeals can take considerable time to produce a published award. The rules are live now, and the guidance on how they work may take a few years to emerge.

Nilo Effori is a sports lawyer and a partner at Brandsmiths.

John Healey has vowed not to let AI “leave workers behind” as he unveiled more than £600m in investment ahead of next week’s Budget, amid mounting concerns over AI-driven job losses.

The Treasury will commit £10m a year to studying the impact of AI on employment, alongside hundreds of millions of pounds for cyber security, British tech companies and domestic AI infrastructure.

The announcement comes just days after Barclays revealed plans to cut 5,000 jobs as part of an efficiency drive involving AI, adding to fears that the technology could accelerate redundancies across Britain’s biggest employers.

Healey said the government would take a “distinctively British approach to AI”, balancing its potential to boost economic growth with the need to protect workers.

“I understand and share the concerns of working people, so I am setting out a distinctively British approach to AI – one that doesn’t leave workers behind and defends our national interest, while ensuring the benefits of AI-enabled growth are felt right across the country,” he said.

The package, announced on Saturday ahead of Wednesday’s Budget, includes an additional £23m over three years for the AI Economics Institute, which will examine the technology’s effects on productivity and jobs.

It follows warnings from AI minister Kanishka Narayan that Britain must avoid repeating the painful transition experienced by workers during the Industrial Revolution.

AI security and British tech

The largest share of the funding will go towards strengthening Britain’s defences against emerging AI threats.

The Treasury has allocated £165m to a National AI Biosecurity Initiative, including £100m for a new laboratory using AI to detect biological threats and develop medical countermeasures.

The facility will also receive up to £200m in AI model credits from OpenAI and Anthropic, alongside partnerships with Google DeepMind and British life sciences firm Basecamp Research.

A further £120m will go to the AI Security Institute, while £60m will fund a National Cyber Shield using AI agents to strengthen cyber defences.

Ministers will also establish a £70m centre to identify vulnerabilities across critical national infrastructure.

The investment comes amid growing concern over the risks posed by increasingly autonomous AI systems.

Financial Conduct Authority chief executive Nikhil Rathi warned this week that emerging technologies were putting threats to financial markets “on steroids”, while regulators have called for greater oversight of AI failures and security risks.

The Chancellor is also committing an additional £60m to the Sovereign AI Fund to support British AI companies, expanding its remit to robotics, autonomous systems and advanced manufacturing.

Narayan said Britain could not afford to rely entirely on overseas technology.

“By backing British science, advanced chips and our own AI companies, we can strengthen our national security, rebuild Britain’s industrial strength and create good, skilled jobs across the country”, he said.

The package also includes £30m for local AI partnerships, a new cyber security training centre in Manchester and £15m for a competition rewarding AI innovations tackling health problems.

Julian David, chief executive of techUK, welcomed the investment, saying it would help British AI companies “grow here, not abroad”.

Frank and Percy with Ian McKellen at London Film Festival, review and star rating: ★★★★

Aged 87, Ian McKellen is gleefully avoiding being typecast by the sort of grandad-in-armchair roles most working actors of his age are weighed down with. And what a joy it is to see him careering about flirting with men 50 years his junior in Frank & Percy. In the drama, McKellen plays an older gent who chirpses much younger men he meets on grandad-themed dating websites, and forms a connection with a slightly younger man, played by Roger Allam.

Judged on the very capable work of McKellen alone, Frank & Percy is one of this year’s ripest pleasures. Hilarious as well as incredibly moving, rambunctious, mischievous Percy is a man you linger on. McKellen can still deliver bedroom eyes like his current accomplishment is the first man he’s ever made advances on, and it’s all especially appealing given he spends the movie cavorting around in Gen Z fashion (woolen peaked caps, tinted glasses, eccentric trainers). Oh, to have the zeal and self-belief of Ian McKellen at any age, let alone his!

Frank and Percy: Allan’s doe eyes

Adorably, there’s fact to this fiction: director Sean Mathias dated McKellen for a decade from 1978 to 1988, and is around the same age as Roger Allam’s Percy (City AM interviewed Mathias in 2023 for the release of the Frank and Percy stage show). You wonder which bits are made up and which are true in this gentle drama, following an aged pair of single gents who meet on Hampstead Heath while walking their dogs and form a friendship.

As for Allam, he does a very good pair of doe eyes as Frank, who looks like he’s processing a thousand thoughts a second as he contemplates the new worlds platformed by progressive, sexually-liberated Percy.

Mathias’ handsomely shot film has the old duo gallivanting around north London, Percy bounding in and out of his achingly middle class Georgian townhouse apartment and the duo perusing farmer’s markets and charity shops. It is a little twee, but honestly only a little bit; Martin Sherman’s screenplay (adapted from Ben Weatherill’s original stage play) is too filthy and hilarious to linger too long on sentiment. 

Ian McKellen shines

One of the funniest scenes follows Frank meeting a series of young admirers in a pub who he’s formerly spoken with online, including a potential suitor played by Ncuti Gatwa in a cameo role (yes, 34-year-old Ncuti Gatwa, who has a granddad fetish). Another, a suited corporate, asks Percy to call him his all sorts of explicit sexual things and McKellen, in a genius performance, raises an eyebrow just enough to illicit the terrible horny hopelessness of it all. To online date at any age is ghastly, but to grapple with it in your 80s! It’s brilliant in revealing the strange ways LGBTQ men can dehumanise one another in the pursuit of intimacy (as a gay man, I can attest to this). 

Sherman’s gently-does-it plot mostly swerves harder hitting stuff to prioritise queer joy. I think that’s right. Premiering at this year’s London Film Festival, Frank and Percy clearly doesn’t carry the emotional heft of Andrew Scott’s Elsinore, about the actor Ian Charleson who played Hamlet at the National Theatre in the months before his death from AIDS, but it does also platform a brilliant, lesser-known story (this time, about elderly LGBTQ love), and in that sense, it feels similarly fresh.

Frank and Percy is released in UK cinemas in 2027

The Supreme Court has blocked Tesco from appealing a key ruling in a long-running equal pay claim brought by more than 16,000 shop workers.

Tesco is one of several UK supermarkets caught in a legal battle over allegations that it underpays its store workers, mainly women, compared with distribution centre workers, who are mostly men.

The case, launched in 2018 by claimant-focused law firms Harcus Parker and Leigh Day, now involves thousands of retail employees in separate cases against Asda, Next, Sainsbury’s, Morrisons, and the Co-Op. It is reportedly worth a potential £4bn.

In the case against Tesco, the claims were divided into three stages, but the back-and-forth stems from the Employment Tribunal deciding to use generic training documents, rather than individual daily duties, to define ‘work’ at the hearings.

Tesco appealed through multiple courts to stop the Tribunal from using this definition. Both the Employment Appeal Tribunal and the Court of Appeal partially allowed Tesco’s appeals, but both rejected its main argument that the Tribunal’s overall methodology should be overturned.

The retail giant sought to appeal to the Supreme Court, but the UK’s top court rejected the case earlier this month and refused its application.

As a result, the case will proceed to trial under the Employment Tribunals’ established methodology for defining ‘work’.

Kiran Daurka, employment partner at Leigh Day, said: “This is a significant outcome for the 16,000 Tesco workers we represent and brings Tesco’s challenge on this issue to an end.” He added, “We remain focused on securing equal pay for our clients in the wider litigation.”

A Tesco spokesperson said: “The jobs in our stores and distribution centres are different. These roles require different skills and demands which lead to variations in pay, but this has absolutely nothing to do with gender.

“We are committed to rewarding our colleagues fairly for the jobs they do and work collaboratively with our colleagues and unions to ensure the pay and benefits we offer are fair, competitive and sustainable. Our position in relation to these claims remains unchanged and we continue to strongly defend them,” they added.

Next’s recent dodge in its equal pay case

Last month, retail giant Next won an appeal in its equal pay case, allowing it to pay warehouse workers more than shop-floor staff, and warned that its defeat “would have represented a hammer blow to retail employment in the UK”.

This follows a 2024 Employment Tribunal ruling that the FTSE giant failed to show that paying its sales consultants, most of whom are women, lower hourly rates than staff in its male-dominated warehouses was not sex discrimination.

The retailer was on the line for a £30m payout before it appealed.

But the Employment Appeal Tribunal overturned the landmark decision, citing recruitment and retention pressures that do not apply to sales workers.

With fiscal headroom under pressure, expect targeted support and modest tax rises in the Autumn Budget, leaving bigger decisions for next year, writes Philip Shaw.

John Healey’s first Budget on 28 October will test how the Government reconciles its ambitions with financial reality. Although the UK economy is on course to grow this year, the public finances leave little room for immediate generosity. We therefore expect a broadly neutral package that maintains the gradual fiscal tightening inherited from Rachel Reeves, with targeted spending financed by modest tax increases and larger decisions deferred until 2027.

Waiting could give the Chancellor a better foundation for those decisions. A new Spending Review would help ministers match their priorities to available resources, while forthcoming welfare reports could provide political cover for reforms and savings. An easing of the Gulf conflict might also relieve financial pressures. Meanwhile, next year’s shift in the fiscal target year could improve headroom by £6.7bn, based on the 2026 Spring Forecast.

The financial buffer could grow

For now, however, that headroom looks vulnerable. March’s forecasts implied a buffer of £24bn against the rule requiring a current budget surplus and £27bn against the debt rule, both of which remain in place despite the change in political leadership. Since then, higher gilt yields, interest rate expectations and inflation could have eroded up to £15bn of the Chancellor’s room for manoeuvre, limiting his ability to accommodate new commitments.

Will productivity forecasts change?

Productivity could eventually offer some relief, although we would not count on an immediate improvement in the forecasts. Revised official figures suggest output per hour grew considerably faster after the financial crisis than previously thought, potentially strengthening the outlook for tax revenues. With those revisions currently stopping at 2024, however, and changes to estimated hours worked complicating the picture, the Office for Budget Responsibility may prefer to await fuller evidence.

Its nearer-term forecasts are likely to send mixed signals. Growth this year has repeatedly exceeded expectations, making the OBR’s 1.1 per cent projection look low, but inflation also looks set for an upgrade this year and next. At Investec, our own inflation forecast for 2027 is 3.3 per cent. Higher earnings could bolster tax receipts, although uncertainty over how wages respond to rising prices makes the fiscal implications harder to judge.

Against that backdrop, household support should focus on those most exposed to higher energy costs. We expect targeted assistance rather than another expensive universal price cap, with a reported increase in the warm homes discount from £150 to £250 costing £600m. Extensions to electricity VAT relief, the fuel duty freeze and the temporary 5p duty cut are

also possible, underlining how difficult supposedly temporary concessions can become to withdraw.

The potential impact of new housing policies

Housing is another likely priority, through the Government’s “Your First Home” scheme. Eligible first-time buyers of participating new-build properties would receive a government-backed equity loan of 20 per cent, initially interest-free, alongside a deposit requirement of 2.5 per cent. Household income and local property price caps would target the support, while additional funding for council housebuilding could help address constraints on the supply of affordable homes.

Clarity should come

The Budget should also clarify how existing political commitments will be delivered. Prime Minister Andy Burnham has promised to prevent people relying solely on the state pension from becoming income taxpayers as pensions rise against a frozen personal allowance, but the mechanism and cost remain unspecified. Resources may also be allocated to regional devolution, while a £1.2bn annual defence equipment funding gap needs addressing separately from longer-term defence ambitions.

Help for businesses

For businesses, measures to encourage recruitment of young people, potentially through National Insurance relief, could accompany business rates reductions for smaller high street retailers. Such support would nevertheless need funding, and inherited plans already imply demanding spending restraint outside health and defence. We doubt ministers will try to balance the books by pencilling in future cuts so steep that their credibility becomes questionable.

Tax rises therefore look likely, although manifesto promises sharply constrain the choices. Employee National Insurance, income tax rates, VAT rates and the main corporation tax rate are protected, together accounting for more than three quarters of central government tax revenues. Alternatives include widening tax bases by charging National Insurance on earnings above retirement age, increasing gambling duties or requiring online marketplaces to collect VAT.

Sector-specific tax options

Banks and oil companies could also face additional taxes, while Capital Gains Tax changes remain possible through smaller rate increases or ending forgiveness at death. Full alignment with income tax appears to have been rejected, however, and entrepreneurs reinvesting in Britain might receive relief. Lowering the proposed mansion tax threshold also appears off the table, further narrowing the Chancellor’s revenue-raising options.

In conclusion: Expect little change

Ultimately, we expect a holding Budget that preserves confidence while addressing immediate needs and explaining how longer-term ambitions become affordable. Restraint now would allow the Chancellor to develop credible, funded plans for more substantial decisions next year, when conditions may be more favourable. The test is whether he can demonstrate progress towards the Government’s ambitions without making promises that the economy and public finances cannot support.

Baillie Gifford US Growth Trust has survived the third attempt by activist hedge fund Saba Capital to oust its board.

Shareholders quashed the efforts of the Boaz Weinstein-run fund to take control of the £1.1bn investment trust by a narrow margin, with 52.8 per cent voting against Saba’s resolution to appoint three of its nominees to the board.

Shareholders voted to retain the current board, a decision which chair of the company Tom Burnet argued reflected the “clear support” for the trust’s leadership and dislike for Saba’s repeated attempts to make changes at the top.

He said: “Repeatedly revisiting matters on which almost all of our independent shareholders have plainly already expressed their view places an unnecessary burden on the company, diverting management time and resources from the delivery of the company’s strategy and the creation of long-term shareholder value and incurring significant costs.”

US Growth Trust, whose portfolio includes the likes of SpaceX and Anthropic – noted that the votes against the resolution reached 99.2 per cent upon excluding the support of Saba and its ally Sessa Capital.

Saba swoops in

But the two hedge funds did successfully block two special resolutions on the disapplication of pre-emption rights, which would have given the board the right to issue or sell new shares without first offering them to existing shareholders, and share buybacks.

The resolutions required 75 per cent to pass, with both only receiving 63 per cent of votes in favour.

Burnet said the trust “looks forward to working constructively with Saba and Sessa” and is looking to secure a long-term solution with Saba, its largest shareholder.

The hedge fund’s latest attempt to wrest control of the fund is the latest in a string of efforts in the last two years to take over or shut down struggling investment trusts. It also follows several attempts by US Growth Trust to reach a settlement with Weinstein, including offering his fund an exit at net asset value of his stake in the trust.

In April, Edinburgh Worldwide Investment Trust (EWIT) – which was also managed by Edinburgh’s Baillie Gifford’s – conceded defeat to Saba, bringing its 17-month long battle to an end.

It succeeded in ousting EWIT’s board and chair Johnathan Simpson-Dent for its own three nominees.

Meanwhile, last month Gore Street Energy Fund narrowly survived an attempt by the notorious US hedge fund to wind-down.

Supermarkets have been caught off guard by the government’s “shambolic” campaign to urge Brits to stock up on supplies of food and water, industry sources told City AM. 

Retailers were not told the details of the government’s “Be Ready” campaign until days before it was announced and expected it to be a more “low key” affair, the people said.

Government officials briefed retailers on the date of this announcement only last week, the people said, telling bosses the campaign would be “low key” and fronted by security minister Dan Jarvis.

Though retailers were caught off guard by Streeting’s involvement, the defence secretary was not directly involved in the campaign’s launch and made his comments in response to media questions on the topic.

A bid to rip up European football’s rules on homegrown player quotas – likened to the landmark Bosman ruling – has been dismissed in a surprise move by a Belgian court.

The case, brought by Royal Antwerp and former player Lior Refaelov, had been expected to be upheld after the European Court of Justice gave it qualified backing in 2023.

Antwerp and Refaelov argued that homegrown quotas should be deemed illegal on the grounds that they infringed European freedom of movement and competition laws.

But the Court of First Instance of Brussels ruled that the rules were proportionate, justified by public interest objectives and did not excessively restrict the mobility of overseas players.

The decision has been welcomed by sports law experts concerned by the reluctance of European lawmakers to recognise the specificity of sport in the Bosman and Diarra rulings. 

“The judgment of the Belgium Court in the Royal Antwerp case on the legality of homegrown player rules should be welcomed by all those who have been calling for a common-sense approach to the application of European competition law and free movement principles to sporting rules,” Darren Bailey of Charles Russell Speechlys told City AM. 

He added: “At a time when uncertainty of outcome and competitive balance, two critical elements of what make sport special, are under threat from financially powerful superclubs, the approach of the Belgium Courts may be a sign that the concerns of European institutions and governments across Europe on the need to more robustly recognise the specificity of sport in legal disputes over its rules might finally have been heard by the judges.

“It is to be hoped that this case can pave the way out of a damaging disconnect between the European judiciary and sport which has undoubtedly contributed to many of the challenges confronting the sector today – not least an excessive pipeline of legal challenges which has created a culture of defensive regulation which is not in the sport or public interest.”

Royal Antwerp decision ‘a notable shift’

The Royal Antwerp ruling threatened to have major implications for Uefa nations, potentially including England, who require clubs to have a minimum number of nationally-trained players, as well as for Uefa rules governing the Champions League and other club competitions.

Uefa and all member FAs would have been forced to rewrite their rulebooks if the challenge had been upheld, while European football chiefs would also have faced a massive class action lawsuit, potentially running into the billions of pounds.

Jean-Louis Dupont, the lawyer who achieved the Bosman ruling that upended the transfer system three decades ago, was among those representing Royal Antwerp and Refaelov.

It was the latest major challenge to football’s regulatory framework in the European courts and followed the Diarra ruling, which forced Fifa to rewrite its global transfer rules and spawned the multi-billion-pound Justice For Players class action.

Bailey, the FA’s former director of governance and regulation, added: “In a notable shift of approach to recent cases, the Belgium Court, following a detailed analysis of the football impacts of the rules, found they could not be characterised as anti-competitive by object. 

“This was a significant finding since it opened the opportunity for the footballing authorities to justify the rules as being necessary and proportionate to the pursuit of legitimate public interest goals.

“Pleasingly, the court found it indisputable that the rules have the legitimate/public interest of encouraging the training of young players and maintaining competitive balance.”

Over 250 films, 33 world premieres, and 88 participating countries… City AM’s culture desk have rounded up the movies we saw at this year’s London Film Festival, which has wrapped for another year.

From legal dramas to terrifyingly prescient films about AI, alternative histories and horrors, here are our thoughts on the releases this year, and when you can see them too, as well as links to the full reviews.

London Film Festival: the movies to book

Wild Horse Nine

‘Two bumbling hitmen contemplate life and death on an ill-fated holiday’ could be the synopsis of Martin McDonagh’s near-perfect 2008 debut In Bruges, but in this instance it is in fact a synopsis of his new film Wild Horse Nine.

John Malkovich and Sam Rockwell replace Brendan Gleeson and Colin Farrell, each of them demonstrating large enough feet to fill those sizeable shoes. Opening in the American embassy in Chile in 1973, Wild Horse Nine is a kind of alternative history, following two boorish CIA agents, Chris Carlisle (Malkovich) and Lee Chesterfield (Rockwell) as they embark on a mission to Easter Island. Carlisle hints to anyone who will listen that he was involved in some historic event; Chesterfield wishes he’d keep his mouth shut, at least when they’re in public.

McDonagh is a master at combining high and low culture, with jokes about dwarfs playing basketball nested beside a broad Shakespearean sweep about the terrible passage of time and the futility of Western imperialism. I’m not sure it hits quite the same highs as In Bruges or Banshees, but Wild Horse Nine is another sad, funny, moving film by an astute chronicler of the human condition.
Read the full Wild Horse Nine review, in cinemas 6 November

Artificial

It isn’t typically a film’s duty to push a political agenda, but with Artificial, the biopic of OpenAI co-founder Sam Altman, there is a clear call to action. It is inevitable that people will ask: ‘What can this film do?’

Luca Guadagnino’s film is a disturbing portrait of AI, following the tech entrepreneur Sam Altman, who launched AI chatbot ChatGPT in 2022. Some leading scientists have claimed that the power and potential of these programmes means they could destroy humanity by the end of the 2020s.
A decade ago that would have been the stuff of science fiction movies, but in autumn 2026, Artificial feels terrifyingly prescient.

It is also very good. Andrew Garfield is superb as a psychopathically cocksure Altman. The Spider-Man actor nails how the business leader is impossible to decipher, always full of nervous energy, forever gyrating his hips, casting strange Cheshire cat grins, and glancing his eyes toward the sky. Neither emotionally or physically can you ever quite catch up.

“Rogue” AI agents from OpenAI are already threatening online security with the latest example being a flood of requests from their AI robots causing Wikipedia to temporarily go down. Artificial will surely be the talking point film of 2027, and is the closest look we’ve had at the charismatic, terrifying men at the heart of the AI revolution.
Read the full Artificial review, in cinemas 22 January

The NT at London Film Festival

Elsinore

Despite the rise of stories depicting the epidemic, the horrors of AIDS are still underrepresented in film and TV. Russell T Davies’ It’s A Sin brought freshness by focusing on fleeting moments of joy, and Simon Stone’s Elsinore borrows from that playbook with this magnificent story that follows one victim’s remarkable life.

Andrew Scott will now be celebrated not for his LGBTQ storytelling in All of Us Strangers, but for Elsinore, his focused, magnetic account of the true tale of Ian Charleson, the actor who played Hamlet at the National Theatre in 1989, seven weeks before he passed away from the disease.

Scott, who produces and stars, is devastatingly good as the man who would rather “die of Hamlet than of AIDS,” delivering agonisingly realistic blow-by-blow accounts of the pain Charleson was experiencing. Beresford’s script follows Charleson’s true, remarkable tale, as the actor prepares to take on the sword-bearing Prince of Denmark in spite of regular sicknesses that cause him to be bed bound in the weeks leading to opening night.

Almost 20,000 men died of AIDS in the UK alone before effective treatment came in in the mid-1990s. Andrew Scott is surely due an Oscar for the agonising detail examined in Elsinore, which sketches out a fresh rulebook for a new era of LGBTQ storytelling.
Read the full Elsinore review, in cinemas January 29

Prima Facie

In London, only three per cent of reported rapes lead to a suspect being charged. It is a fact so shocking that even people with no interest in the courts recite it. It is the problem that formed the backdrop of Suzie Miller’s very good play of the same name as this film, starring Killing Eve actor Jodie Comer, who in 100 minutes of theatre astonishingly played every character from the court judge to the victim.

Prima Facie follows Tessa Ensler, a criminal defence barrister who has become rich protecting men who are probably guilty of crimes by finding legal loopholes. But an incident in her personal life forces her to rethink the morality of her work.

Wicked’s Cynthia Erivo takes over from Comer for Susanna White’s big screen adaptation, alongside a supporting cast. Erivo is totally arresting as Ensler, bringing the sort of muscular fortitude that demonstrates how this young working class woman would graduate to this kind of job that’s typically reserved for the private schooled elite. She is also brilliant at conveying Ensler’s vulnerability; as she experiences a personal breakdown, Erivo’s angular, cocksure barrister softens, her eyes becoming wide chasms of overwhelm.

A terrific depiction of the injustices so many women face, and the truly harrowing plot.
Read the full Prima Facie London Film Festival review, in cinemas 13 November

Paper Tiger

Miles Teller and Adam Driver play Jewish brothers Irwin and Gary Pearl as they navigate a sepia-tinged 1980s New York. Irwin is the archetypal blue-collar worker, still a little in thrall to his retired cop brother. So when Gary arrives bearing a too-good-to-be-true business opportunity, Irwin jumps at the chance. The opportunity: helping a bunch of fresh-off-the-boat Russians with their oil disposal business in the dilapidated Brooklyn docks. What could go wrong?

The rest of the movie follows the brothers as they attempt to escape from the snare of these terrifying gangsters, the noose tightening at every turn.
Paper Tiger is at its heart a family drama. The Pearl brothers are both rivals and co-dependents; both have it all, yet they are willing to risk everything for a chance to get rich quick. The American Dream, baby!

The leads are predictably brilliant and the pacing is propulsive. There’s a sense of inevitability as these characters rattle towards their fates to the sound of ticking clocks and thumping machinery. It’s strange, then, that Gray’s ending feels borrowed from made-for-TV cop dramas, the final scenes visually stunning but narratively flat.
Read the full review for Paper Tiger review, in cinemas 5 February

More from London Film Festival…

Inherit

Our obsession with looking – and remaining – young is stretched to its horrifying logical conclusion in slick Thai horror film Inherit.

The Manasvanich family is in crisis over a chemical leak at their factory, which may or may not be causing birth defects in the local population: the last thing they need is an unexpected visit from a long-lost octogenarian relative. But when Grandma Woranart turns up, she is no little old lady – she’s a bombshell in eveningwear who makes everyone both horny and uncomfortable.

It doesn’t take long for everyone to realise that Grandma has sold her soul to an ageless centipede demon, and soon the chase is afoot: can the Manasvaniches exorcise this evil spirit before she claims another vessel – and will this secretive family survive intact?

It’s a smart and scary satire of our obsession with flawless skin, one that will feel as relevant in Birmingham or Bristol as it will in Bangkok.
Read the full Inherit review, in cinemas TBC

Rogue Trooper

Duncan Jones returns with Rogue Trooper, a lovingly crafted if strangely earnest love letter to pulp science fiction adapted from the cult-classic British anthology comic 2000 AD.

It’s rendered in computer animation and the first thing you notice is just how much Rogue Trooper looks like a video game, with an animation style that will be familiar to anyone who’s picked up a controller in the last ten years or so.

The first half of the film is essentially one long action sequence: the soldiers take out a fortress-sized tank, abseiling away as the thing explodes. Or they have a firefight amid a field of hallucinogenic gas, performing stealth take-downs while silhouetted against a dramatic psychedelic backdrop.

Its real strength, however, lies in its voice acting. Aneurin Barnard is wonderfully likeable as the lead and he’s supported by talent including Matt Berry (brilliant as always), Reece Shearsmith, Diane Morgan (slightly wasted), Jemaine Clement and Sean Bean. It’s briskly entertaining from start to finish and infused with such breathless adoration for science fiction that it’s hard not to be won over.
Read the full Rogue Trooper review, in cinemas TBC

Nightborn

British-Finnish production Nightborn revels in all the terrible functions of the human body: the blood and the guts and the secretions that we pretend are not the very fabric of our being. Around this theme Nightborn crafts a darkly funny allegory exploring the tribulations of new motherhood, with a particular focus on postnatal depression and postpartum psychosis.

We follow young-ish couple Saga and Jon (Seidi Haarla and Rupert Grint) as they arrive in a new home, having relocated from England to a huge, dilapidated house in her native Finland. But after Saga conceives their child during a spirited woodland romp, things quickly go south.

Nightborn’s biggest achievement is how effectively it places you in the mind of this struggling mother – we share her visceral dislike of her repulsive baby, with its guttural, animal-like cries and its clawed little fingers. Everybody else, however, thinks the baby is fine. A little too hairy, maybe, but mostly fine. So why does it crave human blood, wonders Saga?

There are also glimpses of the film Nightborn could have been but Bergholm seems unwilling to fully commit, instead leaving us alone for minutes at a time with a screaming infant, which isn’t much fun at all.
Read the full Nightborn review, which is in cinemas 30 October

The London Film Festival returns in October 2027

John Healey is not expected to rock the boat in his maiden Budget next week. Looking at the combustible bond market, that’s probably just as well, writes Ali Lyon.

John Healey is, the well-worn cliche goes, walking a tightrope.

Boxed in from three directions, the Chancellor could certainly have hoped for an easier backdrop in which to give his maiden Budget. From his left flank he will have to bat away the incessant demand for more public spending from backbench MPs and defence hawks. From his right, he will encounter the country’s business owners and workers, ensuring he makes good on his promise not to raise income tax, national insurance or VAT. All the while, he must stick to his predecessor’s fiscal rules and leave “a buffer against uncertainty” – or risk a market revolt.

With bond yields across the developed world sitting around multi-decade highs, it is this latter group that poses the most immediate risk to the Chancellor’s fate. Investors still – despite France and the US’s relentless profligacy – demand a higher interest rate for holding the UK’s debt than any other major economy. And that means that the Exchequer is now forced to fork out more than £110bn a year just to pay the interest on its insatiable appetite for the bond market’s cash.

Next to none of that, it should be said, is down to decisions made by Healey himself. Almost every recent occupant of No. 11 Downing Street, no matter their political creed, must shoulder part of the blame: after all, one’s interest bill is always going to be higher if the UK has more debt attracting that interest. Just as responsible, though, is the succession of inflationary geopolitical shocks – be that Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, the fiscal stimulus used to carry us through the pandemic and the US’s invasion of Iran – that leaves Healey battling against global forces pulling in the wrong direction. But that doesn’t change the fact it is the current Chancellor, now only in his 14th week in post, who must maintain credibility with the dispassionate, fickle investors willing to lend him their cash.

“The market is very tense,” says Cavendish’s head of equity strategy, Roger Lee. “It’s febrile. The public finances are such that… the scope for additional borrowing – certainly at any sort of reasonable rate – is virtually none.”

Healey’s Hippocratic Budget

The upshot is that, speak to any fixed income investor or economic analyst, and they will tell you that this must be a Budget that takes a fiscal Hippocratic oath: over and above anything else, it must do no harm.

“I would certainly prefer a Budget that avoids the temptation of having to raise taxes for the sake of doing something, and stick with the plans as as they are for now,” RSM UK’s economist Thomas Pugh tells City AM. “And I think that’s roughly where we are. Above all, we need to convince markets that the UK is not the next France, while also giving some support to households and businesses over winter.”

Pugh’s sentiment – very much the consensus view among investors – is largely the product of several recent Chancellors giving Healey helpful examples of what not to do. Especially instructive are the two hamfisted fiscal events overseen by his immediate predecessor, Rachel Reeves.

Her favoured ‘smorgasbord’ approach, of raising a mixture of small taxes while juicing borrowing for investment, generated unreliable revenues and cultivated a wave of sentiment-sapping speculation. Her maiden attempt in 2024 triggered a large gilt sell-off, as bond investors adjusted to £30bn of additional borrowing implied by her plans.

Simultaneously, the spectre of Liz Truss’s ignominious 2022 mini-Budget still haunts the corridors of the Treasury. The radical overhaul, for which she and Chancellor Kwasi Kwarteng dispensed of the Office for Budget Responsibility’s oversight and increased borrowing by £72bn, remains the undisputed pin-up for what can happen when you take the bond market for granted.

Inaction today may be unappealing to a new Prime Minister eager to improve living standards for the median voter. But, in the straitened, logic-bound world of fixed income, there is plenty to be said for, basically, doing nothing.

How is the UK economy doing?

Against a barrage of macroeconomic headwinds, the UK economy has been a standout performer relative to its peers. Official gross domestic product (GDP) figures have, almost without fail, beaten economists’ understandably dreary estimates this year. We have enjoyed the fastest growth of any G7 country this year, and even our long-suffering labour market is showing signs of life.

Fiscally, we are off monetary authorities’ naughty step too. Britain’s deficit reduction plan is more ambitious than its spendthrift peers, which James Carter, co-head of fixed income at W1M, says has helped gilts to outperform almost all government bonds going into next week.

“The ‘moron premium’ embedded in UK gilts has been steadily eroding over recent months,” he tells City AM, adding that political and economic woes afoot in the likes France have helped boost the UK’s credibility. “The Budget is another opportunity to reinforce that rehabilitation.”

If a “do nothing, kicking the can” Budget, as Cavendish’s Lee frames it, is what bond market participants want, it is also what they expect. There is a near unanimous belief among investors that Wednesday 28 October will come and go without any significant plans for more bond issuance emerging.

“I suspect we’ll just see chess pieces moving around the board at not a huge amount coming out of it,” says Oliver Faizallah, head of fixed income research at Raymond James, “I feel like Healey and Burnham now get the fiscal situation, and they don’t want to make any rash decisions because they know the bond market will be extremely nervous about it.”

Any rabbit could trigger ’emergency Budget’

As overwhelming as that view appears to be, the precarious state of the UK’s public finances mean that there remain areas of concern. In Faizallah’s eyes, any attempt at breaking “the spirit of the fiscal rules” would risk a negative reaction, even if technically it conformed to them.

Early on in the 12-week Budget preparation period, the Chancellor was rumoured to be considering approving fresh bond market-funded borrowing to fund so-called ‘public financial institutions’, or PuFins. While not a breach of the letter of the spending rules, the gilt investors would “see through that”, Faizallah says.

Worries also abound that Healey may succumb to the age-old tradition of pulling a ‘rabbit out of the hat’, and save an unexpected spending announcement for the speech itself. That could be an uplift in defence spending, bringing the UK closer to its plan to devote three per cent of GDP to defence by 203. Or it could be a step towards Burnham’s avowed goal to bring more utilities into public ownership.

To do anything along those lines would be to miscalculate the bond market’s capacity for more borrowing, warns Lee, even if ministers could technically frame it as investment. “Issuance is issuance,” he says. “I think the risk is also that they mismatch between your tax raising proposal, which has uncertainty in terms of how much it will yield, versus a spending commitment that is certain.”

Were any of that to happen, then the tinder-box bond market could re-ignite to such an extent that Healey is forced to patch it up. “If we do get that, then the bond market will fight back,” says Faizallah. “And I think there will need to be a revision of some sort – going back to the drawing board.

“But that’s not our base case – Healey’s too long in the tooth for that.”

The Betting and Gaming Council (BGC) told City AM that the comments, which appeared in a draft report by the Social Market Foundation (SMF), raised concerns about whether the impact on jobs and high streets had been properly assessed.

“The reported internal comments raise serious questions about the evidence being used to justify further tax increases and whether the full consequences for jobs, businesses and high streets have been properly considered”, a BGC spokesperson said.

The row comes as Chancellor John Healey considers raising Machine Games Duty, a tax on gambling machines in betting shops, casinos and other venues, in next Wednesday’s Budget.

The SMF has called for the duty to double from 20 to 40 per cent, arguing that the move could raise up to £458m annually while helping to address gambling-related harm. In one exchange, SMF director Theo Bertram questioned a claim that jobs lost through gambling venue closures would be offset by employment elsewhere. “Is this overly optimistic? What’s the basis for the confidence that they will find jobs elsewhere?” he wrote.

Chief economist Gideon Salutin replied that the analysis did not guarantee affected workers would find alternative employment, but maintained that overall employment would grow.

The draft also acknowledged that gambling operators could close venues in response to higher taxes, while Salutin confirmed that bingo halls and seaside arcades would be affected.

The BGC said the comments strengthened its warnings about the potential economic consequences of a further tax increase.

Independent modelling commissioned by the industry body from EY estimates that doubling the duty could put almost 1,500 betting shops and 34 casinos at risk, cost up to 16,000 jobs and leave the Treasury £124m worse off.

Since entering Downing Street in July, John Healey has faced criticism from some business chiefs over an economic vision that seems similar to Rachel Reeves.

Officials attached a figure to this cost, with the impact for households and businesses running into the billions of pounds, as one Treasury source said. The analysis covered pension pots, financial markets and other crucial investment decisions. 

When asked about what’s coming in the Budget, Healey has tended to shake his head, frown and tell reporters that speculation had “real-world impacts”. He said an early Budget on 28 October – a month earlier than last year’s – would help squash the rumour mill, a decision welcomed by a range of key business voices. 

It’s a far cry from Budget 2025.

Healey learns from Reeves’ mistakes

Reeves, who is still a sitting MP despite maintaining some distance from Westminster, got dealt a difficult hand. While higher inflation and stronger wage growth figures helped to boost tax receipt projections, her fiscal buffer was all but wiped out by a £16bn productivity growth downgrade by the Office for Budget Responsibility, the fiscal watchdog.

The decision to revise output forecasts, made months before the Budget was delivered, led to a huge split between Treasury policymakers and independent analysts at the OBR. The two months before the Budget led to what has widely been perceived as an exercise in kite-flying, whereby tax ideas are leaked to the media to gauge public opinion and investors’ reactions. Bank stocks and government bond yields yo-yoed as media outlets pumped out new briefings sourced from Whitehall. 

Reeves also had herself to blame as her fiscal arithmetic set the conditions for high levels of speculation. Speaking to City AM last year, former OBR official Sir Charlie Bean said was “asking for trouble” by leaving herself with headroom of just £9.9bn at the previous fiscal statement in March 2025. By the autumn, half of that buffer was gone following an embarrassing Labour U-turn on £5bn welfare cuts, regardless of the OBR’s decision to downgrade growth forecasts. 

Reeves learned her lesson, building in a headroom against a borrowing target of about £23.6bn. Healey can now partly reap the benefits. Even as the Iran war has put public finances under strain, he is not expected to make significant tax increases given his headroom is estimated at around £12bn as a result of higher borrowing costs and a raft of spending pledges on defence investment and the cost of living. 

Nevertheless, Healey has taken every precaution to ensure businesses and families are not pushed to take rash, irreversible decisions such as withdrawing cash from pension pots, selling businesses or overhauling spending plans. It has also been widely reported that the Chancellor has introduced unprecedented security measures to stop Budget leaks, borrowing protocols from his old job at the Ministry of Defence. This has included changing software settings and limiting the number of people who could access documents, according to the Financial Times.

An endeavour to keep plans a secret has spoken to Healey’s care for security and discipline. All eyes will be laser-focused on whether he applies these attributes to his administration of public finances and the UK economy.

The IFR’s costs will be recouped via a tax on clubs from next year, with those teams earning the most set to contribute the biggest portion of the £20.3m annual levy.

The levy represents around 0.2 per cent of football’s annual revenues of £9bn in 2025-26, the IFR said. Championship clubs not in receipt of parachute payments will pay around £45,000, League One teams £9,000 and League Two sides £6,000.

That levy is made up of £18.3m in annual operating expenses, phased recovery of the government’s costs incurred in setting up the IFR, and a £1m fund for litigation.

If the IFR requires additional funds for litigation – for instance, if it faced a legal challenge to any possible decision to disqualify Manchester City’s owners – it would request an advance from the Treasury, with that sum to be recouped via an increased levy in future years.

Total sales at retailers fell 0.4 per cent in September, according to the Office for National Statistics (ONS), a bigger drop than the 0.1 per cent forecast by City economists.

It follows a surge in August, which the ONS revised upwards to 0.7 per cent from 0.5 per cent previously. September’s slowdown was triggered by a slump at non-food stores and online spending, where volumes declined 0.4 per cent.

Firms reported lower sales and footfall as customers cut back on non-essential purchases. It comes as new data from GfK shows UK consumer confidence suffered its biggest fall since the Brexit vote in 2016.

The firm’s long-running consumer confidence index fell 11 points to -24 in September. Neil Bellamy, consumer insights director at GfK, said there was “an extraordinary collapse” in confidence.

Paul Dales, chief UK economist at Capital Economics, said: “October’s sharp fall in consumer confidence and the dip in retail sales volumes in September show that times are getting tougher for households just as the all-important festive period for retailers is just around the corner.”

Retail industry braces for the Budget

Retailers have been on fragile footing ahead of the Chancellor John Healey’s maiden Budget, set to take place on the 28 October.

Growing fears of inflation and rising interest rates have worsened consumer sentiment, prompting businesses to warn that they cannot encourage spending any more without tax cuts. 

Bosses have urged the government to exclude high street shops from the highest business rates multiplier and roll back recent hikes to employer national insurance contributions (NICs).

Thierry Garnier, chief executive of B&Q owner Kingfisher, wrote in City AM that the company’s provision of work experience placements for young people “depends on what the Chancellor decides in this Budget”.

Automotive fuel was the sole major sector to buck the September slump for retail sectors, showing volume growth despite climbing prices at the pump.

Brits have been forced to swallow higher fuel prices following the spike in oil prices driven by the US-Iran war. The pressure on fuel prices is expected to continue into the final quarter with the average price of diesel in the UK reaching a record high of £2.01 per litre in early October.
