Avenda Health said it designed Surgery Mode to enhance how surgeons use 3D AI mapping during non-robotic and robotic surgeries, alongside new tools to simplify patient case management and physician workflows.

The launch builds on peer-reviewed research predicting that Unfold AI could cut positive surgical margins in half, substantially reducing cancer recurrence. In the study, the system outperformed MRI and other modalities in assessing whether cancer had spread beyond the prostate, assisting surgeons in making nerve-sparing decisions.

In Surgery Mode, physicians can now access enlarged 3D views for clearer visualization, adjust the cancer estimation map to match the camera angle on the surgical console, review underlying MRI slices during the procedure, and access capsule risk scores from within a dedicated surgical view.

Avenda Health claimed that Unfold AI is the only platform implementing multimodal AI to analyze a patient’s MRI, biopsy, pathology, and PSA together. It produces a personalized 3D map of the cancer’s extent to provide surgeons with more precise visualization of tumor boundaries.

While Unfold AI has served as a decision-support tool during preoperative consultations, the latest expansion gives surgeons an enhanced version of these maps during prostate procedures. The suite of improved workflow tools also gives physicians and staff greater visibility into the status of each patient case.

  • Redesigned patient list and case filters: Improved patient organization and updated case status labels let users search for cases in progress, add new patients, and filter by status to see where each case stands at a glance.
  • Improved administrative control: New built-in tools let staff verify insurance approvals and confirm administrative steps are complete before 3D map generation.
  • Streamlined case management: Care teams can now add and view patient notes directly from the patient list and update the assigned physician on a patient report.

Unfold AI helps doctors identify tumor extent

Avenda Health said the expanded features extend Unfold AI’s reach across the prostate cancer care pathway, including active surveillance, focal therapy, surgical interventions, and radiotherapy. Its interactive 3D maps serve as a visual guide for patient counseling and decision support, helping patients and physicians confidently select their treatment path.

Now, with Surgery Mode, the same patient-specific mapping technology can be used to provide clear visual boundaries in the operating room, actively guiding surgical procedures such as robotic prostatectomies.

Unfold AI predicts the cancer’s spread into nearby anatomy with 92% accuracy, compared with 52% using MRI alone. That spatial clarity is central to helping surgeons determine whether a nerve-sparing or non-nerve-sparing surgery should be performed.

Avenda noted that additional research demonstrated that Unfold AI improves physician identification of tumor extent, increasing sensitivity from 37% to 97%. By expanding Unfold AI from preoperative decision support into the operating room, the company said it is developing more precise views of prostate cancer that can support physicians across different stages of care.

Credit: Daimon Robotics

Vision has become central to modern robotics, but cameras alone cannot tell a robot everything it needs to know about physical contact. When handling flexible objects, inserting components, or manipulating delicate items, robots need information about forces, slippage, and contact that visual systems may miss. 

Daimon Robotics wants to provide the infrastructure to help robots develop that capability. 

Rather than focusing exclusively on tactile sensors or developing a single foundation model, the company is building a pipeline that connects tactile sensing, data collection, simulation, and AI models. Its goal is to turn physical interactions into useful training data that helps robots perform manipulation tasks more reliably. 

“By building tactile intelligence, we’re actually playing the role as an infrastructure provider,” Daimon’s Partner & VP of Technology Dr. Zhu told The Robot Report. “We’re not aiming to be a foundation model developer. We are providing the infrastructure for doing so for those downstream customers.” 

That distinction is central to Daimon’s strategy: develop the tools and data infrastructure that other companies can use to build more capable robotic systems.

Building a pipeline for tactile data

Collecting useful tactile data at scale presents a challenge. Unlike visual data, which can be captured relatively easily with cameras, tactile data depends on physical contact. The resulting information varies with an object’s material, geometry, the forces applied, and the task being performed.

Daimon is developing a pipeline to capture and process these interactions, with tactile feedback operating at 30 Hz. The company is also working to connect real-world data with simulation, allowing physical interactions to inform training in virtual environments. 

The sim-to-real gap remains a significant challenge, particularly when accurately reproducing physical properties such as friction and contact forces. Daimon’s approach starts by calibrating simulations against real-world measurements before transferring collected data into simulated environments. 

“Let’s be frank; it’s not good enough. It’s kind of terrible,” Zhu said of the current state of simulation, referring to the gap between simulated and real-world environments. 

Daimon is developing tactile simulations that account for physical properties measured through real-world testing. The goal is to improve the fidelity of those simulations and make it easier to transfer learned capabilities to physical robots. 

The company has discussed collecting more than 10,000 hours of data, with its longer-term Daimon-Infinity initiative targeting more than 1 million hours of tactile embodied data. 

Zhu also emphasized the importance of working with companies developing robotic models and applications. 

“Doing everything ourselves was not enough,” he said. “Collaborating internationally in different downstream scenarios is really important.”

That collaboration helps Daimon understand what other developers need from its sensors, data-collection devices, software, and evaluation tools.

Credit: Daimon Robotics

From tactile demonstrations to industrial applications

Daimon is targeting manipulation tasks such as assembly and packaging, where robots must respond to physical contact rather than simply follow predetermined trajectories. 

A robot might need to determine whether a component is properly seated, detect when an object slips, or adjust its movements when a part behaves unexpectedly. Tactile feedback can help it respond to these conditions. 

The company demonstrated applications involving delicate manipulation at IROS 2026, including applying heat-transfer designs to tote bags and threading bracelets. It also showed a robot collecting and packaging broken glass, illustrating how models trained on data from varied scenarios can be prompted to perform specific tasks. 

Daimon uses its Umi device to collect data from human interactions. Zhu said the company’s demonstrations were powered by foundation models trained on data collected across multiple scenarios, rather than being built solely around individual robot demonstrations.

The company has identified Lenovo Capital and Inovance Technology as key partners. Zhu said Daimon has also moved beyond proof-of-concept projects into industrial assembly lines and warehouses, although he declined to name specific customers because of nondisclosure agreements. 

The commercial test is whether tactile sensing and the models built around it can improve performance consistently in production environments, where robots must handle variations in objects, materials, and operating conditions. 

Moving beyond visual perception

Daimon’s broader strategy centers on developing models that can use tactile information to understand and respond to physical interactions. 

Its Daimon-TWM effort focuses on a tactile-grounded world model intended to help robots reason about physical interactions, rather than relying on visual perception alone. 

Recognizing an object is only part of manipulation. A robot must also understand how its actions affect that object and adjust when the physical result differs from expectations. Tactile feedback can help close that loop by providing information about contact and the consequences of an action. 

Zhu described two roles for tactile sensing in robotic systems: helping models reason about physical properties and enabling rapid adjustments during contact-intensive tasks. The latter can require high-frequency feedback, with Daimon targeting control at 30 Hz. 

The company is also exploring how data collected through human interactions can help train models for different robot configurations, including humanoids and dual-arm manipulators. 

But collecting data and training models are only part of the problem. Developers must still demonstrate that these systems generalize across different objects, materials, robots, and operating conditions. 

Scaling touch for robotics

The broader question facing the robotics industry is what infrastructure is needed to make physical AI work reliably outside controlled demonstrations. 

Companies are investing heavily in vision-language-action models, simulation, and large-scale robot training datasets. Touch adds another dimension, particularly for robots that must manipulate objects through physical contact. 

Daimon aims to build part of the infrastructure connecting sensing, data, simulation, and intelligence. Its strategy is to support the companies developing robotic systems rather than compete directly with them to build the next general-purpose robotic brain. 

Its success will depend on whether that approach measurably improves manipulation, reduces the effort required to develop new applications, and supports deployments across different industrial environments. 

Zhu was careful not to overstate the capabilities of today’s models. Even when trained on large datasets, he said, their ability to generalize remains limited. 

“The model is not as intelligent as we think,” Zhu said. “It has some generalization ability, but it was in-domain generalization sometimes.”
He added that embodied-intelligence models are still in development, and that collecting data from similar tasks can help them generalize to new applications. 

For Daimon, the challenge is turning that emerging capability into reliable performance across a broader range of real-world tasks.

]]> Finnish SpaceTech unicorn ICEYE has announced two new partnerships aimed at expanding its satellite intelligence capabilities across defence and environmental monitoring.

The company signed a Letter of Intent alongside Nokia and Ukraine’s Ministry of Defence to explore sovereign satellite communications, while also announcing a collaboration with German startup OroraTech to develop an integrated wildfire intelligence solution.

This follows a period of notable growth for the Espoo-based scale-up. In June 2026, ICEYE secured €450 million in primary Series F funding, valuing the company at more than €10 billion, with a further €300 million revolving credit facility secured in May.

This funding activity can be placed alongside adjacent 2026 European SpaceTech funding announcements, including €51 million for Luxembourg and US-based Hydrosat to expand thermal satellite intelligence, €34 million for the UK’s SatVu to scale its thermal observation constellation, and €61 million for Switzerland’s SWISSto12 to develop satellite and communications infrastructure.

In Finland, Helsinki-based Kelluu also raised €15 million to expand its autonomous aerial intelligence capabilities.

Together with funding for France’s UNIVITY (€27 million) and Germany’s AIRMO (€5 million), these 2026 rounds account for approximately €643 million in the general SpaceTech sector, including ICEYE’s primary financing.

Founded in 2014 by Rafal Modrzewski and Pekka Laurila, ICEYE specialises in synthetic aperture radar (SAR) satellite technology, providing Earth observation data and intelligence to governments, defence organisations, insurers and emergency management agencies.

The company originated from research at Aalto University and launched its first SAR satellite in 2018, becoming an early pioneer in miniaturised radar satellites.

The first of the two announcements centres on a Letter of Intent signed by ICEYE, Nokia and Ukraine’s Ministry of Defence to explore cooperation on secure satellite communications. Announced during the Finnish Prime Minister’s visit to Ukraine, the initiative aims to strengthen the country’s defence capabilities by developing communications infrastructure that Ukraine can independently own and control.

The agreement builds on an earlier partnership between ICEYE and Nokia, announced on October 1st 2026, to develop secure, high-performance broadband communications systems using low Earth orbit (LEO) satellites. Designed for governments, these systems would support defence, border security, emergency services and disaster response, while giving participating countries control over their satellites, ground infrastructure and terminals.

Rafal Modrzewski, CEO and Co-founder of ICEYE, said: “Ukraine needs secure, sovereign and high-performance satellite communications systems that it controls. We have a proven track record of delivering sovereign missions at speed to help build that capability. ICEYE has proudly supported Ukraine since 2022, and we remain committed to continuing that support today.”

ICEYE has supported Ukraine with satellite intelligence since 2022, making the proposed communications collaboration a potential extension of an existing relationship. The latest agreement remains exploratory, with no deployment timetable or financial commitments disclosed.

Alongside its defence-related developments, ICEYE has also partnered with Munich-based OroraTech to expand its wildfire intelligence services. The collaboration will combine OroraTech’s thermal satellite data with ICEYE’s SAR observations, creating a platform intended to help organisations monitor wildfires from their earliest stages through to damage assessment and recovery.

Founded in 2018 by Thomas Grübler, Rupert Amann, Florian Mauracher and Björn Stoffers, OroraTech develops space-based thermal intelligence for wildfire detection and monitoring. The startup has expanded its satellite network and provides information to governments and organisations managing wildfire risks worldwide.

As per our coverage, OroraTech secured a €37 million Series B extension in 2025.

Until now, ICEYE’s wildfire intelligence capabilities have primarily focused on assessing building-level damage during active fires. By incorporating OroraTech’s thermal observations, the company aims to extend its services to include identifying initial hotspots, tracking fire progression and assessing threats to communities and critical infrastructure.

The combination brings together two complementary technologies. OroraTech’s thermal satellites can detect heat anomalies and monitor active fires, while ICEYE’s SAR satellites can capture observations through clouds, smoke and darkness, helping assess damage to buildings and infrastructure even while a wildfire is ongoing.

Dr. Ignacio Zuleta, Chief Technology and Product Officer at OroraTech, commented: “Our thermal satellite intelligence provides that critical visibility from the earliest stages of an event, detecting hotspots and tracking fire activity as it develops. By bringing that intelligence together with ICEYE’s SAR capabilities, we can help decision-makers maintain a more continuous understanding of a wildfire, from first detection through its impact on communities, infrastructure and the surrounding environment.”

The integrated solution targets several sectors, including government emergency management, utilities and insurance. Emergency services could use the intelligence to inform evacuations and coordinate firefighting resources, while energy providers could monitor threats to electricity networks and other infrastructure. Insurers could also use the data to identify exposed properties, assess damage and prioritise claims.

According to ICEYE, the technology could help accelerate disaster response by providing more timely information on wildfire progression and its consequences. The company says its integrated approach could support damage assessments for disaster declarations within 24 hours, compared with processes that can otherwise take weeks.

Taken together, the two announcements are one of many examples of how ICEYE is expanding its satellite capabilities beyond Earth observation imagery into a broader range of intelligence and communications services.

]]> Phononic Vibes, a Milan-based noise management company that designs and manufactures noise and vibration products for rail, energy, industry, construction and mobility, has secured a €25 million financing round. The company has also launched its new identity and website today. 

The round was led by Jolt Capital, a Paris-based private equity firm specialising in DeepTech growth companies, through Jolt Capital V, a fund targeting €1 billion and nearing final close. Eureka! Venture SGR, CDP Venture Capital SGR, and Simest SpA also participated in this round. The transaction includes the acquisition of 360 Capital’s stake, which it has held since the company’s Seed round. In 2020, the company announced the closing of a €2.3 million funding round.

Andrea Traversone, Managing Partner at Jolt Capital, said, “Noise control is reaching a turning point. Conventional products have hit their physical limit, and infrastructure needs quieter assets with less weight and space. Phononic Vibes is a company combining breakthrough science, a patented design engine and manufacturing at scale. We are excited to back the team in building a global leader in noise and vibration control. This is Jolt Capital V’s first investment in Italy, a country with an increasingly dynamic and vibrant deeptech ecosystem.”

Founded in 2018 by Luca D’Alessandro, Giovanni Capellari, and Stefano Caverni as a spin-off of Politecnico di Milano, the company manufactures in Italy and leads a group of established European manufacturers, including Matis, founded in 1979.

The company designs and manufactures noise and vibration products that do the same job with less material. According to the company, every noise barrier, enclosure, and silencer on the market obeys the mass law: more quiet means more material. Phononic Vibes claims to break it.

It designs metamaterials, structures whose shape does the work mass used to do. Its products weigh up to 30% less while delivering the same acoustic performance, or they perform better at the same weight.

At the core of the company is a proprietary design engine, protected by 18 patent families. “It turns the physics of metamaterials into certified products, drawing on application libraries that grow with every project, so each new market starts from proven designs rather than a blank sheet,” the company mentioned in the press release 

The company highlighted that Deutsche Bahn certified its transparent noise barrier for the German rail network, the first see-through panel it rates as highly absorbing. Phononic Vibes. It also reports that Mercedes-Benz uses its technology in series production, which the company says is the first metamaterial in a series-production car. Contractors such as Webuild and Eteria choose its barriers because they install faster. Its revenue has doubled every year since 2018, reaching break-even in 2025.

Luca D’Alessandro, CEO and co-founder of Phononic Vibes, said, “Weight has always been the price of quiet. We have shown it is a design choice, with two of Europe’s most demanding customers. With Jolt Capital by our side in this new chapter, and the continued support of our existing investors Eureka! Venture SGR, CDP Venture Capital and Simest, we can accelerate our international growth, expand into new applications and make lighter noise control the standard across data centres, rail, energy and industry. I would also like to thank 360 Capital for believing in us from the early days, when we were still working at the desks of Politecnico di Milano, and for being part of the journey that brought us here.”

The company plans to use this capital to scale its proprietary design engine internationally, expand its technology into new applications and strengthen its delivery capabilities.  Phononic Vibes also notes that targeted acquisitions will complement this strategy by extending the reach of its technology and bringing additional industrial capabilities to the group.

]]> As Ukraine continues to defend itself against Russia’s invasion, European startups are developing technologies ranging from autonomous drones and air-defence systems to satellite intelligence, with venture capital playing an increasingly important role in supporting defence innovation.

EU-Startups’ reporting on European DefenceTech and adjacent dual-use technologies has identified more than €1.8 billion in financing across 22 European startups in 2026, as of October.

Drawing on EU-Startups’ coverage, we’ve put together a list of European startups that secured funding in 2026 and are contributing to Ukraine’s defence efforts, alongside the investors backing them. Together, this list represents over €1 billion of funds raised for direct intervention in Ukraine.

And stay tuned: we have an upcoming EU-Startups Podcast episode featuring one of the startups on this list!

The Defenders

DOD Solution – Estonia/Ukraine: Founded in 2023, DOD Solution is an Estonian-Ukrainian DefenceTech startup developing AI-powered autonomy for unmanned systems. Its AURA AI platform combines onboard computing and software to provide autonomous navigation, target recognition and tracking, even when GPS signals or communications are unavailable. Unlike technologies still awaiting frontline validation, AURA AI has already been used in combat in Ukraine.

In September 2026, the company raised €1.8 million in pre-Seed funding from Angel One Fund, Better Angle, Defence Builder Fund, Network VC, Newfund, UAID Fund, WildField Ventures and 4C-Next Holding AG, alongside strategic investor Draganfly. The financing will support product development and further integrations with Ukrainian drone manufacturers.

Frankenburg Technologies – Estonia: Founded in 2024 and headquartered in Tallinn, Frankenburg Technologies develops affordable, mass-manufacturable missile defence systems intended to counter drones and other aerial threats. Co-founded by Taavi Madiberk and Marko Virkebau, the startup is developing its Mark I short-range interceptor missile, with an emphasis on reducing production costs and increasing manufacturing capacity. Its operations extend across eight countries, including Ukraine, reflecting its ambition to manufacture defensive systems closer to where they are needed.

In February 2026, Frankenburg secured €30 million in Series A funding led by Plural, with participation from SmartCap, bringing its reported total funding to €40 million.

ICEYE – Finland: Founded in 2014 and headquartered in Espoo, ICEYE develops and operates synthetic aperture radar (SAR) satellites capable of capturing high-resolution imagery regardless of weather conditions or daylight. Its technology supports defence intelligence and battlefield monitoring, including for Ukraine’s armed forces, which benefit from satellite imagery to improve situational awareness.

In January 2026, ICEYE expanded its cooperation with Ukraine’s Ministry of Defence to provide additional space-based intelligence. In June, the company announced a €450 million primary Series F investment led by General Atlantic, with investors including Solidium, Tesi, Varma, Ilmarinen, Lifeline Ventures, Nokia, QIA and TCV. The Scaleup Europe Fund, managed by EQT, was subsequently identified as a co-lead. Including secondary transactions, the financing exceeded €1 billion.

Occam Industries – United Kingdom: Founded in 2025 and based in London, Occam Industries develops autonomous drone technology designed to reduce reliance on human pilots in battlefield conditions. Its OccamX platform uses computer vision to enable FPV drones to navigate and track targets without continuous manual control or GPS connectivity. Occam has also completed initial testing through Ukraine’s Brave1 defence innovation cluster, opening the door to integration trials with Ukrainian drone manufacturers and potential deployment with the country’s armed forces.

In February 2026, the startup raised €3 million in pre-Seed funding led by Presto Tech Horizons, with participation from Antler, Freedom Fund, TYR.vc and defence-sector angel investors.

PDKINEMATICS – Lithuania: Founded in 2025 and headquartered in Vilnius, PDKINEMATICS develops precision-guidance systems for unmanned aerial vehicles, helping drones operate more accurately in environments affected by electronic warfare. Its flagship Gannet technology enables UAVs to release munitions from higher altitudes without sacrificing accuracy. The startup has partnered with Ukrainian drone manufacturer Bavovna.ai, integrating its systems into platforms already deployed in battlefield conditions.

In June 2026, PDKINEMATICS secured €2 million in Seed funding co-led by Coinvest Capital and Iron Wolf Capital, bringing its total funding to €3 million. The investment will support increased manufacturing capacity and further deployments across Ukraine and European defence markets.

Quantum Systems – Germany: Founded in 2015 and based near Munich, Quantum Systems develops AI-powered unmanned aerial systems and software for military reconnaissance and autonomous operations. The company has an established presence in Ukraine, where its drones reportedly completed more than 19,000 missions during 2025.

In July 2026, it announced a €1 billion Series D round co-led by Blackstone, Noteus, Airbus and Advent, with backing from BOND, Fidelity, Wellington Management, A.P. Moller Holding, Elephant Lake Ventures, Balderton and HV Capital. Its Ukrainian operations are also expanding: in October 2026, EU-Startups reported plans for tens of thousands of Germany-funded interceptor drones to be manufactured in Ukraine.

Shotling – Denmark: Danish DefenceTech startup Shotling develops short-range counter-drone systems designed to protect military personnel, vehicles and infrastructure against FPV drones and loitering munitions. Its electrically driven rotary shotgun system uses a high-capacity magazine and is designed for integration into mobile or stationary defence platforms. The technology addresses a challenge encountered by Ukrainian forces: intercepting inexpensive attack drones without relying on disproportionately costly defensive systems.

In February 2026, Shotling announced €700k in pre-Seed financing led by Myriad Defense Fund, with participation from IPO CLUB’s Fund II America 2030 and a non-dilutive match-loan from EIFO. The startup has reportedly received support from Ukrainian frontline units and defence companies, although operational deployment details have not been disclosed.

Special Mention

Varangians – Sweden: Beyond the startups developing defence technologies, Stockholm-based Varangians represents a more direct route for European venture capital into Ukraine’s DefenceTech ecosystem. Co-founded by Pär Lager, Andreas Flodström and Jonas Rydin alongside a Swedish family office, the investment fund announced a close of more than €10 million in June 2026, specifically to support Ukrainian defence innovation.

Its portfolio includes Norda Dynamics, which develops autonomous drone piloting technology for communications-denied environments; Himera, specialising in electronic-warfare-resistant secure communications; and Sine Engineering, which builds UAV communication and positioning systems capable of operating under jamming and interference.

]]> Cognitive Credit, the London-based provider of corporate credit data, analytics and AI technology, has secured a €35.73 million ($40 million) strategic growth investment.

The investment round was led by global growth equity firm Summit Partners, with continued participation from existing investor ETFS Capital. The investment follows an €8.93 million ($10 million) Series B led by ETFS Capital in September 2024, and a €7.17 million (£6 million) Series A led by Fitch Ventures in November 2021

“High-quality data at speed and scale is critical to powering AI workflows that credit professionals will increasingly rely on for high-stakes decisions,” said Chris Bon, a Partner at Summit Partners who has joined the Cognitive Credit Board of Directors.

Founded in 2017 by Robert Slater, Cognitive Credit was built by ex-credit analysts who experienced first-hand the limitations of relying on tools designed for equity markets, at a time when no credible alternative existed for the credit space. The company set out to address what it saw as a long-overdue digital transformation in corporate credit markets, one of the world’s largest asset classes with nearly €12.5 trillion ($14 trillion) raised in 2025 alone, according to OECD’s Global Debt Report 2026.

Cognitive Credit’s integrated web application provides support across the credit research workflow, combining verified data, advanced analytics and domain-specialist generative AI capabilities. Its platform is powered by proprietary data developed through the analysis of hundreds of thousands of financial reports to give analysts on-demand access to audit-grade credit models and primary reporting libraries across 3,500+ corporate bond and loan issuers in the US, Europe and emerging markets.

“Cognitive Credit is purpose-built for credit analysis and leverages institutional-grade technology to provide speed, precision, and auditability across thousands of issuers and to support leading banks and asset managers in use cases where accuracy and verifiability are critical. We’re excited to partner with Robert and the team as they further expand their presence and offering and help credit professionals put AI to work with confidence,” added Bon.

Cognitive Credit’s product suite includes a web application, an Excel add-in that streams proprietary financials directly into existing spreadsheets, a REST API for integration into institutional tech stacks, and a Claude Connector that allows analysts to query issuers and surface financial insights directly from within the Claude environment.

The company says all the outputs are fully auditable and traceable to source, a critical differentiator for institutional clients. This emphasis on verified data could be the reason why the company has managed to power analytical workflows for more than 80% of the top 25 global asset managers by AUM and all top 10 global debt league table investment banks. In a statement, Summit Partners says Cognitive Credit has achieved 240% active user growth and more than doubled its global bond and loan issuer coverage.

“Demand for credit-specialist technology will continue to accelerate from here, and we are pleased to partner with Summit Partners on our next phase of growth. With the imminent launch of DealConnect, ongoing innovation in our AI deployments, and many additional capabilities planned for 2027, we’re offering credit teams the highest quality data and analytics they require for differentiated analysis and high impact decision-making,” said Slater, founder and CEO of Cognitive Credit.

With this strategic investment, Cognitive Credit will accelerate its commercial expansion into the US and advance its next generation of products. These include the imminent launch of DealConnect, designed to enable on-demand access to detailed credit models for private issuers that report via secure data rooms, and the pending deployment of agentic credit analysis. The company also plans to continue expanding its issuer coverage into new credit markets.

The post OPINION: Robotics are essential for Europe’s energy transition appeared first on EU-Startups.

]]> Europe’s energy transition story is usually told through assets: more renewable generation, smarter grids, electric vehicles and battery storage. Yet while much of the debate focuses on financing and building infrastructure, a different challenge is emerging beneath the surface: operating and maintaining a rapidly expanding asset base over the next several decades.

But the high-margin subsidised programmes that kick-started the industry are being phased out, and operators are facing a new reality of low-margin operations at scale. Combined with the demographic squeeze on the European workforce, the industry looks ripe for automation. Maybe even for robots.

The problem is well-known and systemic. Transmission networks are aging – some 40% of Europe’s distribution grids are over 40 years old – and cross-border capacity is set to double. Offshore wind is moving further from shore and into deeper water. Solar is multiplying faster than construction and maintenance teams can keep up with.

The jobs required to operate all of this are highly skilled or physically demanding and impossible to scale quickly: rope-access technicians, electrical engineers, subsea specialists, offshore crews. You cannot train a generation of them in a hiring cycle, and Europe’s demographics make the recruitment harder every year.

On the other side sits the newest trend in AI. “Physical AI” – large models and computer vision wrapped around a machine that moves – feeds hope for something close to a science-fiction solution. Capital has followed: foundation models for robotics, task-specific platforms, middleware to run fleets. What was research five years ago is now in early production across several industries, also by European energy operators. Among European energy operators, though, the pilot is still the standard unit of deployment.

Reality moves slower, but the underlying idea – raise output and de-risk demographics at the same time – is understood, and it does not require full autonomy to pay off. For now it is about making the people already on the payroll more productive: engineers delivering higher inspecting output, system designs that remove the need to send a crew into a hostile environment, machines that facilitate maintenance work with little manual additions. These advancements create capacity without waiting years for new workers. The infrastructure can keep scaling even when headcount cannot.

The build is financed but the operating cost is the open question

Europe is entering a period of extraordinary expansion. Solar capacity needs to grow 107% by 2030, wind 84%, electricity demand 60%, and transmission must roughly triple – with nearly €600 billion of grid investment needed between now and the end of the decade. In practical terms that means around 150 million solar panels and 150,000 wind turbines to install and then keep running, alongside an existing asset base that is getting older.

For most of the last two decades this was very lucrative, derisked through subsidised feed-in tariffs over up to 20 years. As feed-in tariffs phase out and CfDs roll in and new builds compete at market prices, operating on thin margins becomes normality.

The hardware got cheap, the margin moved

For years robotics was simply too expensive for this work. That has inverted, though not quite in the way the headlines suggest.

LiDAR is projected to fall from around €4,297 ($5,000) to €1,203 ($1,400) by 2040, actuators have roughly halved, battery packs sit near €92.81/kWh ($108/kWh), and inference at the edge costs cents per hour.

Autonomy has matured alongside it: transformer-based approaches have cut the demonstrations needed to teach a new task from tens of thousands to a few dozen, and most of the training now happens in simulation before anything is flown or driven near a live substation.

None of this favours European hardware manufacturers directly. Chinese robot makers undercut European prices by 20 to 30%, and in some cases by up to 50%. For investors, the profits need to be made on the intelligence. Two software layers decide whether a fleet of cheap sensors and commodity actuators actually becomes useful to an energy operator, rather than an expensive way to generate footage nobody watches.

The first is physical observability: the ability to reliably capture, attribute and continuously refresh real-world asset conditions. A thermal camera, microphone or LiDAR scanner only creates value when the observation can be tied to a specific transformer, switchgear compartment or span, stored in context, and compared against its operating history.

The challenge is therefore not simply collecting more data, but capturing the right signals at the right frequency and linking them to the correct asset. In critical infrastructure, where access is difficult, hazards are high and failure modes are rare, this observability layer becomes the prerequisite for any meaningful intelligence.

The second is spatial interpretation: turning what a camera sees into something an energy operator can act on. A generic vision model can flag discolouration on a turbine blade; a system built for energy assets can place that defect on the span, compare its progression against the rest of the fleet, check it against the threshold that triggers a mandatory inspection, and decide whether it justifies pulling a technician forward or waiting for the next weather window.

That judgement comes from fusing thermal, visual and historical inspection data against a specific asset class, and from having seen enough of those assets to know what normal looks like. Together, they form a loop that gets more valuable with every site added, because the data behind it cannot be bought off a shelf.

Why now is the time to act

Two regulatory dates give this some urgency. The EU Machinery Regulation applies from 20 January 2027, and it treats AI safety components as high-risk, requiring certification through a notified body. The AI Act’s obligations for robots operating in critical infrastructure follow on 2nd August 2028, covering transparency, technical documentation and post-market monitoring. Companies that can show compliance evidence alongside their product will move faster through procurement than those retrofitting it under deadline pressure.

Components will likely keep coming from Asia, and much of the underlying AI research from the US. Both enable value creation within Europe. The layer that captures the profits orchestrates customer needs, European and national regulation, and earns the operator’s trust through tangible results. That is where Europe is genuinely positioned to win, provided founders and investors resist the temptation to compete where the economics do not favour them.

]]> Cygrid, a Berlin-based cybersecurity startup, has exited stealth with a €2.66 million pre-Seed funding round for its identity-enforcement platform that controls access to confidential information. 

The funding round was led by Atlantic, the pan-European pre-Seed fund, with participation from D11Z. Ventures, alongside angel investors including Boris Gorin, VP Product at Zscaler and founder of Canonic Security; Andreas Bermig, CEO of bonify; and Vlad Tropko of AmberVale Capital.

“Dmitry and Dekel are proven builders who combine deep cybersecurity experience with a real understanding of what enterprises need: security that stops the wrong action without slowing the business down. AI agents are widening the identity attack surface faster than any control can keep up. Intelligence-driven enforcement is the only answer that scales. The timing for Cygrid couldn’t be better,” said Marc-Olivier Lücke, General Partner, Atlantic.

Cygrid was founded in January 2026 by Dmitry Kharchenko and Dekel Paz, both of whom served in the Israeli Military Intelligence. The pair identified a security blind spot created by the rapid proliferation of AI agents inside enterprises, and Cygrid solves this by changing how identity and access management works at the enterprise level.

Unlike conventional identity and access management tools, which grant access at sign-in and stop there, Cygrid enforces limits continuously, checking each action an agent takes and blocking or narrowing it in real time. It also maps human, non-human and AI agent identities into a single intelligence graph, correlating what each identity is entitled to, what it actually does, and on whose behalf it acts. The company argues this approach lets it revoke a forgotten token in seconds and stop a risky AI agent command before it executes.

“Access control tells you who can log in. It says nothing about what they do next. Every identity in an enterprise can act, and once a token is valid, not one control in the stack can stop the action. Cygrid is the platform that does: it decides what each identity may do and enforces it before anything executes,” said Kharchenko, CEO and co-founder, Cygrid.

In just nine months after incorporation, Cygrid is already serving 19 design partners across FinTech, e-commerce, and SaaS verticals, with six in production. In one early deployment, a Berlin-based D2C company discovered AI agents and third-party app connections its own security team was unaware of, and used Cygrid to remediate more than 100 risky findings.

The fundraise follows a rise in attacks on trusted identities. According to Palo Alto Networks, machine identities now outnumber human ones by 109 to 1, with 79 of those being AI agents. A CrowdStrike report from 2026 found that 82% of cyber detections involve no malware whatsoever; the attackers simply exploited trusted identities such as leaked tokens or compromised agent providers.

With more than 80% of Fortune 500 companies already deploying AI agents and nearly a third of employees using connected agents without organisational approval, according to Microsoft’s Cyber Pulse report 2026, Cygrid sees an urgent, wide-open opportunity.

The startup will use the fresh capital toward expanding its enforcement capabilities, growing its team, and scaling go-to-market operations across Europe. It aims to become the European alternative to US and Israeli providers of AI identity security.

“This funding allows us to scale that approach and help organisations move from reactive identity security to continuous, real-time enforcement, so they can adopt AI agents at full speed without losing control of what those agents can do,” added Kharchenko.

“Intuitivo was born from a teacherʼs request and continues to be developed together with teachers. Our goal is simple: to give time back to those who teach,” said João Guimarães, co-founder and CEO of Intuitivo.

Founded in 2021 by Guimarães, Duarte Oliveira and Diogo Silva, Intuitive is a digital assessment platform designed to enable educators to create, schedule and grade tests and deliver feedback to students. It covers everything from primary school to higher education.

Teachers on the platform can build assessments from scratch, draw from a shared exercise library, or use AI to convert old PDF tests into fully interactive, auto-graded digital versions. Students, on the other hand, access their tests through a single link, no need for an account or software installation.

The platform also gives teachers real-time monitoring during live assessments, built-in anti-cheating mechanisms, and automatic performance statistics broken down by student, class and exercise. Intuitive is solving a well-documented problem ,with OECD’s TALIS 2024 survey revealing that actual teaching accounts for just 43% of a teacher’s working time, with Portugal ranking first among the 44 countries studied in time spent on assessment and grading.

Intuitivo estimates it helps teachers save around 165,000 hours of working time in the 2025/26 school year alone. The startup counts 75,000 registered teachers among its users and has secured more than 200 contracts with municipalities, school clusters and private schools, covering more than 500 schools across Portugal.

While it frees up teachers from administrative tasks, school leadership also benefits from its centralised dashboard to track results and teacher adoption across an entire institution.

The fresh funding will be used to deepen product development and nearly double its headcount from 11 to 20 employees before the end of this year. The startup also plans to use the funding to expand beyond Portugal and break into Brazil, a market estimated at 2.2 million teachers, roughly twelve times the size of its home market.

“Brazil is the natural step: it speaks our language, has more than 2 million teachers, teachers there adopt digital tools easily, and some already use Intuitivo. We want to take what we have built in Portugal there, on a much bigger scale,” added Guimarães.

]]> The CLARITY Act was designed to set clearer rules for how digital assets are classified and overseen in the US. Its failure in the Senate leaves American investors without that framework for now, and anyone watching the Ethereum price USD chart saw the reaction within hours.

The much-lauded CLARITY Act failed to advance in the US Senate on Tuesday, September 15, in a severe setback for the digital assets and crypto industry. It fell 11 votes short of the 60-vote threshold it needed to move onward in the 100-seat chamber. Primarily put forward by Republican lawmakers, three of them voted against it, joining every Senate Democrat in opposition, and the motion failed. The impact will be felt by anyone who trades digital assets, in the US and abroad.

How did markets respond to the Clarity Act failure?

Markets responded quickly to the news. Binance market data showed Bitcoin dropping 5% after the vote. At the time of writing (September 18), it had rebounded slightly, climbing to $78,180 from a $75,390 low on Tuesday, September 15. Ether stood at $2,515, up from $2,378 the day after the vote. Share prices of several crypto firms also fell, with Coinbase and Circle each down about 10%, according to Cointelegraph.

This will push any further decisions on it until after the mid-term elections, which will take place in November. A key fight to take control of the House and Senate, it could potentially be pushed back until 2029 should Democrats make it a priority and stop it dead in its tracks.

What was the Clarity Act?

The CLARITY Act was an attempt to provide a US federal framework for digital asset markets. For years, there has been confusion over where digital assets lie in the US and who has oversight for them. Primarily, this was the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) and the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC).

Where value is derived from network use and trading, in spot markets, jurisdiction would have been given to the CFTC. The SEC would have had an overview of digital securities in which the value depended on a specific company’s managerial efforts.

How have banks reacted to the Clarity Act news?

The US Banking lobby has already pledged its support to keep fighting for the bill. This is mainly because it still leaves questions around stablecoin yields unanswered. A joint statement from the Independent Community Bankers of America and American Bankers Association noted that “as lawmakers consider next steps, we encourage them to adopt targeted changes to stablecoin yield policy.”

It is likely this will now pivot the conversation to how banks can begin to implement the GENIUS Act. Signed into law in 2025, it has barred stablecoin issuers from offering rewards. Yet it does allow third parties, such as exchanges, to pay yields. The Independent Community Bankers of America has warned that this could drain as much as $1.3 trillion from community bank deposits.

Stablecoin builders outside the US are watching this fight closely: EU-Startups reported in July 2025 that London fintech Due had raised €6.3 million and launched a stablecoin API for borderless payments, the kind of product whose US reach depends on how Washington settles yield.

How did crypto exchanges react?

The major crypto exchanges were keen to point out that by no means does this signal the end for the CLARITY Act. Binance added that “With the November midterm elections approaching, lawmakers have limited time to resolve disagreements and secure the votes needed to move the bill forward. A renewed attempt would still have to navigate Senate procedures and any remaining legislative steps, including resolving differences with the House-passed version before legislation could reach the president.” They then closed this with “The immediate result is a stalled bill, not necessarily a permanently dead one.”

Other crypto companies also released statements on the event. Ripple described this as a “tremendous missed opportunity” in a statement on their website. They went on to add that “Consumers and market participants still deserve predictable standards and protections. Responsible businesses should not have to rely on years of litigation or live under the threat of one to understand how the law applies to them. And the United States should not concede leadership in the future of finance because policymakers were unable to establish a durable framework. Ripple will continue advocating for market structure legislation and engaging constructively with policymakers.”

This will only add to the volatility the crypto market has displayed over the last few months. Rising oil prices and expectations that the Federal Reserve would hike rates, which it did on Wednesday, September 16, have also weighed on sentiment.

Further dampening the mood were comments signaling that investors should not write off the prospect of another rate raise before the year is out. This was the first rate rise in three years, taking them to 3.75%-4%, according to the Federal Reserve’s September 16 statement, as reported by CNBC. After the September 16 decision, Fed Chair Kevin Warsh said that “inflation is too high and has been for too long“, then branded the move a “sober” and “responsible decision“. He then highlighted that inflation remains a problem, showing that more may yet be due to come.

]]> Not all economy seats are created equal. Depending on the airline and aircraft, passengers could have anything from a relatively spacious 34 inches of seat pitch to a more cramped experience.

For long-haul travellers, those few extra inches can make a noticeable difference, especially on overnight flights. To help, we’ve compared economy class seat pitch across major international airlines to find which carriers offer the most legroom.

Japan Airlines and All Nippon Airways top the list of most generous legroom in economy class, with seat pitches reaching 34” (86 cm) on selected aircraft. 

Here’s how the leading carriers compare, and how to identify the roomiest seats before you book.

Also read: 10 tips and seat map tools to avoid the worst seats on a plane Also read: 10 tips and seat map tools to avoid the worst seats on a plane

Seat pitch varies around the world

Economy seat pitch varies widely between airlines and aircraft. The comparison below shows the maximum reported standard economy seat pitch on selected long-haul aircraft operated by 20 major international airlines.

These are main-cabin economy seats, excluding extra-legroom seats which often cost extra.

Which airlines offer 34 inches of economy seat pitch?

Japan Airlines

Japan Airlines (JAL) is a top choice for passengers who want extra space without paying for premium economy.

Its JAL SKY WIDER economy seats, installed on selected international Boeing 787, Boeing 777 and Boeing 767 aircraft, provide more space than more densely configured economy cabins.

The airline has also introduced new economy seating on its Airbus A350-1000 long-haul aircraft.

JAL’s published international economy seat guide distinguishes between aircraft and seat products. Check the aircraft type assigned to your flight.

Passengers can also compare individual configurations using AeroLOPA’s Japan Airlines seat maps.

All Nippon Airways (ANA)

ANA offers up to 34” (86 cm) of economy seat pitch on selected Boeing 787-9 aircraft.

The airline says its redesigned slimline seats provide this spacing while preserving passenger comfort. Their construction also improves knee clearance without requiring additional cabin space.

ANA’s official international economy seat specifications confirm the 34” measurement for its 206-seat Boeing 787-9 configuration.

However, not every ANA aircraft has the same economy cabin. Travellers should check the aircraft configuration and not assume the maximum seat pitch applies to the whole fleet.

Other airlines offering generous economy legroom

Korean Air

Korean Air also offers comparatively generous economy seating on selected long-haul aircraft.

Many of its economy cabins provide about 33” (84 cm) of seat pitch, well above the 30–31 inches commonly found on more densely configured aircraft.

As with other international airlines, dimensions depend on the aircraft type and seating configuration.

Emirates

Emirates is another airline worth considering, particularly for long-haul passengers travelling on its Airbus A380.

Most Emirates economy configurations have 32” (81 cm) seat pitch. The airline operates several aircraft configurations, each with different seating arrangements.

Passengers should check the seat map for the aircraft operating their flight to confirm legroom.

JetBlue

Among US airlines, JetBlue stands out for its spacious economy seating, even on domestic flights. Its standard economy product, branded Core, offers 32” of pitch on many aircraft. 

The airline also sells EvenMore seats with additional legroom, which often costs extra.

Singapore Airlines

Singapore Airlines offers approximately 32” (81 cm) of economy seat pitch on most of its long-haul aircraft and no less than 79 cm.

Like others on our list, Singapore Airlines has different cabin layouts on the same aircraft type. Passengers should check which version operates their flight.

Cathay Pacific

Cathay Pacific is another long-haul airline that offers economy seating with 32” pitch on selected aircraft.

Its Airbus A350 and Boeing 777 aircraft have different cabin configurations, and available space depends on the installed seating product.

Passengers travelling through Hong Kong can compare the aircraft assigned to competing flights before selecting their seats.

Qantas

Qantas offers approximately 31”–32” of economy seat pitch across selected long-haul aircraft, including its Boeing 787-9 Dreamliners and Airbus A380s.

Seat pitch can vary by aircraft and row, so passengers should check the individual seat map when booking.

Does seat pitch really measure legroom? 

Seat pitch measures the distance between a fixed point on one seat and the same point on the seat directly ahead or behind it. While it is a useful metric for comparing cabin configurations, it doesn’t measure the actual clearance available for passengers’ knees. 

Seat design, cushion thickness, recline and the position of the seatback pocket can all affect comfort. Two economy seats with identical pitch may feel different because of their construction.

Slimline seats can provide extra knee clearance by reducing seatback thickness. Conversely, a bulky seatback, entertainment equipment or a poorly positioned literature pocket can reduce usable space.

Seat width also matters, particularly on long flights. An aircraft with 32” pitch and wider seats may feel more comfortable than one with 34” pitch but narrower seating.

Passengers should also consider whether the seat reclines, the position of the armrests and the amount of space beneath the seat ahead.

How to find the economy seats with the most legroom

The best way to find a spacious economy seat is to check the aircraft configuration before booking.

Independent aircraft seating guides provide detailed cabin maps showing seat positions, window alignment, lavatories, galleys and other features. AeroLOPA lets you identify the specific cabin of the aircraft that typically operates your flight with a flight number search, making your booking decision easier. 

Travellers can use these maps, along with the airline’s seat map in the booking platform, to compare cabin products and the onboard passenger experience before booking flights and selecting seats.

Exit-row and bulkhead seats may offer additional legroom, although they can come with restrictions. Some have fixed armrests, reduced storage or limitations on reclining. Passengers should also check whether additional-legroom seats are priced differently, as many airlines sell these as a pricier economy plus product.

Here's why the US, China, India and private companies are investing in lunar exploration.

]]> The Moon has never stopped capturing imaginations, but for decades it seemed largely absent from humanity’s plans. That is changing fast.

Governments are preparing new crewed lunar missions, private companies are building hardware capable of reaching deep space, and a new race is emerging over who will shape the next era of exploration.

NASA is aiming to return astronauts to the lunar surface in 2028, having completed the crewed flyby in 2026. China is planning to land its astronauts on the lunar surface before 2030, and India says it will follow suit around a decade later.

For the first time, private space companies are developing to the point where they can discuss their own missions to the Moon or even Mars.

Here’s why nations and companies are racing back to the Moon

Why they went to the Moon in the first place

Before answering the question of why “everyone wants to go back to the Moon,” it’s useful to answer why they went there in the first place.

In the 1960s, the Cold War, geopolitical competition, and Kennedy’s internal politics were central.

Although the Apollo missions conducted important scientific experiments and returned invaluable lunar samples, public attention focused overwhelmingly on the symbolism of humanity’s first steps on another world.

That said, developing the entire Apollo ecosystem was in itself a major scientific windfall.

In 1957, the USSR’s Sputnik shocked the US. In 1961, the Soviet Union sent Yuri Gagarin into orbit before the United States could launch its first astronaut, securing another major propaganda victory in the Space Race, a feat that remains central to Russia’s national narrative.

Today’s context has substantially changed

Now, there are two credible missions to return to the Moon, and while the world has changed, it continues to bear many striking parallels to the 1960s.

Some actors are familiar, such as the United States and its NASA, while others are gone (the USSR).

Russia inherited the Soviet space programme, but it no longer possesses the resources or momentum that once enabled direct rivalry with NASA and currently has no clear independent pathway to a crewed lunar landing.

Russia’s greatest likely contribution is that of a major junior partner to China’s missions. Europe and Japan have major space programmes, but they contribute to the US-led Artemis mission.

India is perhaps the country worth watching the most after the US and China. Like China, it has powerful motivations to one day send a crewed mission independently to the Moon.

At the same time, there are powerful and capable private companies like SpaceX and Blue Origin that can contemplate their own self-funded or privately funded missions.

The canceled SpaceX dearMoon (Yusaku Maezawa’s privately funded project) lunar flyby and SpaceX’s long-term plans to visit Mars are examples.

All this means that the motivations of each of these countries and major companies should be discussed separately as they have different motives.

Why the US wants to return to the Moon

The US accomplished what it wanted with the Apollo programme; it established that it was the pre-eminent spacefaring nation. The inability of the USSR to challenge that, followed by its collapse, meant its position was secure without another expensive new programme.

But China is now challenging the US for that mantle. If the US does nothing and lets China go to the Moon, then it will always be able to claim it was the first, but the conversation becomes past tense. This could reinforce notions of the US as a country in decline.

Many analysts argue that returning astronauts to the Moon before China would help the US reinforce its position as the world’s leading space power.

It should also be stressed that the US has other motivations that include science and industrial base, but China still looms large.

Japan is enormously important, perhaps the third most important after the US and China. However, it has chosen to support the US effort instead of going it alone.

Unlike in the 1960s, mining and other commercial interests are becoming increasingly important. In 2023, Reuters reported, “NASA is looking to develop resources on the moon that initially include oxygen and water, and eventually may expand to iron and rare earths, and has already taken steps toward excavating moon soil in 2032.”

Japan prepares world-first mission to bring back samples from Mars moon Phobos Japan prepares world-first mission to bring back samples from Mars moon Phobos

Why China and India want to go to the Moon

For many observers, putting astronauts on the Moon would be highly symbolic for China. It fits into broader narratives of national rejuvenation and the country’s ambition to establish itself as a leading technological and geopolitical power.

China plans to put astronauts on the Moon before 2030; delays to the Artemis mission mean the missions are now likely to be very close.

Russia currently appears unlikely to mount an independent crewed lunar programme, making cooperation with China its most realistic route to returning cosmonauts to the Moon.

Working as a junior partner with China allows Russia to claim it remains an important actor in space.

Perhaps the most overlooked major space power is India.

India has said it will put astronauts on the Moon by 2040, making it the third major power with a declared crewed lunar ambition.

India’s motivations differ from China’s but similarly include national prestige, technological development and the desire to demonstrate its emergence as a major global power.

The big two companies: SpaceX and Blue Origin

Private companies, especially US-based ones, change the narrative significantly. These companies are essential to national efforts like Artemis, but they are also forces in their own right.

SpaceX has a goal of long-term expansion of human spaceflight, Elon Musk’s dreams of colonizing Mars, and sees commercial opportunities (e.g., mining, tourism). Blue Origin is similar and is guided by Jeff Bezos’s vision, tourism, and plans for long-term space industrialization.

Other notable companies include Intuitive Machines, Firefly, and Astrolab, although SpaceX and Blue Origin are the two companies with (or developing) the needed hardware.

These companies do not yet have confirmed self-funded programmes to land people on the Moon. However, as the canceled dearMoon mission shows, once SpaceX has its Starship fully operational, it can start chartering lunar flybys within a short time.

]]> Look up at the sky, and you will notice that most commercial aeroplanes are painted predominantly white. Although some airlines use colourful designs, distinctive logos and bold patterns, white remains the most common colour for aircraft around the world.

Why are most airplanes painted white?

It’s not because airlines lack imagination. Instead, there are several practical reasons why airlines choose white paint, ranging from reducing heat absorption to making aircraft easier to inspect and maintain.

Here’s why airlines around the world continue to choose white aircraft over darker or more colourful alternatives.

White paint helps keeps aircraft cooler

One of the main reasons airlines paint their aircraft white is that white surfaces reflect more sunlight than darker colours. This helps reduce the amount of solar energy absorbed by the aircraft, keeping its exterior cooler when parked on the ground or flying in direct sunlight.

Dark colours, such as black and navy blue, absorb more solar radiation and can become significantly hotter. On an aircraft, this additional heat can affect the temperature of the fuselage and the materials used in its construction.

Keeping the aircraft cooler can help reduce thermal stress on certain materials and components, particularly those exposed to prolonged sunlight.

It can also limit the amount of heat transferred into the cabin, potentially reducing the demand on air-conditioning systems while the aircraft is on the ground. Although a white exterior does not eliminate the need for cooling systems, it offers a simple and effective way to manage heat.

Why white aircraft are easier to inspect and maintain

Aircraft safety depends on regular, detailed inspections. Engineers must look for signs of damage, corrosion, fluid leaks and other faults that could affect an aircraft’s airworthiness.

A white exterior provides a useful background against which many types of damage and contamination can be identified. Oil, hydraulic fluid, soot and other dark substances are often easier to spot on a white surface than on a darker one.

Cracks, dents and areas of discolouration may also be more noticeable, depending on their location and the lighting conditions./i

White paint does not make every defect visible, and engineers use specialist inspection techniques to detect problems that cannot be seen with the naked eye. Nevertheless, a light-coloured exterior can make routine visual checks more straightforward.

This is particularly valuable for airlines operating large fleets, where efficient maintenance procedures are essential for keeping aircraft safe and reducing time spent out of service.

Also read: ANA’s new Chiikawa Jet takes off on first passenger flight in Japan Also read: ANA’s new Chiikawa Jet takes off on first passenger flight in Japan

How white paint helps airlines reduce maintenance costs

Aircraft painting is an expensive process. Before an aircraft can be repainted, its existing finish may need to be stripped, the surface prepared, and new layers of primer and paint applied. The work requires specialist facilities, skilled technicians and considerable time.

White is often a practical choice because fading, discolouration and minor cosmetic imperfections can be less conspicuous than they are on certain darker or more elaborate finishes.

Some coloured paints, especially those exposed to intense sunlight, may fade unevenly over time. Maintaining a consistent appearance can therefore require additional attention.

White paint is not necessarily cheaper in every situation, and the overall cost depends on the paint system, design, preparation work and maintenance schedule.

However, a predominantly white livery can simplify repainting and touch-ups, particularly when an airline operates many aircraft with the same basic design. For airlines working to control operating costs, even small savings across a large fleet can be worthwhile.

Why aircraft leasing companies prefer white airplanes

Many airlines do not own every aircraft they operate. Instead, they lease aircraft from specialist companies, allowing them to expand or adjust their fleets without purchasing every aeroplane outright.

A neutral white exterior makes an aircraft easier to transfer between operators. When a lease ends, the aircraft may need to be repainted in the next airline’s colours. A simple base colour can make the transition between liveries more straightforward, depending on the existing paint scheme and the condition of the aircraft.

White also provides a versatile background for different airline logos, colours and designs. This makes it a practical starting point for aircraft that may change operators several times during their working lives.

For lessors and airlines, flexibility can help reduce the complexity and cost of preparing an aircraft for its next role.

Also read: How are aircraft liveries designed, and why are they so important to airlines? Also read: How are aircraft liveries designed, and why are they so important to airlines?

Does white paint make aircraft damage easier to spot?

Bird strikes, lightning strikes and other incidents can leave marks or damage on an aircraft’s exterior. A white surface can make some resulting stains, scorch marks and other visible changes easier to identify.

White paint can also help ground crews notice certain leaks or unusual deposits during routine inspections.

However, visibility depends on the type of damage, its location and the surrounding materials. Some cracks, structural defects and other faults will not be obvious regardless of the aircraft’s colour.

The main advantage is that white provides a relatively consistent, light-coloured surface that can support visual inspection, rather than replacing the specialist checks required for aviation safety.

Why some airlines choose colourful aircraft liveries instead

Despite these advantages, airlines are not required to paint their aircraft white. Many use striking liveries to establish their brand identity and stand out from competitors.

Bright colours, distinctive tail designs and special-edition paint schemes can make an airline more recognisable to passengers. Some aircraft feature extensive coloured areas, while others combine a white fuselage with a colourful tail and logo.

These designs allow airlines to balance practical considerations with marketing and customer recognition. The choice of paint also depends on the airline’s brand, operating conditions, maintenance requirements and budget.

Modern paint technology means that airlines can use a wide range of colours while still meeting the technical and operational requirements of aircraft maintenance.

Why most airlines still choose white aircraft

Airlines paint their aircraft white for several practical reasons. White reflects sunlight, helping limit heat absorption, and can make certain stains, leaks and visible signs of damage easier to identify.

It can also offer maintenance advantages and provide a neutral base for aircraft that may be sold, leased or transferred between operators.

Although colourful liveries remain an important part of airline branding, white offers a useful combination of practicality, flexibility and visual simplicity. What appears to be a straightforward design choice is, in reality, a decision shaped by engineering, maintenance, economics and the everyday demands of commercial aviation.
