]]> Kosmos 2612 and ICEYE-X36: What happens when a satellite gets too close? https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/news/kosmos-2612-and-iceye-x36-what-happens-when-a-satellite-gets-too-close/ Sat, 24 Oct 2026 17:57:00 +0000 https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/?p=54346 Russia's Kosmos 2612 manoeuvred repeatedly near commercial radar satellite ICEYE-X36, prompting fresh concerns about the vulnerability of commercial spacecraft in orbit.

The post Kosmos 2612 and ICEYE-X36: What happens when a satellite gets too close? appeared first on AGN.

]]> A Russian military satellite’s unusually close approach to a commercial spacecraft supporting Ukraine has raised fresh concerns about the vulnerability of satellites to interference or attack in orbit.

Russia’s Kosmos 2612 carried out a series of manoeuvres near ICEYE-X36, a radar imaging satellite operated by Finnish-founded company ICEYE, between 15 and 19 October.

Satellite tracking specialist Marco Langbroek, who monitored the encounter, described it as “a worrisome cat-and-mouse-game”. 

On 17 October, he calculated that the spacecraft were already within one to two kilometres of each other and warned that they could come within a few metres in the following hours.

“That is very worrisome,” Langbroek wrote, describing the rendezvous and proximity operation as “completely non-consensual”. He questioned whether the manoeuvres might signal an anti-satellite attack.

The encounter was also photographed by US spatial intelligence company Vantor, which said an image captured by its WorldView Space system on 17 October showed Kosmos 2612 approximately one kilometre from ICEYE-X36.

Subsequent orbital observations suggested a close approach on 18 October, although the precise separation remains uncertain. There is no confirmed evidence that an attack took place.

A rare view of concerning activity in orbit. From Oct. 16–18, a Russian satellite made several close approaches to a U.S. commercial satellite. This image, collected by Vantor’s WorldView Space capability on Oct. 17, shows Russian Cosmos 2612 at an estimated distance of about 1 km from ICEYE-X36. “This image captures a reality long recognized by our national security leaders—space is becoming increasingly contested. Seeing one spacecraft repeatedly maneuver close to another raises serious concerns about capability and intent.”—Dan Smoot, Vantor CEO. With WorldView Space, Vantor’s non-Earth imaging capability lets us collect images of other spacecraft in orbit, helping us better understand how they’re operating and spot activity that warrants a closer look. Read @axios’s exclusive coverage: https://t.co/oix2OaIEwt Explore WorldView Space: https://t.co/FmXyUumK21

— Vantor (@vantortech) October 22, 2026

The incident highlights a problem confronting satellite operators. A spacecraft may be able to detect another satellite approaching, but that does not mean it can escape or defend itself. Most satellites carry no weapons and have limited fuel for manoeuvring.

So what could a hostile satellite actually do? Could it disable another spacecraft without destroying it? And what protection is available when the threat is already hundreds of kilometres above Earth?

When getting close becomes a threat

Satellites routinely pass near other objects in orbit. Operators track those encounters to assess collision risks and, when necessary, adjust their spacecraft’s trajectory.

But Kosmos 2612’s movements were different from an ordinary close pass.

According to Langbroek, the Russian spacecraft began making a series of orbital adjustments on 30 September, followed by further manoeuvres on 12, 15 and 16 October. These brought its altitude, orbital period and other characteristics increasingly close to those of ICEYE-X36.

The Russian satellite had been launched from Plesetsk in April. Its subsequent movements suggested a deliberate effort to approach the ICEYE spacecraft rather than a chance encounter between two objects travelling through space.

In an updated analysis published on his SatTrackCam blog, Langbroek estimated that the closest approach occurred early on 18 October, possibly within a few hundred metres or less. He cautioned that uncertainties in the available orbital data made a precise calculation difficult.

Also read: Russian satellite activity raises concerns for Starlink Also read: Russian satellite activity raises concerns for Starlink

The encounter was also captured from space. US spatial intelligence company Vantor said its WorldView Space system photographed Kosmos 2612 on 17 October, when the Russian spacecraft was estimated to be about one kilometre from ICEYE-X36.

Space is becoming “increasingly contested” warn experts

The image was collected using Vantor’s non-Earth imaging capability, which allows its satellites to photograph other spacecraft in orbit. Such observations can complement ground-based tracking and help analysts examine unusual orbital activity.

“This image captures a reality long recognized by our national security leaders – space is becoming increasingly contested. Seeing one spacecraft repeatedly maneuver close to another raises serious concerns about capability and intent,” said Vantor CEO Dan Smoot.

LeoLabs, which tracks spacecraft and orbital debris using a network of ground-based radars, later reported that Kosmos 2612 had been drifting away from ICEYE-X36 since 18 October.

However, the company cautioned that the Russian spacecraft could resume its rendezvous and proximity operations, or RPO, and that other recently launched Russian satellites might undertake similar activity.

“Usually these events don’t just end on one,” LeoLabs’ Adam Marsh told The New York Times, according to a statement subsequently shared by the company.

By 21 October, Langbroek reported that Kosmos 2612 had manoeuvred back towards ICEYE-X36’s orbital altitude after initially moving away. The spacecraft were then approximately 480 kilometres apart.

The episode is particularly sensitive because ICEYE’s radar satellites can produce images of the Earth’s surface in darkness and through cloud cover, making their services valuable for monitoring military activity.

But a deliberate approach does not, by itself, prove an intention to attack.

How satellites can be attacked

Anti-satellite weapons, commonly known as ASAT weapons, are designed to damage, disable or destroy spacecraft, or interfere with their ability to perform a mission.

The most direct method is a missile launched from Earth to intercept a satellite. Such weapons have already been demonstrated by several countries. 

China destroyed one of its own weather satellites in 2007. India carried out an anti-satellite missile test in 2019.

In November 2021, Russia destroyed its defunct Kosmos 1408 satellite, creating more than 1,500 pieces of trackable debris, according to US Space Command.

The problem with destroying a satellite is that the fragments do not simply fall harmlessly to Earth. Many remain in orbit, travelling fast enough to damage other spacecraft. A single interception can therefore create hazards for satellites belonging to countries that had nothing to do with the attack.

Also read: What happens when a satellite runs out of fuel? Also read: What happens when a satellite runs out of fuel?

There are also less destructive ways to interfere with spacecraft.

Electronic jamming can disrupt the radio signals used for communications or navigation. Spoofing involves transmitting misleading signals, potentially causing a receiver to calculate an incorrect position or accept false information. Cyberattacks may target ground stations, communications links or spacecraft control systems.

These attacks do not necessarily require another satellite to be nearby. Some can originate from equipment on Earth.

A spacecraft operating in close proximity presents a different kind of risk. Depending on its design and capabilities, it could inspect another satellite, interfere with its operations or potentially cause physical damage through contact.

The difficulty is determining what an approaching spacecraft is equipped to do. A satellite capable of inspecting another vehicle may use some of the same manoeuvring technologies needed for an attack.

That overlap between peaceful servicing and potentially hostile activity makes behaviour and intent difficult to judge.

Can a satellite get out of the way?

A satellite cannot simply turn around and fly in another direction.

Spacecraft travel in carefully calculated orbits, often at several kilometres per second. Changing that path requires propulsion, and the result may not be immediately obvious. 

Depending on the manoeuvre, a satellite may need to move into a slightly higher or lower orbit to alter its speed relative to another object.

Many satellites carry thrusters for routine orbital adjustments and collision avoidance. Others have little or no ability to manoeuvre.

Even those with propulsion have limited fuel. Repeated evasive manoeuvres could shorten a satellite’s useful life, while moving away from one threat might create a new collision risk or interrupt its normal operations.

There is another complication. Collision avoidance normally involves an object whose future path can be predicted with reasonable confidence. 

A satellite deliberately changing course to follow another spacecraft is a different challenge.

The threatened operator must decide whether to move, when to act and whether the approaching spacecraft is likely to respond with another manoeuvre.

ICEYE’s response to the October encounter illustrates the importance of resilience. The company told Aviation Week that it was aware of the situation and monitoring it closely, while emphasising that its constellation was designed to maintain service continuity. It did not disclose the operational status of ICEYE-X36. 

For companies operating large constellations, distributing services across many satellites can reduce the consequences of losing one spacecraft. That does not prevent an attack, but it can make the overall network harder to disable

A growing problem for commercial operators

The Kosmos 2612 encounter also raises a question that extends beyond spacecraft technology: what happens when a privately operated satellite becomes involved in a military confrontation?

Commercial satellites now provide imagery, communications and other services that armed forces depend upon. ICEYE-X36 is particularly significant because of the role radar imagery can play in supporting Ukraine.

In an assessment published on 21 October, US intelligence and surveillance company Integrity ISR argued that the Russian satellite’s manoeuvres demonstrated the ability to approach, remain near and then withdraw from another spacecraft.

But the company also warned against drawing conclusions about intent from orbital movements alone.

The distinction matters. There is no confirmed evidence that Kosmos 2612 damaged ICEYE-X36. Yet the encounter demonstrated how closely one spacecraft can approach another without the targeted operator necessarily having an effective means of stopping it.

Space law offers no straightforward equivalent of the rules governing encounters between military aircraft or ships. The Outer Space Treaty establishes important obligations for states, but it does not prescribe a universal minimum separation distance between satellites.

For operators, the immediate priorities remain better tracking, secure communications, reliable collision avoidance and spacecraft networks that can continue functioning when individual satellites are lost or disrupted.

The latest encounter has shown why those precautions matter. A satellite does not have to be destroyed for its operator to face a serious security problem. 

Sometimes the challenge begins when another spacecraft comes close enough to make its next move impossible to ignore.

]]> Flying in luxury no longer necessarily means booking first class on a major airline or chartering a private jet. A small group of airlines offer aircraft with all-premium cabins, fewer passengers and top-shelf service throughout.

The latest entrant is Magnifica Air, a US start-up planning to introduce its new “Private Class” service in 2027. The airline intends to combine spacious Airbus cabins, private airport facilities and personalised hospitality with flights sold by the seat.

Magnifica joins a market already served by all-business-class airlines such as La Compagnie and beOnd, as well as semi-private operators including JSX and Aero.

The concept has a mixed history. Several all-premium airlines launched in the 2000s but failed to survive. Today’s operators are pursuing different markets, from transatlantic business travel to luxury holidays.

Magnifica Air: A new take on private luxury

Florida-based Magnifica Air plans to operate Airbus A220-300 and ACJ321neo aircraft with approximately 45–54 seats. 

Its proposed cabins include private suites and premium recliners. The A220 will feature two suites, while the larger A321neo will have four. The airline also plans to eliminate overhead luggage bins to create a more spacious interior.

Passengers will use private airport facilities, with dedicated security screening, lounges and transfers to the aircraft. Magnifica aims to let travellers arrive about 30 minutes before departure.

The airline is positioning its “Private Class” product between commercial first class and private charter. It plans to sell individual seats on a luxury jet, instead of requiring travellers to hire an entire aircraft.

Magnifica plans to begin operations in 2027, though its aircraft interiors, regulatory approvals and commercial launch are still works in progress.

La Compagnie: All-business-class flights across the Atlantic

French airline La Compagnie has operated all-business-class transatlantic flights since 2014.

The carrier uses Airbus A321neo aircraft with 76 seats, all of which convert into fully flat beds. Its routes connect Newark with Paris, Milan and seasonal services to Nice.

La Compagnie offers scheduled airline service and uses commercial airport terminals rather than private airport facilities. Its main attraction is an exclusively business-class cabin, often marketed at fares below those of larger international airlines.

The airline has survived for more than a decade in a market where several earlier competitors failed.

Its narrowbody aircraft let it operate transatlantic routes with fewer passengers than a conventional widebody would need to fill.

beOnd: Luxury flights to and from the Maldives

beOnd launched in 2023 with an all-business-class product aimed primarily at luxury leisure travellers.

The Maldives-based airline operates Airbus A319 and A321 aircraft with 44 and 68 seats respectively. Both feature lie-flat seating, premium dining and cabins designed around long-haul comfort.

beOnd serves destinations including Zurich, Munich, Milan and Dubai, connecting affluent travellers with the Maldives.

Unlike La Compagnie, which serves a substantial corporate travel market, beOnd concentrates on passengers travelling to high-end resorts.

Its smaller aircraft and limited capacity support an exclusive passenger experience.

JSX: Semi-private flying in the United States

US operator JSX offers a different interpretation of premium flying.

The company operates public charter flights using regional jets, generally configured with around 30 seats. Passengers book individual seats and use smaller private-terminal FBO facilities instead of larger airport terminals.

JSX advertises check-in as little as 20 minutes before departure. Its onboard product includes comfortable seating, complimentary refreshments and a more personal service than passengers typically encounter on short domestic flights.

The operator offers more convenience than luxury. For travellers flying shorter routes, avoiding crowded terminals and lengthy airport procedures can be as valuable as the onboard experience.

JSX is not a conventional scheduled all-business-class airline. It operates as a public charter, unlike operators like La Compagnie and beOnd.

Aero: Private aviation without chartering the whole aircraft

Aero offers luxury flights sold by the seat aboard smaller aircraft with premium interiors.

The company targets affluent leisure travellers flying to selected resort and holiday destinations, particularly in the western United States.

Its service includes private-terminal arrangements, limited passenger numbers and personalised onboard hospitality.

Aero also offers private charter services, but its shared flights let customers buy individual seats.

The product is closer to private aviation than conventional airline business class, although passengers still share the aircraft with other travellers.

The all-business-class airlines that didn’t survive

All-premium airlines have a difficult history, particularly on transatlantic routes.

In the mid-2000s, Eos Airlines, MAXjet and Silverjet launched services designed to compete with the business-class cabins of established international carriers.

Eos operated spacious Boeing 757 cabins between London and New York. MAXjet pursued a lower-cost business-class model, while Silverjet offered premium flights linking London with New York and Dubai.

All three ceased operations between 2007 and 2008, affected by rising fuel prices, financial pressures and competition from larger airlines.

Other ventures also disappeared or changed direction.

French all-business-class carrier L’Avion was acquired by British Airways and incorporated into OpenSkies, which subsequently adopted a mixed-cabin model.

British Airways itself operated an all-business-class Airbus A318 service between London City and New York until 2020.

While smaller, premium-only cabins appealed to a select group of travellers, these operators struggled with the economics of operating limited fleets and route networks.

Can today’s all-premium airlines succeed?

The current generation of premium operators has adopted different business models.

La Compagnie competes for transatlantic business travellers. beOnd targets luxury holidaymakers. JSX and Aero concentrate on convenience, smaller airports and private-aviation-style service.

Magnifica Air intends to combine premium commercial airline cabins with private airport facilities, positioning itself between these existing models.

All face the same basic financial challenge. Aircraft with fewer seats must generate sufficient revenue per passenger to cover operating costs.

They also compete with established airlines investing heavily in private business-class suites, improved lounges and premium onboard services.

For passengers willing to pay more for comfort, privacy and convenience, options exist beyond commercial airline business and first class. One downside is that these carriers serve fewer routes than their larger commercial counterparts.

While few details were disclosed, the carrier did specify that the campaign is aimed at replacing its ageing fleet of Boeing 777-200ERs.

Replacing an ageing Boeing 777-200ER fleet

American Airlines currently has 47 Boeing 777-200ERs in its fleet, and are among the oldest aircraft types it owns. With an average age of just under 26 years, they far exceed its other widebody types including the 777-300ERs (13 years) or its even younger 787s.

Revenue up across all markets, though transatlantic lags behind

American Airlines saw improved yield and revenue performance across all markets, particularly the US & Canada and Latin America.

Despite a decrease in capacity of -0.3%, American Airlines still managed a nearly 21% increase in revenue in its Latin America market.

Its largest capacity increases were in the Pacific, a market the company seems bullish about. It hopes to revitalise its Los Angeles hub with a somewhat newfound purpose as its Pacific gateway.

]]> Replacement Red Arrows: What aircraft could supplant the iconic Hawk T1? https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/news/raf-hawk-trainer-replacement-contenders/ Sat, 24 Oct 2026 08:42:00 +0000 https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/?p=53954 Several aircraft are competing to replace the Red Arrows' Hawk T1 display aircraft, with the Boeing-Saab T-7 Red Hawk among the leading contenders.

The post Replacement Red Arrows: What aircraft could supplant the iconic Hawk T1? appeared first on AGN.

]]> In May 2026, hopes of a British-designed successor to the RAF‘s Hawk fleet faded when aerospace start-up Aeralis collapsed.

With no domestic contender remaining, the replacement for the RAF’s Hawk T1 and Hawk T2 aircraft is now likely to be based on an overseas design.

The Hawk has been one of Britain’s most successful military aircraft programmes and export successes.

However, with the Hawk T1 due to retire from RAF service around 2030 and the wider Hawk fleet approaching the end of its operational life, a replacement will need to be selected in the near future.

The programme to find a Hawk replacement

In 2026, the UK Ministry of Defence issued a request for information to replace its Hawk aircraft. It requires a new trainer for its Red Arrows to serve as an aerobatic aircraft and a replacement for its 28 (now 27) Hawk T2 trainers.

The MoD is likely to select a common platform for the two aircraft variants, so whichever design wins the T1 competition will likely also be the one winning the T2 competition.

The MoD has said the aircraft should be “designed to support the transition to fifth- and sixth-generation air systems, ensuring UK pilots are equipped with the skills needed for modern and future combat environments.”

Prospective contractors were to place their submissions by the 11 September. A key requirement was for Britain to have a significant workshare.

BAE-Boeing-Saab T-7 Red Hawk

BAE Systems has announced a partnership with Boeing to offer the T-7 Red Hawk (designed for the US Air Force) to the Royal Air Force. This is widely viewed asthe most likely option for the Hawk T1 and T2 replacement.

BAE stated in July, “The agreement marks a significant milestone in the partnership between the three companies and commits to a new UK-based final assembly and integration facility.”

The T7 is undergoing flight testing, is set to enter serial production, and is soon to enter service with the US Air Force. The type would be a comparatively low-risk option and an aircraft that has been designed for future improvements.

BAE CEO ​Charles Woodburn said, “Our offer represents a modern, integrated training solution which aligns with the ambition of the Defence Investment Plan, while ​strengthening the UK’s sovereign industrial capability.”

Italy’s Leonardo M-346 Master

The Leonardo M-346 Master is a popular and capable trainer that has the benefit of being a mature aircraft and would help the UK build on its close relationship with Italy.

The Master is regarded as one of the leading alternatives to the T-7.

The Italian Air Force selected the M-346 for its national aerobatic team, the Frecce Tricolori, in 2024. These will replace the team’s existing fleet of ten Aermacchi MB-339s. The team will receive the first in 2027 and transition in 2028.

Overall, the Leonardo M-346 offers lower development risk as the T-7 is not yet mature. It is also already in service with the air forces of Italy, Israel, Poland, Singapore, Qatar, and Greece.

The contracting British party is Babcock.

Also read: Hawk turns 50 – best-selling jet trainer ‘from the cockpit’ Also read: Hawk turns 50 – best-selling jet trainer ‘from the cockpit’

Other, less likely, options

The other two bidding aircraft are the Lockheed Martin KAI TF-50 and the Turkish Aerospace Hürjet. These are generally considered by industry experts as being less likely to win, especially the Hürjet.

Lockheed and South Korea’s KAI are offering a version of the popular T-50 Golden Eagle family. The aircraft first entered service in 2005, and variants have since been exported to Poland, Indonesia, Iraq, the Philippines, and Thailand.

Like the M-348, the Golden Eagle is also a mature design offering low risk. Notably, since 2010, South Korea’s Black Eagles aerobatic display team has also used the T-50B Golden Eagle as its display aircraft.

Turkey is also offering the Hürjet single-engine advanced trainer, which it is delivering as an advanced trainer, aerobatic display aircraft, and for light-combat missions.

Its unclear if the jet would realistically be ready within the RAF’s 2030 timeframe.

In 2025, Spain approved a budget of around $3.6 billion to purchase up to 45 upcoming Hürjet jets, showing there is some solid export interest in the jet.

However, this is in the context of deeper Spanish and Turkish military-industrial cooperation.

While the outcome of the competition remains uncertain, the RAF’s requirement is likely to be shaped by a combination of training capability, programme risk, industrial participation and value for money. W

ith Hawk retirement approaching in the next decade, the eventual winner will not only become the RAF’s next advanced jet trainer but could also take on one of British aviation’s most visible roles as the aircraft of the Red Arrows.

Meanwhile, easyJet is taking a family-friendly approach, offering eligible parents a £66.50 contribution towards their baby’s first passport when booking their next easyJet holiday.

JetBlue and Virgin Voyages introduce adults-only travel

Dubbed “Do Not Disturb”, the new package from JetBlue Vacations and Virgin Voyages has been designed exclusively for travellers aged 18 and over.

The four-day package combines child-free round-trip JetBlue flights with a Virgin Voyages cruise and includes VIP experiences and optional add-ons throughout the holiday.

The package costs US$2,750 for two travellers and includes flights from New York’s JFK Airport to Fort Lauderdale-Hollywood International Airport in Florida, as well as the cruise.

Jamie Perry, President of Paisly, which powers JetBlue Vacations, said the collaboration was designed to deliver an adults-only experience from start to finish.

“From the flight to the transfer to the cruise itself, we’ve thought about the entire journey so our customers can simply show up, settle in and enjoy some uninterrupted time away.”

In 2023, Corendon Dutch Airlines introduced an “only adults” zone for passengers aged 16 and over on selected Amsterdam-Curaçao flights.

In 2013, AirAsia X introduced a designated quiet section with age restrictions (passengers aged 12 and above) on selected A330 long-haul services. easyJet’s offer to help cover babies’ first passport costs

Family travel is on the rise

According to easyJet, around 585,000 families welcome a new baby each year in England and Wales, and infants travelling this year have increased by 10% compared to 2025, with 22,000 more infants flying across its network in 2026.

City break bookings have seen a notable boost among young families, the carrier said.

The airline’s initiative to cover passport fees addresses practical and financial hurdles parents face when planning their first trip with a baby.

easyJet’s research shows that while almost 4 in 5 parents surveyed (82%) described their baby’s first holiday as a landmark moment, over a third (36%) identified the first passport photo as one of the biggest challenges to getting there.

“Travel has a unique way of bringing families together,” said Stuart Wright, Customer Director at easyJet holidays.

]]> Artemis II crew faced cabin leak scare minutes before crucial Moon burn https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/news/artemis-ii-cabin-leak-scare/ Fri, 23 Oct 2026 15:29:00 +0000 https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/?p=54373 Artemis II pilot Victor Glover reveals how a false cabin leak warning nearly disrupted NASA’s historic Moon mission before its record-breaking journey.

The post Artemis II crew faced cabin leak scare minutes before crucial Moon burn appeared first on AGN.

]]>

NASA’s Artemis II astronauts received a suspected cabin leak warning just 15 minutes before a critical engine firing that would send them towards the Moon, raising the possibility that their historic mission could be cut short before it had even left Earth’s vicinity.

The incident, which occurred on 2 April this year, was disclosed by Artemis II pilot Victor Glover during a discussion with former astronaut Chris Hadfield at the Starmus VIII festival in Tenerife on 18 October.

The warning came as the Orion spacecraft approached the lowest point of its elongated orbit around Earth, preparing for the manoeuvre that would commit its four astronauts to a journey around the Moon.

“If it had happened five minutes later, we may not have been able to have that burn,” Glover told the audience, according to Space.com.

The crew and mission controllers had to establish whether the warning indicated a genuine loss of cabin pressure. A real leak could have forced the astronauts to abandon their lunar journey, put on their spacesuits and prepare for an early return to Earth.

The warning was eventually determined to be false, allowing Orion to complete its engine firing and begin a journey that would carry humans further from Earth than ever before.

A warning at the worst possible moment

Artemis II had launched on 1 April aboard NASA’s Space Launch System rocket, carrying commander Reid Wiseman, pilot Glover, mission specialist Christina Koch and Canadian Space Agency astronaut Jeremy Hansen.

Rather than heading directly for the Moon, Orion first entered a highly elliptical orbit around Earth. The trajectory gave the astronauts and flight controllers time to check the spacecraft’s life-support systems, communications and handling before committing to deep space.

By 2 April, Orion had travelled roughly 38,000 miles from Earth and was returning towards the planet for its planned translunar injection burn.

The manoeuvre was timed to take place near the spacecraft’s closest approach to Earth, at an altitude of about 100 miles. 

At that point, Orion was travelling rapidly, making it an efficient place to fire the engine and gain the additional speed needed for the lunar journey.

Glover recalled Hansen looking through the window as Earth grew closer beneath them.

“I think we’re going to run smack dab into the middle of Earth,” Hansen remarked, according to Glover’s account reported by Space.com.

The crew also had to contend with an environment containing more orbital debris and satellites as Orion descended towards its lowest altitude.

Then came the cabin leak alert.

Determining whether the warning was genuine became an immediate priority. The astronauts could not ignore a possible loss of cabin pressure, but delaying the engine firing could also mean missing the planned opportunity to head towards the Moon.

NASA flight director Judd Frieling subsequently confirmed during an April briefing that the alert had been a false alarm.

A record-breaking journey beyond the Moon

The successful burn began a mission that would take the four astronauts farther from Earth than any previous human crew, surpassing the record established by Apollo 13 in 1970.

As Aerospace Global News reported following Orion’s safe return, the spacecraft reached a maximum distance of 252,756 miles from Earth, exceeding Apollo 13’s record by more than 4,000 miles.

During the lunar flyby on 6 April, Orion passed approximately 4,067 miles above the Moon’s surface. The astronauts photographed the lunar landscape and carried out observations intended to support future exploration.

Over the nearly 10-day mission, Orion travelled more than 694,000 miles, completing life-support checks, spacecraft handling exercises and scientific investigations.

The mission also marked the first time humans had travelled beyond low Earth orbit since the Apollo programme ended in 1972.

Artemis II was not designed to land on the Moon. Its primary purpose was to demonstrate that Orion and its supporting systems could safely carry astronauts into deep space and bring them home.

A major contribution came from the European Space Agency’s European Service Module, built under ESA leadership and largely assembled by Airbus Defence and Space in Bremen. It supplied propulsion, electrical power, air, water and thermal control during the flight.

The module performed with sufficient precision that two planned trajectory correction burns were no longer needed, according to ESA officials.

Orion’s return clears the way for future missions

Artemis II concluded on 10 April when Orion splashed down in the Pacific Ocean off San Diego, completing NASA’s first crewed lunar mission in more than half a century.

The spacecraft endured temperatures of approximately 5,000°F during atmospheric re-entry, followed by a planned communications blackout lasting just over six minutes. Its parachutes then deployed successfully, bringing the crew safely to the ocean.

The cabin leak warning, now described publicly by Glover, offers a reminder of how easily the mission’s outcome might have changed.

Artemis II went on to break the record for the greatest distance travelled from Earth by humans before returning safely on 10 April. 

The incident also showed why NASA had taken the precaution of checking Orion’s critical systems in Earth orbit before sending four astronauts on their journey around the Moon.

]]> Airport fees still outweigh fuel costs for Eurowings despite Middle East crisis https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/news/eurowings-airport-airline-fees-fuel-costs-middle-east-crisis/ Fri, 23 Oct 2026 14:02:29 +0000 https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/?p=54349 Rising fuel prices may dominate aviation headlines, but Eurowings says airport fees, taxes and charges remain an even bigger obstacle to keeping flights affordable and maintaining winter routes.

The post Airport fees still outweigh fuel costs for Eurowings despite Middle East crisis appeared first on AGN.

]]> Airport fees and charges remain a bigger cost burden for Eurowings than fuel, even as the Middle East crisis drives up Jet A-1 prices and disrupts supply, the German airline has said.

Speaking at Routes World 2026 in Frankfurt, Tobias Bracht, head of network and airport relations at the low-cost carrier, said airport charges and government-imposed fees comprised a large slice of the airline’s cost base and therefore were key factors in determining which routes airlines could sustain through a winter season.

Fees and charges outweigh fuel costs

Since the outbreak of war between the US and Iran in the spring of this year, the price of jet fuel surged and the focus has been on how airlines and their balance sheets will weather the storm. 

But while the fuel price is undoubtedly a concern for carriers, Bracht highlighted how fees and charges remained a significant burden – one that surpassed fuel even in the current high-cost environment. 

“We are all talking about … fuel, but even in today’s really high cost fuel environment, the fees and charges part is still significantly larger than fuel costs,” he said. 

That is particularly relevant for Eurowings, since the cost burden for carriers operating in Germany is higher than in other European countries.

Winter flying brings its own cost challenges

Looking ahead to the winter schedule, which begins on Sunday, these fees often continue to be levied even when demand drops off and revenue falls.

Bracht added that airlines were increasingly focused on whether winter flights could cover their variable costs, such as taxes, fuel and variable salaries for crew, rather than whether they could generate a positive earnings contribution once all the fixed costs were included.

“We have already incorporated and accepted that the flight itself will not make a positive EBIT from itself, but we rather see it as a marginal contribution towards the total year result, so that the summer doesn’t have to carry the total cost burden of winter.”

Bracht said roughly two thirds of his airline’s total costs were variable, with fees and charges accounting for about half of that portion.

In Germany, he said, government charges and airport costs each accounted for approximately half of the fees-and-charges category.

However, it is fuel that has attracted more of the attention, with the US-Iran conflict continuing to create uncertainty for airlines over energy prices, supply and operations. 

Airport fees and taxes remain a more substantial cost consideration for airlines such as Eurowings, even under the current fuel-market conditions – not least since fuel prices can fluctuate with global market conditions, while airport fees, passenger taxes and other government charges are often fixed, even during periods when demand and revenue are weaker.

Seasonal flexibility could support winter flying

Speaking to delegates at the event, the head of network urged governments and airports to look at the cost structure and consider lowering fees for off-season flights when demand and revenue is much lower. 

Bracht said the ability to reduce costs during the winter was complicated by the different approaches taken by governments and airports.

“Where it gets really, really tough is, of course, on the government side, where governments might take a more holistic approach and don’t care as much about seasonality.”

Many airports served by Eurowings continue to apply broadly uniform fees and charges throughout the year, regardless of the seasonal differences in airline demand.

Some airports, however, have begun to introduce greater flexibility, charging airlines more during the busier summer season while reducing charges during winter.

“This is a step towards bringing more flights in the winter,” he said.

.sie-field-hero{position: relative; 
 left: 50%;
 right: 50%;
 margin-left: -50vw;
 margin-right: -50vw;
 width: 100vw; 
 min-height: 480px;
 max-height: 560px;
 background-size: cover;
 background-position: center 40%;
 background-repeat: no-repeat; 
 background-color: #003B73;
 overflow: hidden;
 margin-bottom: 0;}
.sie-field-hero--no-image{background: linear-gradient(
 135deg,
 var(--field-color, #003B73) 0%,
 color-mix(in srgb, var(--field-color, #003B73) 65%, #000) 100%
 );}
.sie-field-hero__bg-img{position: absolute;
 inset: 0;
 width: 100%;
 height: 100%;
 object-fit: cover;
 object-position: center 40%;
 z-index: 0;
 display: block;}
.sie-field-hero__overlay{position: absolute;
 inset: 0;
 z-index: 1;
 background: linear-gradient(
 to top,
 rgba(0, 20, 50, 0.90) 0%,
 rgba(0, 20, 50, 0.60) 38%,
 rgba(0, 20, 50, 0.25) 65%,
 rgba(0, 20, 50, 0.12) 100%
 );
 display: flex;
 align-items: flex-end;
 padding-bottom: 52px;}
.sie-field-hero__inner{width: 100%;
 max-width: 1100px;
 margin: 0 auto;
 padding: 0 32px;}
.sie-field-hero__label{display: block;

 font-weight: 500;
 color: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.75);
 margin-bottom: 12px;
 letter-spacing: 0.03em;}
.sie-field-hero__label a{color: inherit;
 text-decoration: none;}
.sie-field-hero__label a:hover{color: #fff;
 text-decoration: underline;}

 margin-bottom: 14px;

 letter-spacing: 0.03em;}
.sie-field-category-badge i{font-size: 11px;

.sie-field-hero__title{font-size: clamp(30px, 5vw, 54px);

<span><span>sandoel</span></span>
<span><time datetime="2021-12-07T08:55:30+01:00" title="Tuesday, December 7, 2021 - 08:55">Tue, 12/07/2021 - 08:55</time>

<div class="ecl"><h2><strong>What is the Conference?</strong></h2>

<p>The <strong>Conference on the Future of Europe </strong>is the first transnational discussion with Europeans on how to address Europe’s challenges together. This is an opportunity to think about what citizens and&nbsp; civil society want for the European Union.</p>

<p>&nbsp;</p>
</div>

  <div class="eac-body lc-stripe-wrapper-text"><h2><strong>How does the Conference work?</strong></h2>

<p>Europeans can share ideas via the <a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/?locale=en" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">Multilingual Digital Platform</a>, and both national and&nbsp;<a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/assemblies/citizens-panels" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">European Citizens' Panels</a>. These contributions feed into the&nbsp;<a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/pages/plenary" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">Conference Plenaries</a>.</p>

<p>The Conference&nbsp;offers a new public forum for an open, inclusive, and transparent debate with citizens around a number of key priorities and challenges.</p>

<h2><strong>How can you participate?</strong></h2>

<ul>
	<li><!--[if !supportLists]--><!--[endif]--><a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/processes?locale=en&amp;pk_source=pdf_document&amp;pk_medium=link&amp;pk_campaign=europarl" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">share your own ideas or support others’ ideas</a> on the multilingual digital Conference platform</li>
	<li><!--[if !supportLists]--><!--[endif]-->organise your own events and promote it by adding them to the <a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/?locale=en&amp;pk_source=pdf_document&amp;pk_medium=link&amp;pk_campaign=europarl" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">Conference platform</a></li>
	<li><!--[if !supportLists]--><!--[endif]-->take a look at the <a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/meetings" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">events organised by people across the EU</a></li>
</ul>

<h2><strong>What will the outcome be?</strong></h2>

<p>All of the ideas gathered and reports on events are published on the platform openly and transparently. These reports will then directly influence the discussions in the European Citizens’ Panels as well as in the Plenaries, where citizens will enter into a dialogue with national and European decision makers.</p>

<p>By spring 2022, the Conference will provide guidance on the future of Europe to the European institutions</p>

<p><a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/pages/getinvolved" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">Get involved and make your voice heard when it comes to education, culture, youth, sport, and more</a>.</p>

<p>Follow on Twitter at&nbsp;</p>

<ul>

                        <div class="eche-officer-question">Your institution has a strategy and an overarching structure supporting internationalisation</div>
                        <div class="eche-report-button-js eche-report-detail-close"><i class="fa fa-plus-circle fa-3x"></i></div>

                <div class="eche-officer-question-wrapper eche-report-question-wrapper-show">

                    <div classs="eche-officer-must">
                                                <h3>Must have</h3>
                                                <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">The internationalisation strategy is available and prominently displayed on your website</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>Internationalisation is an important driver for institutional change, and has a great influence on the major activities of a higher education institution (HEI) i.e. education and research. The importance of internationalisation is recognised, and most institutions have a strategy for internationalisation. However, for a strategy to be efficient, and for it to drive the HEI's activities regarding internationalisation, there is a need for its acceptance from across the whole institution. In addition the strategy could also be accessible to external collaborative partners. It is highly important to have the institution's internationalisation and modernisation strategy published and easily accessible to all.</p>                      </div>
                    <div class="eche-officer-best">
                                                <h3>Best practices</h3>
                                                <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">It promotes incoming and outgoing student and staff mobility</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>Mobility is important to the development of the institution as a whole as well as for the individual participants. Therefore the HEI should make mobility and international cooperation a central element in its institutional policies, and explicitly and consistently promote and support student and staff mobility. Non-discrimination policies and further emphasis on the promotion of mobility for under-represented groups should also form an integral part of the institutional support structures.</p>                         <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">It promotes engagement in European and international cooperation projects</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>The institution's internationalisation strategy and policy should explicitly and consistently promote the development of cooperation with partners in other EU and non-EU countries. The activities and co-operation projects agreed by the HEI should be based on identified needs. In addition they should identify geographical and subject priorities of the internationalisation strategy.</p>                         <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">Specific support measures are provided to staff working at all levels of the institution with outgoing and incoming participants. For example:  allocation of additional resources, training on intercultural competences and other relevant aspects of the mob</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>The institution should allocate additional resources to support staff working at all levels of the institution with outgoing and incoming participants, such as allowing staff adequate time to carry out work with outgoing and incoming participants and providing administrative back-up (e.g. with financial management). Trainings/webinars/projects could be organised on intercultural competences and communication, management of mobility projects’, enhancement of internationalisation at home/intercultural, or other activities suggested by the staff and supported by the hierarchy. As part of the institutional modernisation and internationalisation strategy, concrete support measures should be defined at both institutional and departmental levels.</p>                         <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">Incentives are provided to staff involved in international activities</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>Participation in such international projects should be seen as an important aspect of the professional development of the staff and of the modernisation of the HEI. It should, therefore, be considered a key component in staff evaluation. As part of the institutional modernisation and internationalisation strategy, concrete support measures should be defined at both institutional and departmental levels to encourage and recognise staff participating in such projects, as well as allow adequate time to carry out this work.</p>                      </div>

                        <div class="eche-officer-question">Your institution has established a framework of Inter-Institutional Agreements for Erasmus+ mobility</div>
                        <div class="eche-report-button-js eche-report-detail-close"><i class="fa fa-plus-circle fa-3x"></i></div>

                    <div classs="eche-officer-must">
                                                <h3>Must have</h3>
                                                <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">They are based on areas of mutual interest</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>It is vital that Inter-Institutional Agreements are based on areas of mutual interest. These agreements should identify shared quality requirements specific to the planned exchanges, including concrete proposals as to how these activities will contribute to the development of learning and teaching in participating institutions. The involvement of academic staff is key to ensuring that the selection of partners is based on sufficient knowledge of the area. Each HEI should decide who is responsible for initiating, signing and implementing these agreements and the list of responsible persons should be available on the website for contact and consultation purposes.</p>                         <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">They are based on the compatibility of study programmes</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>Inter-Institutional Agreements should be based on a comprehensive understanding of the partner HEIs, the compatibility of study programmes, quality levels and standards considered adequate for student and staff mobility activities. For example, selected partners should have learning, teaching and assessment procedures that can be accepted by the sending institution without requiring mobile students to do any additional work or take examinations upon returning from the receiving institution. The compatibility of the programmes should be reflected in the learning outcomes to be achieved.</p>                      </div>
                    <div class="eche-officer-best">
                                                <h3>Best practices</h3>
                                                <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">They are based on shared quality requirements, student and staff selection for mobility and clear timelines at all stages of the mobility</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>A key role of Inter-Institutional Agreements is to set out agreed, shared quality criteria and clear timelines for all stages of the mobility.<br>Shared quality criteria may include, but are not limited to: selection criteria for the nomination of students and staff, recommended language skills, grading systems, measures for preparing, receiving and integrating Erasmus+ participants. These might be expanded with geographic and subject-specific criteria.<br>In terms of the timelines set out for the mobility activities, particular attention should be paid to:</p><ul><li>The nomination of mobile students by the sending HEI,</li><li>The acceptance of nominees, and</li><li>The issuing of the Transcript of Records after the study period abroad by the receiving HEI. This is normally issued within five weeks after the end date of the mobility period.</li></ul>                      </div>

                        <div class="eche-officer-question">Your institution expresses its commitment to equal access and opportunities to mobile participants</div>
                        <div class="eche-report-button-js eche-report-detail-close"><i class="fa fa-plus-circle fa-3x"></i></div>
                    </div>
                </div>
                <div class="eche-officer-question-wrapper eche-report-question-wrapper-show">
                    <div class="eche-report-border"></div>
                    <div classs="eche-officer-must">
                                                <h3>Must have</h3>
                                                <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">There are specific provisions e.g. in the general policies, rules and regulations of the institution</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>In signing the Erasmus Charter for Higher Education, the institution agrees to respect <strong>in full</strong> the principles of non-discrimination as set out in the Programme. The institution must clearly demonstrate through its policies, rules and regulations that equal access and opportunities to mobile participants from all backgrounds. Which means that all individuals or groups will be treated equally, irrespective of their characteristics. In accordance with Article 21 of the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union, there should be no discrimination "based on sex, race, colour, ethnic or social origin, genetic features, language, religion or belief, political or any other opinion, membership of a national minority, property, birth, disability, age or sexual orientation". For more information, see: <a href="http://www.europarl.europa.eu/charter/pdf/text_en.pdf">http://www.europarl.europa.eu/charter/pdf/text_en.pdf</a></p>                      </div>
                    <div class="eche-officer-best">
                                                <h3>Best practices</h3>
                                                <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">The principle - that extra fees are not being charged to incoming mobile students - is implemented</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>The receiving institution must <strong>not </strong>charge any type of fees to incoming mobility students for the tuition, registration or examination of these students or for their access to laboratory, library and other facilities offered to local students.<br>In certain cases, however, mobile students may be required to pay small fees for insurance, student unions, use of miscellaneous materials (e.g. photocopies, laboratory products) on the same basis as these are charged to local students. Students should be made aware of these extra costs before the start of mobility. Fees may only be charged in the case of full degree mobility or for students registered in joint degree programmes.&nbsp;</p>                         <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">All students and staff (incoming and outgoing) are treated equally in all academic and service matters</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>In accordance with equal access and opportunities, all students and staff should be treated equally in all academic and service matters. Clear appeal procedures should be in place to ensure equal treatment. There should be individuals - such as mentors and counsellors - available to offer support.</p>                         <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">It provides incoming mobile participants with access to the same services and facilities available to local students and staff</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>It is vital to ensure that incoming mobility participants have full access to the same services and facilities as local students and staff. For example, mobility participants with special needs can benefit from the support services that the receiving institution offers to its local students and staff.</p>                      </div>

                                                <h3>Must have</h3>
                                                <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">That is up-to-date, ECTS based and available on the institution's website</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>It is important for each HEI to produce an online Course Catalogue, which includes detailed, user-friendly and up-to-date information on the institution’s educational offer and learning environment to enable students to make the right choices and use their time most efficiently, before and during their study period. The Course Catalogue should follow the guidelines set out in the ECTS Users' Guide (http://ec.europa.eu/education/ects/users-guide/index.htm) to increase comparability and transparency. It should be published on the institution's website sufficiently in advance i.e. to enable prospective mobile students to make their choices.</p><p>It should include general information on the institution, its resources and services, as well as academic information on its programmes and individual educational components. The ECTS Users' Guide recommends using the following common structure:</p><ul><li>General information</li><li>Resources and services</li><li>Information on study programmes</li><li>Information on single course units</li></ul><p>The Course Catalogue should also include the names of people to contact, with information about how, when and where to contact them.&nbsp;</p>                         <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">That is updated regularly and sufficiently in advance for prospective mobile students to make their choices</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>The Course Catalogue should be updated regularly and sufficiently in advance for prospective mobile students to make their choices. Ideally, the edition of the Course Catalogue for the upcoming academic year should be available by the early spring of the preceding academic year.</p>                      </div>

                                                <h3>Best practices</h3>
                                                <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">That is up-to-date, ECTS based and available on the institution's website</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>It is important for each HEI to produce an online Course Catalogue, which includes detailed, user-friendly and up-to-date information on the institution’s educational offer and learning environment to enable students to make the right choices and use their time most efficiently, before and during their study period.                         <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>The Course Catalogue should be updated regularly and sufficiently in advance for prospective mobile students to make their choices.                         <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>The purpose of the Learning Agreement is to provide a transparent and efficient preparation of the study period abroad and to ensure that the student will receive recognition in his/her degree for the educational components or traineeship successfully completed abroad. The Learning Agreement:</p><ul><li>Sets out the learning outcomes for the mobility, including both the educational components or traineeship activities to be carried out by the student at the receiving institution/organisation/enterprise, which will be recognised by the sending institution upon successful completion of the study programme abroad and counted towards his/her degree.</li><li>Ensures full recognition for satisfactorily completed activities of study mobility and traineeships in terms of credits awarded, without the need for the student to take any further courses or exams, and documents these credits in the student records, so that they can be identified in a transparent way.</li></ul><p>The Learning Agreement is binding for all parties and constitutes the cornerstone of successful student mobility (for studies, traineeships, and combinations thereof), including quality assurances and the process for transparent transfer of credits. It is not compulsory to circulate papers with original signatures; scanned copies of signatures or digital signatures may be accepted, depending on the national legislation.</p><p>The EU official templates for Learning Agreements for studies and traineeships are available online: <a href="http://ec.europa.eu/education/opportunities/higher-education/quality-framework_en.htm">http://ec.europa.eu/education/opportunities/higher-education/quality-framework_en.htm&nbsp;&nbsp;</a></p>                         <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">Including allocation of responsibility to an academic who has the authority to approve, amend and recognise the Learning Agreements on behalf of the responsible academic body</span>
